text: |x| is almost always taught as “make it positive,” and that description survives exactly as long as the numbers stay simple. The honest definition is geometric: |x| is the DISTANCE from x to 0 on the number line. Distance has no direction, which is why it is never negative — not because a sign was deleted.

So two numbers can share a distance while disagreeing about everything else. |−6| = |6| = 6, but −6 ≠ 6. Absolute value throws away the side and keeps the size; the number itself is unharmed by being measured.

Feed every input to |x| and plot the results. Inputs on the right rise along y = x. Inputs on the left are negative, but their DISTANCES are positive, so the left half rises too — mirror-imaging the right. Two rising branches meeting at the origin: a V.

The corner is the signature. A line has one constant slope; the V has two — it falls at slope −1 until the origin, then climbs at slope +1. The switch happens exactly where the inside of the bars changes sign, and that is the vertex.

y = |x − 2| − 3 is still the same V, standing somewhere else. The −2 INSIDE the bars moves it horizontally; the −3 outside moves it vertically. The vertex is wherever the inside of the bars equals 0 — that is the one input the shift is built around.

A minus in FRONT flips instead of shifts. y = −|x| takes every height and negates it, turning the V upside down into a peak — the vertex becomes the highest point rather than the lowest. Inside the bars: horizontal. Outside: vertical. In front: reflection.

|x| = 5 asks which numbers sit five units from zero. Phrased that way the answer is obvious — there are two, one per side. Phrased as “remove the bars,” only one shows up. The distance reading is what keeps the second solution from disappearing.

The method generalizes by treating whatever sits inside the bars as one object. |x − 1| = 4 says the QUANTITY x − 1 is four units from zero, so x − 1 = 4 or x − 1 = −4. Solve both, and you get both answers.

The pair is the usual case, not the only one. |x| = k has two solutions when k > 0, exactly one when k = 0 (zero is its own mirror), and NONE when k < 0 — because no point on the line sits a negative distance from anywhere.

So the count is decided by the number on the right, before any case-splitting begins. Positive right side: a pair. Zero: a single solution where the inside vanishes. Negative right side: nothing. Reading the right-hand side first saves the whole procedure.

|x| < 3 asks which points are CLOSER than three units to zero — a band around the origin, from −3 to 3. |x| > 3 asks the opposite: points farther out than three units, which is everything beyond −3 on the left and beyond 3 on the right. One band, or two rays.

So the direction of the sign decides the SHAPE of the answer, not just its edges. Less-than gives one sandwich, written with a single chain. Greater-than gives two separate rays, joined by ‘or’ — and it cannot be written as a chain, because no number is on both rays at once.

Some rules change formula partway along. A phone plan charges one rate up to 5 GB and another beyond it; that is one function with two formulas, each labelled with the inputs it governs. The labels are what keep it a function: every input is handed to exactly one formula.

So evaluating happens in two moves, and the order matters: first find which condition the input satisfies, THEN apply that branch's formula. Reaching for the nearest formula and checking the condition afterwards is what produces most piecewise errors.

Graphing a piecewise rule means drawing each formula only over the inputs it governs, then deciding what happens where the branches meet. At the boundary exactly one branch owns the point — the one whose condition includes it — and the graph marks that with a filled dot and the other with an open one.

The open circle is not decoration — it records that the branch approaches a height it never attains. When the two branches meet at the same height the dots coincide and the graph is continuous; when they do not, the graph jumps, and the size of that jump is visible on the page.

Some real rules are piecewise with many pieces, all of them flat. Postage charges by the ounce, parking by the hour, tax by the bracket. Between the jumps the price does not move at all; at each jump it leaps. Graphed, these rules look like a staircase.

Flat between jumps has a consequence worth naming: within one step the price carries no information about the exact input. Learning a letter cost $3 tells you the weight was more than 2 oz and at most 3 oz — a range, never a number. Steps trade precision for simplicity, on purpose.
When two groups come together, count every object in both groups to find how many there are in all.
Nothing is left out and nothing is counted twice — every object gets exactly one number.
Your fingers are always with you. Hold up one group on one hand and the other group on the other hand.
Then count every raised finger, starting from one, to find the total.
A drawing keeps a group still so you can count it carefully.
Draw the first group, then draw the second group beside it, then count everything you drew.
A sum can be acted out: start with a group of children, then let more children join them.
The group grows as each child joins, so the total is larger than the group you started with.
A number sentence records what happened. The plus sign means groups came together.
The equals sign says both sides name the same amount: 3 + 2 and 5 are the same number.
Taking away removes objects from a group. What is left is always less than what you started with.
Count what remains, not what was removed — those are two different numbers.
To show taking away in a drawing, cross out the objects that leave.
The crossed-out marks stay on the page as a record, but only the plain ones are still in the group.
A take-away can be acted out too: children stop playing and go home, one at a time.
Each child leaving makes the playing group one smaller.
The minus sign records taking away, just as the plus sign records joining.
The first number is what you started with, and the second is what left.
Whatever the story, the question "how many are left?" always asks about what remains.
Start at the number you had and count back once for each object that goes.
An add-to story starts with a group and puts more into it.
The starting amount and the amount added are both known, so the total is what is missing.
A take-from story starts with a group and removes part of it.
The start and the amount removed are known, so what remains is the missing number.
A put-together story has two parts that were never apart — they simply make up one whole.
Nothing is added or removed; the two parts are counted together to name the whole.
Before you can solve a story, decide what happened: did the group grow, or did it shrink?
Growing means adding. Shrinking means subtracting. The words of the story tell you which.
A drawing of a story must show two things: how many there were, and what happened to them.
A drawing that shows only the start, or only the change, does not tell the whole story.
Some sums are worth knowing by heart, so you do not have to count them every time.
The sums that make 5 or less come back quickly with practice.
Differences within 5 are worth knowing by heart too.
Each one is the partner of a sum you already know: if 2 and 3 make 5, then 5 take away 3 leaves 2.
Adding one moves to the very next counting number. Taking one away moves back to the number before.
These two facts work for every number, so they never need counting out.
Zero means none. Adding zero puts nothing in, and taking zero away removes nothing.
Either way the group is untouched, so the number stays exactly the same.
Now the sums and differences within 5 come back together, mixed up and out of order.
Mixing them removes the rhythm of a single page, so each fact must be recalled on its own.
A **double** is the same number twice, like a mirror. 6 + 6 = 12.
Doubles land on **even** numbers: 10, 12, 14, 16, 18, 20. Learn them and they're instant.
Neighbors like 7 + 8 are **near doubles**: double 7 is 14, one more is 15.
Near doubles land on **odd** numbers: 11, 13, 15, 17 — one past an even double.
You own four tools: doubles, near doubles, make ten, count on. Pick the fastest for each fact.
Speed comes from choosing, not rushing. See the fact, name the tool, answer.
Adding tens is like adding ones. 3 tens + 4 tens = 7 tens, so 30 + 40 = 70.
The ones digit stays 0 when you add whole tens — only the tens digit changes.
Ones join the ones. 34 + 5: the 5 joins the 4, making 39. The 3 tens don't change.
Add ones to the ones digit — never to the tens digit. 71 + 8 changes only the 1.
Add tens with tens, ones with ones. 34 + 52: tens 3+5=8, ones 4+2=6, so 86.
Split, add, join: 61 + 27 is 60+20 and 1+7 — that's 80 and 8, so 88.
37 + 25: the ones make 12 — too many! Trade ten ones for a rod: 6 tens 2 ones, 62.
The traded rod joins the tens. Never drop it, never keep the ten loose ones.
Subtracting tens is like subtracting ones. 7 tens − 3 tens = 4 tens, so 70 − 30 = 40.
The ones digit stays 0 when whole tens leave — only the tens digit shrinks.
Ones leave the ones. 58 − 5: the 5 leaves the 8, making 53. The 5 tens hold still.
Take ones from the ones digit — never from the tens digit. 65 − 4 changes only the 5.
Take tens from tens, ones from ones. 86 − 52: tens 8−5=3, ones 6−2=4, so 34.
Split, take, join: 95 − 63 is 90−60 and 5−3 — that's 30 and 2, so 32.
62 − 37: only 2 ones, but 7 must leave. Break a rod: 5 tens 12 ones. Now 12−7 and 5−3: 25.
Two traps: flipping to 7−2, and breaking but keeping 6 tens. The broken rod is spent!
Some stories take **two steps**. 18 birds land, 24 more come, then 15 fly off: 18 + 24 − 15 = 27.
The order matters: do the **first thing that happens** first. A word like *then* or *after* points to step two.
Two-step stories often need a trade. 52 stickers, give away 27 (that's 25), then get 13 back: 25 + 13 = 38.
A story can also **add** into a trade. 46 + 17: ones 6 + 7 make 13, so trade a ten → 63.
The hard part is **choosing** the steps. Gained, found, more → add. Gave, lost, used → subtract. Then do them in order.
Beware the keyword trap: *more* does not always mean add. "How many **more** does Sam have?" is a compare — that's a subtraction.
Line a number up in **pairs**. If none is left over, it's **even** (like 8). If one is left alone, it's **odd** (like 7).
Shortcut: check the **last digit**. Ends in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 → even. Ends in 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 → odd.
Two evens always make an even: 4 + 6 = 10. Both pair up cleanly, so their total does too. **even + even = even.**
**odd + even = odd.** One leftover has no partner: 4 + 7 = 11. And doubles are always even — they pair perfectly.
Hundreds add just like ones: 3 hundreds and 2 hundreds make 5 hundreds. The place holds, only the count grows.
When both numbers are whole hundreds, the tens and ones stay zero — a one-column addition wearing a big number's clothes.
When every column's digits fit under ten, add place by place: ones with ones, tens with tens, hundreds with hundreds.
Three little additions side by side make one big one — that is all column addition is when nothing trades.
When the ones column passes nine, ten of those ones bundle into one new ten — the trade moves value left without changing it.
Write the bundled ten above the tens column and add it there. The total is identical before and after the trade.
Tens overflow the same way: ten tens bundle into one hundred and move into the hundreds column.
The rule repeats at every place — ten of a unit make one of the next size up.
Some sums trade twice: ones bundle into a ten, and then the tens — counting that new ten — bundle into a hundred.
Work right to left and each carry arrives just in time for the next column's addition.
Subtraction also works place by place. When every top digit is big enough, each column subtracts on its own.
Ones from ones, tens from tens, hundreds from hundreds — three small take-aways make the big one.
When the ones run short, break one ten open: it becomes ten ones, and the tens column has one fewer ten.
Breaking is trading downward — same value, smaller pieces, so the ones can pay their bill.
When the tens run short, break a hundred: it becomes ten tens, and the hundreds column has one fewer.
The downward trade repeats at every place, just like the upward one did.
A zero in the tens means the ones cannot borrow next door — first break a hundred into tens, THEN break one of those tens into ones.
Two downward trades in a row: the value flows hundreds → tens → ones until every column can pay.
Ten more or ten less touches only the tens digit. See the number, slide that one digit, and you are done — no columns needed.
457 → 467 → 477: the ones and hundreds stand still while the tens count the journey.
A hundred more or less slides only the hundreds digit — an even bigger jump that is even easier to see.
348 → 448 → 548: the tens and ones ride along unchanged.
An open number line turns addition into jumps: big friendly jumps of hundreds and tens, landing where the answer lives.
467 + 30 is three ten-jumps: 477, 487, 497. The line keeps your running total visible.
Trading works because ten of one unit and one of the next are the same amount: 14 tens IS 1 hundred and 4 tens.
A number does not care what form its blocks take — 2 hundreds, 14 tens, 3 ones and 343 are one quantity in two outfits.
A strategy is explained by naming its moves and WHY each is allowed: what traded, where the value went, why the total held.
The words 'because they are equal' are the heart of every correct explanation of trading.
A story hands you the numbers and the action: joining means add, remaining means subtract. Write the equation, then solve it.
The trail log, the summit, the seed jars — every story hides one equation waiting to be written.
You now own several methods: mental slides, open-line jumps, and careful columns with trades. The numbers tell you which to reach for.
Friendly numbers invite mental math; messy trades invite paper. Choosing well is itself a skill.
Adding three-digit numbers is three small additions stacked in a column: ones with ones, tens with tens, hundreds with hundreds.
When no column runs past nine, nothing has to move — each place settles on its own and the sum falls out.
When a column passes nine, it cannot hold the result: ten ones bundle into one ten and move left. That move is the carry.
A carry is packaging, not magic — the amount never changes, only which column holds it. Strand the carry and the total drops by exactly that bundle.
Subtracting three-digit numbers runs the same columns backward: ones from ones, tens from tens, hundreds from hundreds.
While every top digit is big enough, no trading is needed — each column simply gives what it owes.
When a top digit cannot pay, do not flip the subtraction — trade. One ten from the left becomes ten ones, and the column can finally pay.
Flipping to take the small digit from the large one is the most common subtraction bug there is. It gives an answer that no trading could ever produce.
Across two zeros the trade cannot happen in one step: the ones need a ten, but the tens column is empty and must borrow a hundred first.
The borrow passes THROUGH the zero. One hundred becomes ten tens; one of those tens becomes ten ones; and the zero column ends up holding nine.
An open number line trades the column for a journey: start at one number and jump — hundreds first, then tens, then ones.
The jumps can be any size, so choose big ones. Two hundred-jumps beat twenty ten-jumps, and both beat counting by ones.
Compensation borrows from the future: round an awkward number to a friendly one, add the easy way, then give back exactly what you borrowed.
298 + 145 becomes 300 + 145 = 445, and since 298 was handed 2 extra, the total returns them: 443. Borrow 2, repay 2.
Addition and subtraction undo each other, so every subtraction carries its own proof: add the answer back to what you took away.
If 632 − 178 = 454, then 454 + 178 must rebuild 632. Agreement is evidence; disagreement points straight at the slip.
Stories hide the operation inside words: spending takes away, raising adds, and a two-step story does both before it is finished.
Read for the action, not the numbers. Once you know which way each step moves, the arithmetic is the part you already own.
Every method here reaches the same answer, so the real question is which costs least: the column algorithm, the open line, or compensation.
Numbers just under a friendly hundred beg for compensation. Long borrow chains across zeros are the algorithm at its slowest. Choosing well is part of fluency.
Adding is **counting on**. For 4 + 3, start at 4. Hop: 5, 6, 7. You land on **7**.
Each hop is **one more**. Three hops means three more. So counting on is just adding, one step at a time.
Small adds are fast. **+1** is the next number. **+2** is two hops. **+3** is three hops.
Adding **0** changes nothing. 5 + 0 is still 5. Zero hops means you stay right where you are.
3 + 8? Flip it! Start at the **bigger** number, 8. Count on 3: 9, 10, 11. Fewer hops!
Same numbers, either order, **same answer**. 4 + 7 = 7 + 4. So start big and hop less.
Two numbers that fill a ten-frame are **partners of ten**. 6 and 4 are partners: 6 + 4 = 10.
Learn the partner pairs by heart: 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6, 5+5. They make adding fast.
To add 8 + 5, **split** the 5. Give 8 what it needs to make ten — that's 2. Then 3 is left.
Now add the leftover to ten. 10 and 3 more is **13**. So 8 + 5 = 13!
Make ten to add any sum. Remember 8 + 5: fill to ten, add what's left. Now try new numbers.
Always fill the **bigger** number to ten. Fewer dots to move, fewer mistakes.
A teen is ten and ones. 8 + 5 makes 10 + 3 = 13: one ten, 3 ones.
Making ten works for every teen sum. Fill to ten, add the rest, read the teen.
**Subtract** means take away. Start with 7, take away 3, and **4** are left. Write it 7 − 3 = 4.
Taking away makes the number **smaller**. The more you take, the fewer are left.
To subtract, **count back**. For 7 − 3, start at 7 and hop back: 6, 5, 4. Land on **4**.
Don't count the start number! For 9 − 3, hop starts at 8, not 9. Three hops: 8, 7, 6.
Subtraction also finds the **difference** — how many more. 8 is 3 more than 5, so 8 − 5 = 3.
Count up from the smaller to the bigger. The hops you take is the **difference**.
Every subtraction hides an addition. 13 − 5 = 8 because 8 + 5 = 13. Use adds you know!
To subtract, think: what **adds** to make it? 15 − 6 = 9 because 9 + 6 = 15.
Three numbers make a **fact family**. 8, 5, and 13 give four facts: 8+5=13, 5+8=13, 13−5=8, 13−8=5.
Flip the adds, split the total. The same three numbers, four ways.
The **equal sign** = means 'same as', like a balanced scale. 6 + 4 = 10 — both sides are 10.
= does NOT mean 'the answer is next'. It means both sides are the **same amount**.
An **unknown** is a missing number. In 6 + ? = 10, the ? is 4, because 6 + 4 = 10.
Use a fact family to find the unknown. For ? − 4 = 5, think 5 + 4 = 9, so ? = 9.
A story that **joins** groups means add. 7 birds sit. 5 more come. 7 + 5 = 12 birds.
A story that **takes away** means subtract. 12 birds. 4 fly off. 12 − 4 = 8 birds.
Two parts make a **whole**. 6 red and 7 blue marbles: 6 + 7 = 13 marbles in all.
Know the whole and one part? **Subtract** to find the other part. 13 − 6 = 7.
To compare, **subtract**. 9 apples and 5 oranges: 9 − 5 = 4 more apples.
'How many more' means find the **difference** — subtract the smaller from the bigger.
Three groups can join into one total. Add two of them first, then join the third — the answer is the same however you start.
Adding three numbers is really two additions in a row. Finish the first pair before bringing in the third addend.
When two of the three addends make ten, group those two first. Ten plus the leftover is easy to name.
Scanning for a ten-partner pair before adding is faster than working strictly left to right.
When two addends are equal, start with the double you already know, then join the third addend.
Doubles are instant facts. Anchoring on one turns a three-addend problem into a single easy step.
Three addends can be grouped in any order. Whichever pair you join first, the total is the same.
This is why choosing a smart pair is safe: regrouping changes how hard the work is, never the answer.
Since any grouping works, choose deliberately: a ten-partner pair if one exists, otherwise a double, otherwise simply left to right.
Reading the three addends before starting is what separates fast adding from slow counting.
A story with three collections becomes a three-addend equation. Every collection mentioned belongs in the total.
Write the equation first, then choose the easiest grouping to finish it.
Given three addends, decide for yourself which two to join first — and be able to say why that pair was the best choice.
The best pair is the one that lands on a friendly number: ten if possible, otherwise a known double.
Three addends often total more than ten. Making the ten first turns the answer into ten-and-some, which is easy to name.
Passing ten is not a problem to avoid — the ten is the stepping stone that makes the total readable.
Sometimes the total is known and one addend is hidden. Build what you can, then find the gap up to the total.
The gap between the part already made and the total is exactly the missing addend.
You now have three tools for three addends: make a ten, use a double, or just add in order. Read the numbers, pick a tool, and say why.
A strategy is valid when it protects the total. All three tools do — they differ only in how much work they save.
Adding a one-digit number to a two-digit number works the same way as adding small numbers: start at the bigger number and count on.
Counting on is fast for small amounts — count on 1, 2, or 3 rather than starting over from one.
Sometimes adding the ones makes a full ten. When that happens, ten ones bundle into one new ten.
Splitting an addend so part of it completes a ten first makes the rest of the addition easier.
Adding a multiple of ten changes only the tens digit. The ones digit stays exactly the same.
Because only whole tens are being added, the ones never have to be touched or recounted.
When both numbers being added are whole tens, add the tens digits and keep the ones at zero.
Two tens plus three tens is five tens — the same relationship as 2 + 3 = 5, just scaled by ten.
Ten more or ten less than a number can be found without counting: just change the tens digit by one.
This is fast enough to do in your head, because only one digit ever moves.
On a hundred chart, moving down one row adds ten, and moving right one square adds one.
The chart makes the tens-digit-only change from adding ten visible as a simple downward move.
A number line shows addition as a hop forward: start at the first number and hop the size of the second.
The landing point after the hop is the sum — the number line makes the count-on strategy visible.
Any addend can be broken into two smaller parts. Splitting one addend so a piece completes a ten first often makes the whole sum easier.
Breaking a number apart does not change its value — the two smaller parts still add to the same total.
Subtracting a multiple of ten changes only the tens digit, the same way adding one does — just in the other direction.
Because the ones digit is untouched, subtracting ten is as fast as adding ten.
On the hundred chart, moving up one row subtracts ten — the mirror of moving down to add ten.
The chart makes the ten-at-a-time subtraction visible as an upward move, one row at a time.
A strategy is not just a shortcut — it works because it respects what addition and subtraction actually mean. Explaining why keeps that connection visible.
If a strategy always gives the same answer as counting one at a time would, it is a valid strategy, not just a guess.
A story gives two known groups and asks for the whole. Read carefully to find both parts before adding.
The words describe the situation, but the numbers and the relationship between them are what you compute.
A take-away story gives a starting total and how many left, and asks what remains.
The starting number and the amount removed are both known, so what remains is found by subtracting.
Different problems fit different strategies best. Counting on suits small amounts; making ten suits sums that cross a ten; adding tens suits round numbers.
Choosing a strategy is a decision, not a guess — the numbers in the problem hint at which method fits best.

Any triangle sits inside a rectangle sharing its base and height — and it always covers exactly **half** that rectangle. So a triangle's area is **1/2 × base × height**: base 6, height 4 gives 1/2 × 6 × 4 = **12**. The rectangle would be 24; the triangle is exactly half of it.

**Height** always means the PERPENDICULAR distance from the base to the opposite vertex — a straight up-and-down measurement, never a slanted side. A tall, tilted triangle can have a short height if its apex leans far to one side; height is about the drop, not the slant.

A **parallelogram** slices a triangle off one side and reattaches it to the other, forming a rectangle of the SAME base and height — no halving needed. Area = **base × height**: base 6, height 4 gives 6 × 4 = **24**. Unlike a triangle, a parallelogram is already the full rectangle in disguise.

A **trapezoid** has two parallel bases of DIFFERENT lengths. Split it diagonally into two triangles — one using the long base (b1), one the short base (b2), both sharing the height. Adding those triangle areas gives the formula: **1/2 × (b1 + b2) × height**. Average the two bases, then apply the triangle rule.

Same base, same height, three different answers — the SHAPE decides the rule. Base 9, height 4: a **triangle** gives 1/2 × 9 × 4 = 18; a **parallelogram** gives 9 × 4 = 36 (exactly double the triangle); a **trapezoid** needs a second base too. Identify the shape FIRST, then pick its formula.

A trapezoid needs one more piece of information than the others: a SECOND base. Given base 9, second base 5, height 4: 1/2 × (9 + 5) × 4 = **28** — between the triangle's 18 and the parallelogram's 36, which makes sense since a trapezoid is a blend of the two.

An L-shaped figure isn't a single rectangle — but it splits into two. Cut it with one straight line and you get a bottom rectangle and a top rectangle; **add their areas** for the total. A 10-by-8 L with a 4-by-3 corner missing splits into a 10×5 rectangle (50) plus a 6×3 rectangle (18): total **68**.

There's a second, equally valid path: picture the L-shape's **bounding box** — the full rectangle it would be without the missing corner — then **subtract the cut-out** piece. The 10-by-8 example: bounding box 10×8 = 80, minus the 4×3 cut = 12, giving 80 − 12 = 68. Same answer, different route — a genuine check on your work.

A house-shaped figure is a rectangle topped with a triangular roof — two DIFFERENT shape rules, added together. Walls 8 wide, 5 tall: rectangle area 8 × 5 = 40. Roof: base 8, height 3, so 1/2 × 8 × 3 = 12. Total house area: 40 + 12 = **52**. Identify each piece's shape before computing its area.

Not every composite figure ADDS its pieces — some SUBTRACT a piece that's been cut away. A rectangle with a triangular notch removed (like a corner sliced off) LOSES that triangle's area: 10×6 rectangle (60) minus a base-4-height-3 triangle notch (6) leaves **54**. Look for whether a shape is attached (add) or removed (subtract).

Real floor plans often need THREE or more pieces: a main room, an extension, maybe a nook. The rule scales up perfectly — identify every piece's shape, compute each area, then combine with add or subtract as each piece demands. A main room (12×8=96) plus an extension (4×5=20) plus a triangular reading nook (1/2×4×3=6) totals **122**.

The ORDER you add pieces never changes the total — 96 + 20 + 6 gives the same result as 20 + 6 + 96. Group however makes the arithmetic easiest, especially when a subtraction is mixed in: compute every piece first, THEN combine with the correct signs (+ for attached, − for removed).

When a side is perfectly horizontal or vertical, its length comes straight from the coordinates: **subtract the coordinate that changes, and take the distance (never negative)**. From (3, 2) to (8, 2), the y stays at 2 but x goes from 3 to 8 — length 8 − 3 = **5**. The unchanging coordinate tells you the side is horizontal (same y) or vertical (same x).

The same rule works for **vertical** sides, just swap which coordinate you're reading: the x stays the same, and you subtract the y's. It also works with **negative coordinates** — the distance is still the difference, taken as a positive number: from (2, −4) to (2, 3), length = 3 − (−4) = **7**.

Once you can find side lengths from coordinates, area follows the same rules from earlier chapters. A rectangle with corners (2,2), (6,2), (6,4), (2,4): width = 6−2 = 4, height = 4−2 = 2, area = 4 × 2 = **8**. Find the sides first, THEN apply the shape's area formula.

The right angle at a shared corner is what makes this easy: when two sides of a triangle are horizontal and vertical, they're the triangle's **legs**, and you already know how to find their lengths from coordinates. Read the legs first, then apply 1/2 × leg1 × leg2 exactly as before.

Everything from this chapter combines: read side lengths from coordinates, identify each shape, and — if the figure is composite — add or subtract pieces exactly as in Chapter 2. A rectangle (1,1)-(6,1)-(6,4)-(1,4) plus an attached triangle gives one combined coordinate-based composite area.

Combine exactly as before: since the triangle is ATTACHED to the rectangle (not cut from it), **add** the two areas. 15 + 4.5 = **19.5** total. The coordinate reading and the combine-the-pieces skill from Chapter 2 work together on any figure, however it's described.

Unfold a box flat and you get its **net** — six connected rectangles. **Surface area** is the total area of all six faces. A 4×3×2 box has three PAIRS of matching faces: two 4×3 (top/bottom), two 4×2 (front/back), two 3×2 (sides). Sum: 24 + 16 + 12 = **52** square units.

The shortcut formula packages the three pairs: **SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)**. For 4×3×2: 2(12 + 8 + 6) = 2 × 26 = 52 — identical to adding all six faces. The two most common slips: counting each pair only once (getting half), or computing l×w×h (that's VOLUME, a different thing entirely).

A **triangular prism** (like a tent or a Toblerone box) has 5 faces: **2 triangle bases** at the ends, plus **3 rectangles** wrapping around. Each face keeps its OWN formula from Chapter 1 — triangles halve, rectangles don't. Compute all five, then add.

Total surface area = 2 triangle ends + 3 rectangles. For the (3,4,5)×6 prism: 12 + 72 = **84**. Verify by listing all five faces individually — 6, 6, 18, 24, 30 — which also sums to 84. Two routes, same answer, exactly like the L-shapes in Chapter 2.

Surface area answers real questions: **how much wrapping paper covers a gift, how much paint coats a room, how much cardboard makes a box.** The key reading skill: does the problem cover ALL faces (a wrapped gift) or only SOME (painting walls but not the floor)? Count exactly the faces the situation includes.

Volume and surface area answer DIFFERENT questions: volume is what fits **inside** (cubic units); surface area is what covers the **outside** (square units). "How much water fills the tank" is volume; "how much paint coats the tank" is surface area. The units are the tell: cubic for inside, square for outside.

**Volume** counts the unit cubes that fill a box: a 2×3 base holds 6 cubes per layer, and 4 layers stack to 24 cubes — which is exactly **V = length × width × height** = 2×3×4 = 24 cubic units. The formula is layer-counting, compressed.

Volume and surface area part ways here for good: volume is **cubic units** (what fits inside); surface area is **square units** (what covers outside). One box, two numbers: the 4×3×6 box holds 72 cubic units inside and wears 108 square units of surface. Keep the units straight and you'll never mix them.

The formula V = l × w × h keeps working when an edge is a **fraction** — you just pack with SMALLER cubes. A box 3 × 2 × 3/2 fits half-unit cubes: 6 × 4 × 3 = 72 of them, each with volume 1/8, totaling 72/8 = **9** — exactly what 3 × 2 × 3/2 gives directly. Fractions don't break the formula; they refine the cubes.

For a **mixed number** edge like 3½, convert to an improper fraction first: 3½ = 7/2. Then V = 7/2 × 2 × 4 = **28**. The most common slip is quietly dropping the fraction and computing 3 × 2 × 4 = 24 — always convert the mixed number before multiplying.

Volume questions hide in everyday objects: **how much water an aquarium holds, how much soil fills a planter, how many boxes fit in a moving van.** Read the three dimensions (converting any mixed numbers), multiply, and label the answer in cubic units. The whole course's toolkit comes together here.

"How many smaller boxes fit inside" is volume DIVISION: total space ÷ space per box. A van with 48 cubic units of cargo space fits 48 ÷ 2 = **24** boxes of 2 cubic units each — as long as the shapes stack cleanly. Divide volumes to count containers.
Pair the counters into twos. If every counter finds a partner, the number is even; one left standing alone makes it odd.
Pairing is a test you can SEE — the leftover, or its absence, is the whole answer.
You do not need counters forever: the ONES digit carries the verdict. 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 end even numbers; 1, 3, 5, 7, 9 end odd ones.
The tens pair up automatically — every ten is five pairs — so only the ones digit can leave a leftover.
A double like 7 + 7 pairs every counter with its twin across the groups — so a double can never leave a leftover.
Doubles are the even numbers wearing their construction on their sleeve: two equal groups, zero leftovers.
Every even number can be written as a double: split it into two equal groups and name the sum, like 14 = 7 + 7.
Finding the double is un-doubling — asking which number, taken twice, rebuilds the total.
An array lines counters into ROWS (across) and COLUMNS (up and down). Every counter sits in exactly one row and one column.
The grid is not decoration — rows and columns are two honest ways to slice the same total.
To count an array by rows, take one row's number and add it again for every row: 3 rows of 4 is 4, then 8, then 12.
The running total climbs by the same step each time — that steady step IS the row size.
The SAME array counts by columns too: 3 rows of 4 is also 4 columns of 3 — the totals must agree because the counters never moved.
Two counting paths, one answer. When they disagree, a counting mistake happened, not a mathematical one.
The repeated sum is the array written as arithmetic: 3 rows of 4 becomes 4 + 4 + 4. The addend is the row size; the number of addends is the row count.
Reading it back works too — see 5 + 5 + 5 and picture 3 rows of 5 before computing a thing.
Twelve counters make a 2-by-6 array, a 3-by-4, a 6-by-2 — the shape changes freely while the count stands still.
That freedom is useful: choose the slicing that makes the adding easiest, since every honest slicing agrees.
Egg cartons, garden beds, window panes — the world stacks things in rows and columns, and your row-by-row sum totals every one of them.
Spot the array, name the rows and row size, write the repeated sum, and stage the addition. Four moves, any array.

(a + b)² is not a² + b². Squaring a sum means multiplying the whole sum by itself, and the cross terms that appear are the entire content of this course. Drawn as a rectangle, (a + b)² is one a-square, one b-square, and TWO identical strips — and the strips are what the wrong version throws away.

Push the exponent up and the pattern keeps going. (a + b)³ has four terms, not two; (a + b)⁴ has five. In general (a + b)ⁿ expands into n + 1 terms, whose a-powers count down from n while the b-powers count up — and whose coefficients are what the rest of this chapter is about.

Stack the coefficient rows and a triangle appears. Row 0 is a lone 1; row 1 is 1 1; row 2 is 1 2 1; row 3 is 1 3 3 1. Every interior entry is the sum of the two directly above it, and every row begins and ends with 1. The rows are numbered from ZERO, which is the single most common place to slip.

Two facts make the triangle worth trusting. Every row is symmetric, so reading it backwards changes nothing. And the entries of row n add to 2ⁿ — row 3 sums to 8, row 4 to 16 — which is a fast way to check a row you have just built.

Expanding (a + b)⁴ means multiplying four brackets, and from EACH bracket you take either an a or a b. Every term of the answer is one such choice sequence. So the coefficient of a²b² is simply the number of ways to choose which two of the four brackets contribute the b — a counting question, not an algebra one.

That identification is the theorem's engine: the entry in row n, position k, IS C(n, k). Pascal's addition rule is the same statement in disguise — choosing k things from n either uses the last item or does not, which is exactly C(n−1, k−1) + C(n−1, k), the two entries above.

Written out, the identification of the last lesson becomes one line: (a + b)ⁿ is the sum, over k from 0 to n, of C(n,k)·aⁿ⁻ᵏ·bᵏ. Three moving parts — a combination, a falling power of a, a rising power of b — and their exponents always total n, which is the fastest check that a term was written correctly.

The theorem also handles binomials that are not bare letters. For (2x + 3)⁴, take a = 2x and b = 3 and apply the formula unchanged — but every power now acts on the whole quantity, so a² means (2x)² = 4x², coefficient included. Forgetting to raise the 2 is the standard slip.

The theorem's real power is selective. If you want only the b³ term of (a + b)⁷, you need not expand the other seven — set k = 3 and write C(7,3)·a⁴·b³. The whole skill is deciding what k is, and reading it off the power of b every time.

Because rows are symmetric, C(n,k) and C(n,n−k) agree — so mixing up which exponent supplies k sometimes yields the right number by luck. Depending on that luck is how the error survives. Anchor k to the power of b and it never matters.

Let p be the chance of a success and q = 1 − p the chance of a failure. Then (p + q)ⁿ expands into terms C(n,k)pᵏqⁿ⁻ᵏ, and each one is the probability of exactly k successes in n trials. Since p + q = 1, the whole expansion sums to 1ⁿ = 1 — the distribution accounts for every outcome.

With a fair coin every path is equally likely, so the probability of exactly k heads is C(n,k)/2ⁿ. When p is not ½ the paths stop being equally likely and each carries weight pᵏqⁿ⁻ᵏ instead — but the COUNT of paths is still C(n,k), unchanged. The combination counts; the powers weigh.
A **scatter plot** shows **paired data** — two numbers measured on each thing. Each dot uses one measurement for its across-position (x) and the other for its up-position (y). One dot per item.
The two measurements must stay in order: the first number is always the across-value, the second the up-value. Swapping them puts the dot in the wrong place and can hide the real pattern in the data.

**Association** is the overall direction of the dots. **Positive**: as x goes up, y tends to go up (dots rise to the right). **Negative**: as x goes up, y tends to go down (dots fall). **No association**: no clear direction.

Think about what the pairing means. More hours of studying and more problems solved rise together — positive. More time driving and less fuel left in the tank move oppositely — negative. Shoe size and test score have no real link — no association.

Beyond direction, look at three things. **Clusters**: groups of dots bunched together. **Outliers**: lone dots far from the rest. **Form**: whether the pattern follows a straight line (**linear**) or a curve (**nonlinear**).

Form tells you what kind of model fits. If the dots follow a straight path, the form is linear and a straight line summarizes them. If they bend — leveling off or curving up — the form is nonlinear and a line would miss the shape.

When a scatter plot's form is roughly linear, a single straight line can summarize the trend. This **line of best fit** runs through the middle of the cloud, staying as close as possible to all the dots at once.

A good fit doesn't have to touch any dots. What matters is that the line sits in the **middle** of the cloud — roughly as many dots above it as below, each one not too far away. It's a summary, not a connect-the-dots.

To compare two candidate lines, look at the **gaps** between the dots and each line. The better fit has smaller gaps overall — the dots huddle closer to it. Bigger gaps mean a worse summary of the trend.

A tightly clustered cloud can be summarized by a line with very small gaps — a strong fit. A widely spread cloud leaves bigger gaps no matter how you draw the line, so even the best line is a looser summary.

Once you have a good line, describe it with an equation **y = mx + b** — the same form from functions. The **slope m** is the line's steepness, and the **intercept b** is where it crosses the up-axis (its value when x = 0).
The slope tells you how much y changes for each step of x. In y = 2x + 3, every increase of 1 in x raises y by 2. The intercept, 3, is the starting height where the line meets the up-axis.
A line of best fit does more than describe — it **predicts**. To predict y for a new x, plug that x into the equation **y = mx + b**. The line fills in a likely y-value for an x you didn't measure.
The steps are always the same: multiply the slope by the new x, then add the intercept. For y = 3x + 1 at x = 4: 3 × 4 = 12, then 12 + 1 = 13. Order matters — multiply before you add.
In a real situation, the **slope** is a rate: how much y changes for each extra unit of x. The **intercept** is the starting value of y when x = 0. Reading them tells the data's story in words.
The intercept anchors the story at x = 0. In y = 2x + 10, the 10 is the base cost before any data is used — the fee you pay at 0 gigabytes. Slope = per-unit change; intercept = starting amount.

Predictions are most reliable **inside** the range of the data. Stretching far **beyond** it — called **extrapolation** — is risky: the trend may not continue. A line fit to weeks 1–6 may say little about week 50.

Data can also curve outside the range you measured. A plant grows steadily for weeks, then stops at full height — a straight line would keep predicting impossible growth. Real trends often bend once you leave the data.
Some data is **categorical** — not numbers, but groups like dog/cat or child/adult. A **two-way table** sorts each person into a row-and-column box, counting how many fall into each combination.

The margins hold the **totals**. The child row totals 30 (20 dogs + 10 cats); the dog column totals 25 (20 children + 5 adults). The bottom-right corner, 50, is the **grand total** — everyone surveyed.
A **relative frequency** turns a count into a fraction or percent of a total: divide the cell by the total you care about. Of all 50 people, the 20 dog-loving children are 20 ÷ 50 = 0.40, or **40%**.

The total you divide by depends on the question. **Of the whole survey?** Divide by 50. **Of just the adults?** Divide by 20. Same cell, different total — so always ask which group the percent is 'out of'.

Two-way tables reveal **association** between categories. Compare relative frequencies across rows: if children and adults prefer dogs at very different rates, age and pet-preference are **associated**. Similar rates mean little or no association.
The key move is comparing **rates, not raw counts**. Two groups of different sizes can't be compared by counts alone. Turning each into a percent of its own row makes a fair comparison possible.

Chapter 2 fit a line; chapter 3 used it to predict. But real points don't sit ON the line — each one misses by some amount. That miss has a name: the residual, observed minus predicted. It is the line's error, measured point by point.

Every data point gets a residual: positive above the line, negative below, zero on it. A fitted line doesn't erase the misses — it chooses where to put them. Reading those leftovers is how you audit the line.

One residual judges one point. All the residuals together judge the MODEL. Plot each residual against x — flip the line down to a flat zero-axis — and look for a pattern. A good fit leaves patternless scatter; a pattern means the line missed something systematic.

Three diagnoses so far: U = curvature, one-sided = misplaced line, growing spread = the relationship loosens with x. Different diseases, one instrument — and none of them are visible from the fitted line alone. The scatter plot can look fine while the residual plot screams.

If residuals diagnose a line, they can also steer one. Move the line and every leftover changes; the best line is the one that makes them small AND balanced — some up, some down, summing to about zero, with no pattern. Fit by leftover.

This is the idea behind the 'line of best fit' your tools compute: they choose the slope and intercept that make the residuals collectively smallest (squaring them so ups and downs can't cancel). You've been doing by eye what least squares does by algebra.

Circles measure turning, and the ruler is the **central angle** — vertex at the center, sides on two radii. The piece of circle it cuts off is an **arc**, and we simply DEFINE the arc's measure to equal its central angle. A 140° central angle stands on a 140° arc; the whole circle is 360°.

Naming keeps the two arcs straight: **minor arcs** (under 180°) use two letters — arc AB — while **major arcs** (over 180°) borrow a third point to force the long way around — arc ACB. A 180° arc is a **semicircle**, cut off by a diameter. Adjacent arcs simply add, like segment lengths on a bent ruler.

Slide the vertex from the center out to the circle itself: that's an **inscribed angle** — vertex ON the circle, sides two chords. The **Inscribed Angle Theorem**: an inscribed angle measures **half** the arc it opens onto (half the central angle on that arc). An 80° arc is seen at 40° from the circle.

Why half? Draw the radius to the inscribed vertex: it splits the picture into isosceles triangles (two sides are radii), and each base angle gets doubled by the exterior angle at the center. The doubling at the center IS the halving at the rim. One proof, endless mileage.

The animated figure's punchline is a theorem of its own: **every inscribed angle on the same arc is congruent** — slide the vertex anywhere along the major arc and the angle refuses to change, because it always halves the SAME arc. Photographers call it the viewing-angle circle; geometers call it free congruence.

Point the inscribed angle at a **diameter** and the theorem sings: the diameter's arc is a semicircle, 180°, so the inscribed angle is half of that — **exactly 90°, from anywhere on the circle**. That's Thales' theorem, arguably the oldest proved statement in mathematics.

Thales turns every such triangle into a RIGHT triangle whose hypotenuse is the diameter — so the whole right-triangle toolkit (Pythagoras, the trig course) boards the circle. And the two remaining angles? They must complete 180° past the right angle: complements of each other.

A **chord** is a segment with both endpoints on the circle — the diameter is just the chord that happens to pass through the center. Every chord cuts off an arc, and the two are locked together: **congruent chords cut congruent arcs**, and vice versa (in the same circle, or in congruent circles).

The lock runs through the **central angle**: chord ↔ central angle ↔ arc, each pair matched. A 60° central angle is special: its two radii and the chord form a triangle with two equal sides and 60° between them — equilateral, so **the chord of a 60° arc equals the radius**.

Drop a perpendicular from the center onto any chord: it lands on the chord's **midpoint** — and bisects the chord's arc too. Proof: the two endpoint triangles share the perpendicular leg and have matching radius hypotenuses — HL congruence, then CPCTC. One perpendicular, two halves.

Run it backward: given the chord, find its distance. Half the chord and the distance are the legs; the radius is always the hypotenuse. Radius 13, chord 24: half-chord 12, so d = √(169 − 144) = 5. The 5-12-13 triple lives inside every such circle problem.

The converse is a center-finder: **the perpendicular bisector of any chord passes through the center** — the center is equidistant from the chord's endpoints, and the bisector is exactly the set of such points. Two chords, two bisectors, one intersection: the lost center, found. Restorers rebuild broken plates this way.

Put the right-triangle engine to comparative work: **congruent chords sit at equal distances from the center, and equal-distance chords are congruent.** The equation (chord/2)² + d² = r² makes it plain — fix r, and chord length determines distance exactly, both ways.

Unequal chords trade off: from (chord/2)² + d² = r², a LONGER chord forces a SMALLER distance — **the closer the chord, the longer it runs**, peaking at the diameter (distance zero). Ranking chords by length is ranking their distances in reverse.

A **tangent line** touches the circle at exactly ONE point — the point of tangency. (Different creature from the tangent RATIO in trigonometry; the shared name is historical.) The headline theorem: **a tangent is perpendicular to the radius at its point of tangency** — and conversely, a line perpendicular to a radius at its endpoint is tangent.

That right angle recruits Pythagoras. From an external point P, the segment to the center (OP), the radius to the tangency point (r), and the **tangent segment** PT form a right triangle with the right angle AT T — so **PT = √(OP² − r²)**. The hypotenuse is OP, always.

From any external point, exactly TWO tangent lines reach the circle — and their tangent segments are **congruent**: PT₁ = PT₂. Proof in one breath: triangles OT₁P and OT₂P share hypotenuse OP and have equal legs (radii), so HL congruence — then CPCTC hands over the tangent segments.

Zoom out to the whole figure OT₁PT₂: two radii, two congruent tangent segments — **a kite**, straight from the quadrilateral course, with its right angles at T₁ and T₂. Its angle sum forces a clean supplement: **angle P + central angle T₁OT₂ = 180°**, since the two right angles spend the other 180.

Wrap a triangle around a circle so every side is tangent — the circle is **inscribed** in the triangle. The two-tangent theorem fires at all three vertices: each vertex owns a matched pair of tangent lengths, call them x, x at A, y, y at B, z, z at C. Every side is then a SUM of two tangent lengths.

Run it in reverse to find unknown pieces. If AB = 12 and the tangent length from A is 4, then B's tangent length is 12 − 4 = 8 — and B carries that same 8 onto side BC. Tangent lengths are a bookkeeping system: each vertex's number is fixed, and sides just add adjacent entries.

Chapter 1 priced angles ON the circle (half their arc). Move the vertex and the price changes. Two chords crossing **INSIDE** the circle make an angle equal to **half the SUM of the two arcs** they and their vertical partner intercept — the average of the two arcs. Arcs 100° and 40°: angle = 70°.

Push the vertex **OUTSIDE** and the formula flips its sign: two secants (or tangents) from an external point make an angle equal to **half the DIFFERENCE of the far and near arcs**. Arcs 130° and 30°: angle = 50°. Inside averages; outside takes half the spread. The vertex's location picks the sign.

One hybrid remains: a **tangent and a chord** meeting at the point of tangency. The angle between them equals **half the intercepted arc** — the same rate as an inscribed angle, because it IS an inscribed angle in the limit: slide one chord endpoint around until the chord becomes the tangent, and the half-arc rule survives the slide.

The two angles the chord makes with the tangent — one on each side — halve the two arcs the chord creates, and those arcs sum to 360°. So the two tangent-chord angles sum to 180°: supplements, exactly as a straight line demands. The circle's arithmetic and the line's arithmetic agree.

From angles to lengths. Two chords crossing at P inside a circle obey **PA · PB = PC · PD**: the products of the two pieces match. Why: joining the endpoints creates two triangles with equal inscribed angles (same arcs) — similar by AA, from the similarity course — and the proportion cross-multiplies into the product rule.

Outside the circle the same law holds in costume: for two secants from P, **PA · PB = PC · PD**, where both distances are measured FROM P — so each product is the secant's **external part times its whole length**. Same AA-similarity engine, same matched products.

Let one secant rotate until its two intersection points merge: it becomes a **tangent**, and near × far collapses to **PT · PT = PT²**. The tangent-secant law: **PT² = PA · PB** (external × whole). One law, three costumes — chords, secants, tangent — all called the *power of the point* P.

Arc MEASURE counts degrees; arc LENGTH measures distance — and the bridge is a fraction. An arc of θ degrees claims θ/360 of the circle, so it claims that same fraction of the circumference (2πr, from your Grade 7 circle work): **arc length = (θ/360) · 2πr**. Degrees price the share; the radius prices the whole.

The trigonometry course prices the same arc as **s = rθ** with θ in radians — and the two formulas are one. Convert 60° = π/3 rad: s = 9 · π/3 = 3π, exactly the fraction route's answer. Radians BUILD the fraction into the angle unit; degrees keep it explicit. Same arc, two bookkeeping systems.

The same fraction that priced the arc prices the **sector** — the pie slice between two radii. A θ-degree sector claims θ/360 of the circle's area πr² (Grade 7 again): **sector area = (θ/360) · πr²**. One fraction, two purchases: rim distance and interior area.

Radian bookkeeping compresses this one too: with θ in radians, sector area = **½r²θ**. Check it on the quarter-circle: ½(36)(π/2) = 9π — the same 28.27. And notice the pleasing echo: arc s = rθ, sector = ½r·(rθ) = ½ · radius · arc, just like a triangle's ½ · base · height.

A **cyclic quadrilateral** has all four vertices on one circle. Its signature: **opposite angles are supplementary.** Why: opposite angles are inscribed angles opening onto complementary arcs — the two arcs together make the whole 360°, so the two angles halve it: 180° between them.

The proof in one line: angle A halves arc BCD, angle C halves arc DAB, and those arcs tile the whole circle — A + C = ½(360) = 180. The CONVERSE holds too: if a quadrilateral's opposite angles are supplementary, a circle passes through all four vertices. Supplementarity is the entrance ticket.

For similarity, most shapes need conditions checked — matching angles, proportional sides. A circle needs none of that. Every circle's circumference is 2πr and every circle's area is πr² — the SAME two formulas, for every circle there is. Only the radius changes from one circle to the next, and that single number is enough to connect any two circles by exactly one dilation.

Area's formula is πr² — built from r SQUARED, not r alone. That one difference changes everything about how it scales: double the radius and the '2r' piece doubles, but the 'r²' piece quadruples. Circumference and area are both built from the same radius, but they answer to that radius in genuinely different ways.
Two groups can hold MORE, FEWER, or the SAME. Those three words are all of comparing — the rest is finding out which is true.
More means leftovers on that side after pairing. Fewer means running out first. Same means the pairing comes out even.
Matching one to one is the oldest comparing tool: one star takes one heart, again and again, until a side runs dry.
The side still holding things is the bigger group — and HOW MANY it still holds is exactly the difference.
The BIGGER group is the one pairing cannot empty. Say it with MORE: more stars, more hearts, whichever side holds extras.
Bigger is about members, not about space or size — three elephants are fewer than five mice.
The SMALLER group runs out first when pairing. Say it with FEWER: fewer stars means stars ran out while hearts remained.
Fewer is not sad or wrong — it is simply the side of the pairing that finished first.
Sometimes the pairing comes out even: every star finds a heart, and nothing stands alone. Those groups MATCH — they are EQUAL.
Equal is a claim about the pairing, so it survives any shuffling — scatter the stars and they still pair off exactly.
Eyes can compare when the gap is huge — seven against two needs no counting. But close contests fool the eye, especially spread-out groups.
The rule: trust a glance for big gaps, and reach for pairing or counting the moment the race looks close.
Counting both groups turns comparison into a number question: the group whose count comes LATER in the song has more.
Count stars to six, hearts to eight — eight is later than six, so the hearts win, no pairing required.
Two written numerals compare the same way: the one LATER in the counting song is GREATER. 8 beats 6 because counting reaches 6 first.
No stars or hearts needed — the song's order is carried inside the numerals themselves.
The number EARLIER in the song is LESS. 4 is less than 7 because the count says four first, three steps before seven.
Less and greater are two views of one fact: if 4 is less than 7, then 7 is greater than 4 — both at once.
5 pebbles and 5 feathers hold the SAME amount — the numeral 5 does not care what it counts. Same numeral, same group size.
That is what makes numerals powerful: one symbol compares groups of anything at all.
Several numbers line up by the song's order: smallest first, then each next greater, up to the biggest. That is counting order.
Placing them is repeated comparing — each number goes after everything less and before everything greater.
In an ordered line, the GREATEST stands at one end and the LEAST at the other — the song's last word, and its first.
Greatest and least are the line's two ends — everything else lives between them.

A **perfect square trinomial** is a squared binomial in disguise: (x + p)² = x² + 2px + p². Read it backward: given x² + bx, the constant that completes the square is **(b/2)²** — half the middle coefficient, squared. The picture: two b/2 strips wrap the x² square, leaving one small corner to fill.
Spotting one in the wild: x² + 10x + 25 has 25 = (10/2)², so it folds up as **(x + 5)²**. The number inside the parentheses is always **b/2** — the same half that got squared.

You already know how to solve (x + 3)² = 4 — square roots. Completing the square lets you **build** that form from any quadratic. Solve x² + 6x + 5 = 0: move the constant, x² + 6x = −5; add (6/2)² = 9 to **both sides**: (x + 3)² = 4.

Finish with square roots: (x + 3)² = 4 gives x + 3 = ±2, so x = −3 ± 2 — that's **x = −1 or x = −5**. Check: (−1)² + 6(−1) + 5 = 0. ✓ The whole method is: isolate, add (b/2)² to both sides, root, undo the shift.

You've read vertices FROM vertex form — now derive it. For y = x² − 6x + 5, add and subtract (6/2)² = 9 **on the same side**: y = (x² − 6x + 9) − 9 + 5 = **(x − 3)² − 4**. Add-and-subtract keeps y unchanged — there's no other side to balance on.
Why it's legal: +9 − 9 = 0, so y never changed — it just regrouped. The payoff is instant: (x − 3)² − 4 hands you the vertex **(3, −4)** and the minimum value −4 with no formula at all.

x² = −1 has no real solution — every real number squares to zero or more. Mathematicians' fix: invent a new number. Define **i** by **i² = −1**. With it, square roots of negatives make sense: √(−9) = √9 · √(−1) = **3i**.

The rule in general: **√(−k) = i√k** for k > 0 — pull the −1 out as i, then root the rest. And equations follow: x² = −16 now HAS solutions, x = ±4i, because (4i)² = 16 · i² = −16 and (−4i)² does the same.

Keep multiplying by i and a pattern locks in: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = i²·i = **−i**, i⁴ = i²·i² = (−1)(−1) = **1** — and then it repeats. Every power of i is one of just four values, cycling like a quarter turn.
For big exponents, ride the cycle: since i⁴ = 1, only the **remainder of n ÷ 4** matters. i¹⁰: 10 = 4·2 + 2, remainder 2, so i¹⁰ = i² = −1. Remainder 0 means a whole number of laps: the value is 1.

A **complex number** mixes both kinds: **a + bi**, with real part a and imaginary part b. Since it takes two numbers to describe, it lives on a **plane**: real part along the horizontal axis, imaginary part up the vertical. 3 + 2i is the point 3 right, 2 up.

Special positions: a purely **real** number like 5 sits ON the horizontal axis (its b is 0); a purely **imaginary** one like 5i sits ON the vertical axis (its a is 0). Every other complex number floats off both axes.

Adding complex numbers works like combining like terms: **real with real, imaginary with imaginary**. (3 + 2i) + (1 + 4i) = (3 + 1) + (2 + 4)i = 4 + 6i. The two parts never mix — just as 3 + 2x stays 3 + 2x.

Subtraction distributes the minus to **both parts** of the second number: (6 + 2i) − (4 + 5i) = (6 − 4) + (2 − 5)i = 2 − 3i. The classic slip is subtracting the real part but forgetting to subtract the imaginary one.

Multiply complex numbers like binomials — distribute everything (FOIL) — then apply **i² = −1**. (2 + i)(3 + 2i) = 6 + 4i + 3i + 2i². The 2i² becomes **−2**, a real number, so the product is (6 − 2) + 7i = **4 + 7i**.

The pattern to internalize: the **First** and **Last** FOIL terms build the real part (with the Last flipped by i²), and the **Outer + Inner** build the imaginary part. In symbols: (a + bi)(c + di) = (ac − bd) + (ad + bc)i.

The **conjugate** of a + bi is a − bi — same real part, flipped imaginary sign. Multiply a number by its conjugate and the i vanishes: (a + bi)(a − bi) = **a² + b²**, always a real number. For 3 + 2i: (3 + 2i)(3 − 2i) = 9 + 4 = 13.

That real product is the key to **division**: to divide by a complex number, multiply top and bottom by the **bottom's conjugate**. Example: (3 + i)/(1 − i). Multiply by (1 + i)/(1 + i): bottom becomes 1 + 1 = 2, top becomes (3 + i)(1 + i) = 2 + 4i, so the answer is **1 + 2i**.

In Algebra 1, x² = −16 was a dead end: 'no real solutions.' Now you can finish it: x = ±√(−16) = **±4i**. Every equation of the form x² = −k has two purely imaginary solutions, ±i√k — the square-root method never stalls again.

Shifted squares work the same way: (x − 2)² = −9 gives x − 2 = ±3i, so **x = 2 ± 3i** — a real shift plus an imaginary spread. The answers come as a matched pair, one +3i and one −3i around the center 2.

The quadratic formula never needed the discriminant to be positive. For x² − 4x + 13 = 0: D = b² − 4ac = 16 − 52 = **−36**. Then √D = √(−36) = 6i, and x = (4 ± 6i)/2 = **2 ± 3i**. Same formula, new number system.

Finishing matters: x = (4 ± 6i)/2 divides **both parts** by 2, giving 2 ± 3i. Notice the answers are **conjugates** — same real part, opposite imaginary signs. Real-coefficient quadratics always deliver complex roots in conjugate pairs.

Algebra 1's discriminant chart had a hole: 'D < 0: no real solutions.' The full story: **every** quadratic has exactly **two** roots. D > 0: two distinct reals. D = 0: one real, counted twice. D < 0: two complex conjugates. Nothing is ever missing — it just moves off the real line.

So classifying is a one-number job: compute D = b² − 4ac and read its **sign**. Positive → two real crossings. Zero → the vertex kisses the axis. Negative → the parabola floats clear and the pair goes complex.

The old shortcuts survive the trip: for x² + bx + c = 0, the roots still **sum to −b** and **multiply to c** — even when they're complex. x² − 4x + 13 has roots 2 ± 3i: sum (2 + 3i) + (2 − 3i) = 4 = −b. ✓

The product uses the conjugate pattern: (2 + 3i)(2 − 3i) = 4 + 9 = **13** = c. ✓ In general a ± bi sums to **2a** (the imaginary parts cancel) and multiplies to **a² + b²** (always real — which is exactly why c is real).

Run the shortcuts backward: a monic quadratic with roots r and s is **x² − (sum)x + (product)**. Roots 3 ± 2i: sum 6, product 9 + 4 = 13, so the quadratic is **x² − 6x + 13**. Note the sign: minus the sum.

This is also why complex roots of real quadratics **must** come in conjugate pairs: only then do the sum (2a) and product (a² + b²) come out real. One root 4 − i immediately tells you the other is 4 + i.

Four solving methods, one decision: bare x² = k or a ready-made square → **square roots**; friendly integer factors → **factoring**; even middle term, stubborn factors → **completing the square**; anything at all → the **formula**. The discriminant predicts the root type before you commit.

Complex roots aren't tied to any one method — they appear whenever **D < 0**, whichever route you take. x² + 10x + 29: completing the square gives (x + 5)² = −4, so x = **−5 ± 2i** — the negative square announces the complex pair.
A shape is decided by its defining attributes: how many straight sides it has and how many corners. Those are the parts that cannot change.
Count the sides and corners and you can name the shape, whatever colour or size it happens to be.
Colour, size and which way a shape points are non-defining attributes. Change any of them and the shape stays exactly what it was.
A tiny red triangle turned upside down is still a triangle, because its sides and corners never changed.
Sorting by a defining attribute puts shapes into groups that really are alike: all the 3-sided shapes together, all the 4-sided ones together.
Sorting by colour makes groups too, but they are not shape groups — the same shape can end up in different piles.
Two shapes can be joined along a matching edge to make a brand-new, larger shape. The edge where they meet disappears inside.
That is why the new shape has fewer sides than the two pieces had between them — the joined edges are no longer on the outside.
Two squares pushed together side by side make a rectangle: four straight sides, four corners, but longer than it is tall.
The two squares still exist inside the rectangle — composing does not destroy the pieces, it only hides the edge between them.
Six triangles meeting at a single centre point make a hexagon — a shape with six straight sides.
Composing is not limited to two pieces. Any number of shapes can combine, as long as their edges match up.
Filling an outline with smaller shapes means covering it completely: no gaps left uncovered and no pieces stacked on top of each other.
The same outline can often be filled in more than one way, using different pieces — and every correct filling covers it exactly.
Solid shapes can be composed too. A cube, a cone, a cylinder and a sphere take up space, unlike flat shapes that lie on the page.
Solids have flat faces and edges to count, just as flat shapes have sides and corners.
Composing has an opposite: a shape can be cut into smaller shapes. A square cut along its diagonal becomes two triangles.
Decomposing and composing undo each other — the pieces can always be rejoined into the original shape.
Composing and decomposing together let you build new shapes from old ones, then take them apart again — the pieces are never lost.
Whatever you build, name it by its own defining attributes: count the sides and corners of the finished outline.

Two words do all the work. **And** (∩) keeps an outcome only if it passes **both** tests. **Or** (∪) keeps it if it passes **at least one**. So the intersection is always the smaller set — it lives inside the union.

Draw one card from twenty cards numbered 1–20. The twenty outcomes are the **sample space**. An **event** is just a subset of it: "multiple of 3" is the set {3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18}. Because every card is equally likely, a probability is a count: P(A) = (outcomes in A) ÷ 20.

Picture the two events as overlapping circles. The middle holds outcomes in **both**; the outer petals hold outcomes in only one; everything outside is in **neither**. That picture is why counting a union means adding the two circles and then removing the middle once — it was counted twice.
"At least one" means **one or more** — one, two, all of them. It fails in exactly one way: **zero**. So always ask "how many outcomes have zero?" and subtract that from the total.

Every outcome either is in A or is not. So P(A) + P(not A) = 1, giving the **complement rule**: P(not A) = 1 − P(A). This is the workhorse for "at least one", because the opposite of *at least one* is the much smaller, much easier event: **none**.

Notice the pattern. Counting "at least one" directly means adding overlapping cases and repairing double-counts. Counting **none** is one clean multiplication — every trial must miss. That is why the complement route is almost always the short road.
One test decides it. Try to name a **single outcome** that is in both events. If you can name even one, the events are not mutually exclusive. If no such outcome exists, they are.

Two events are **mutually exclusive** when they share no outcome: A ∩ B is empty, so they cannot both happen. Even and odd. Rain all day and dry all day. When events are exclusive, counting a union is pure addition — there is nothing to remove. Most real pairs of events are **not** exclusive.

That subtraction has a name coming in Chapter 4: the **addition rule**. For now, hold the picture. Add the two counts, then remove the middle once. Exclusive events just happen to have an empty middle, so nothing gets removed — they are the easy special case, not the rule.

Adding P(A) and P(B) counts everything in the middle **twice** — once from each event. The rule fixes that by subtracting the middle once. If the events cannot co-occur, the middle is empty and there is nothing to subtract.

Counting outcomes and finding probabilities are the same move, divided by the total. If every card is equally likely, P(A) is just |A|/52. So the overlap correction you learned for **counts** carries straight over to **probabilities**:

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B).

When the overlap is empty, P(A ∩ B) = 0 and the subtraction does nothing:

P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B).

That is the *special* case, not the default. Adding without checking the overlap is the single most common error in this chapter — so before you add, always ask: **can both happen at once?**

A joint probability answers **both** questions at once, so it lives in a single inner cell — never a row, never a column. Its denominator is always the grand total, because the student could have landed anywhere in the table.

A two-way table sorts one group by **two questions at once**. Each of the 200 students lands in exactly one inner cell, so the four inner cells add to 200. The edge totals are just those cells summed along a row or a column.

You met these tables in Grade 8. Now every count in one becomes a probability: divide by the grand total.

Two names for two shapes:

**Joint** probability — one inner cell over the total. P(bus and sport) = 40/200.

**Marginal** probability — a whole edge total over the total. P(sport) = 110/200.

Same denominator, different shaded region. Marginals ignore the second question entirely.

Row total + column total always overshoots, because the crossing cell lives in both. Subtract that cell once and you are left with exactly the shaded students. A quick sanity test: if your "or" probability exceeds 1, you forgot the subtraction.

"Bus **or** sport" on a table means: shade the whole bus row, then shade the whole sport column. The cell where they cross gets shaded twice — once by the row, once by the column.

That is the addition rule in picture form. Add the row total and the column total, then take the crossing cell back once.

"**Neither**" is the complement of "or". Every student is either inside the shaded union or outside it, so:

P(neither) = 1 − P(A ∪ B).

On a table it is the one cell you never shaded. That gives you a free check: the union and the "neither" cell must add to the whole group.

When you are told B happened, cross out every outcome where B is false. Then just count: how many of the survivors are also A? That count over the number of survivors **is** the conditional probability.

P(roll a 6) = 1/6. Now someone tells you the roll came up **even**. The three odd faces are gone — they were never possible after all — and the 6 is one of the three faces still standing.

Information does not change the die. It changes the **set of outcomes you are choosing among**.

Written as a formula:

P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).

Read it as: *of the B-world, how much is also A?* The numerator must be the part of A **inside** B — an outcome outside B is no longer on the table. Both parts are measured against the same original total, so that total cancels.

The bar in P(A | B) is not symmetric. Whatever stands to the **right** of the bar is the group you are standing inside; whatever stands to the left is what you are counting there. Swap them and you have changed the question.

The same 40 students sit in the crossing cell. But *what you are told* decides what you divide by.

Told they take the bus → divide by the bus row: 40/100.
Told they play a sport → divide by the sport column: 40/110.

Same numerator, different denominator, different answer. P(A | B) and P(B | A) are **not** the same number.

Swapping the two sides is the most expensive mistake in probability.

*Almost every flu patient has a cough* does **not** mean *almost every cougher has flu*. The first divides by the flu patients; the second divides by the far larger crowd of coughers.

When a claim conditions on something, ask: **which group is underneath?**

Think of it as a two-stage journey. Stage one: how likely is B at all? Stage two: **given you got there**, how likely is A? Multiply the two stages. The second probability must be measured inside the world the first one created.

Multiply both sides of P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B) by P(B):

P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B).

In words: to get **both**, first get B, then get A *in the world where B already happened*. Half the students ride the bus; 40% of those play a sport; so 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.20 do both.

The rule works from either end:

P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B) = P(A) × P(B | A).

Use whichever conditional you actually know. That freedom is what makes the rule usable — and it is the seed of Bayes' rule, since both products describe the same overlap.

Take the draws one at a time. Write the bag's contents before each draw, and read the probability off *that* bag. Without replacement the bag changes between draws, so the second fraction is never a copy of the first.

A tree turns the multiplication rule into a picture. Each branch carries a conditional probability, so you **multiply along a path** to reach a leaf.

The second-draw branches use denominators of 7, because one marble is already gone. Removing it also changes *which* marble is likelier next — the branches differ depending on the path you took.

Multiply **along** a path; add **across** paths.

"One of each colour" happens two ways — red-then-blue and blue-then-red — and those two leaves are mutually exclusive, so their probabilities add. Every leaf of the tree is exclusive of every other, which is why the four leaves sum to 1.

Ask one question: *does the news change my estimate?* If P(A) was 0.3 before you heard about B and it is still 0.3 after, B was worthless news and the events are independent. If it moves at all — up or down — they are dependent.

Two events are **independent** when learning one leaves the other's probability exactly where it was:

P(A | B) = P(A).

A card's suit and its rank are like this. P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13. Told the card is a heart, the world shrinks to 13 cards — but exactly one is a king, so it is still 1/13.

Independence is **symmetric**. If B tells you nothing about A, then A tells you nothing about B:

P(A | B) = P(A)  ⟺  P(B | A) = P(B).

So you may test whichever direction is easier. Careful: independence is a claim about *information*, not about causation, and it must be checked — never assumed because two things "feel unrelated".

The product test has two steps. **Predict:** multiply the two rates and scale by the total. **Compare:** look at what the cell actually holds. Equal means independent. Any difference at all means dependent.

Put P(A | B) = P(A) into the multiplication rule and the conditional disappears:

P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B)  — **only when A and B are independent.**

That gives a one-line test. Predict the cell from the two edge totals; then look at the cell. If the prediction is wrong, the events are dependent.

The product test works in **both directions**:

– Given a table, compare the actual cell with P(A) × P(B) × total.
– Given that events *are* independent, use the product to **build** the missing cell.

A gap in either direction — cell above or below the prediction — is dependence. Only an exact match means none.

Picture the Venn diagram. Mutually exclusive events are **drawn apart** — no shared region at all. Independent events **must overlap**, and the overlap has to be exactly the product size. Separate circles can never be independent.

These two words sound similar and mean nearly opposite things.

**Mutually exclusive:** A happening makes B *impossible*. P(B | A) = 0.
**Independent:** A happening leaves B *untouched*. P(B | A) = P(B).

So if both events have a real chance of happening, being exclusive is the strongest possible dependence — the news is devastating, not useless.

A test you can apply in one second: could both events happen at once?

– If **no**, they are mutually exclusive, hence dependent (assuming each has a real chance).
– If **yes**, they overlap, and you must still check the product to know whether they are independent.

Overlapping is necessary for independence, but it is not enough.
Draw one empty box per slot. Write in each box how many candidates are still available when you reach it. Then multiply the boxes. If a chosen item is used up, the next box holds one fewer.

Sometimes the sample space is far too big to list. Then you **count** it instead.

Fill the slots one at a time and multiply. Five runners, three medals: 5 choices for gold, then only 4 runners remain for silver, then 3 for bronze.

5 × 4 × 3 = 60 possible podiums.

Two names for the same machinery:

**n!** — arrange **all** n items: n × (n−1) × … × 1.
**nPk** — fill only **k** slots from n items: n × (n−1) × … , k factors in total.

Both assume order matters: swapping two chosen items produces a different result.

Count as if order mattered, then repair. Any k chosen items can be arranged in k! ways, and those arrangements all describe the same group — so the ordered count is exactly k! times too big. Divide by k!.

A podium of gold-silver-bronze cares about order. A **team** does not: {A, B, C} is the same team however you list it.

Those 60 ordered picks contain each team exactly 3! = 6 times — once per ordering. So divide:

60 ÷ 6 = 10 teams.

The formula records that division:

C(n,k) = nPk / k! = n! / (k! (n−k)!).

Ask one question before you compute: **would swapping two of my chosen items give a different outcome?** If yes, use a permutation. If no, use a combination.

Write down two counts before touching a calculator. **Total:** how many equally likely groups exist? **Favourable:** how many of them satisfy the event? Then divide. Use the same counting style for both.

When every group is equally likely, probability is just a ratio of two counts:

P = (favourable groups) / (all groups).
