Lengths scale by the scale factor — but **area scales by its square**. At 1 cm = 4 m, each 1 cm² of drawing stands for 4 × 4 = **16 m²** of real area, because both the width AND the height stretch by 4.
The safest method for a scaled rectangle: convert each **side** to real units first, then multiply. A 2 cm × 3 cm drawing at 1 cm = 4 m becomes 8 m × 12 m, so the real area is 96 m².
A circle has two key lengths. The **radius** r runs from the center to the edge; the **diameter** d crosses the whole circle through the center. The diameter is always **twice** the radius: d = 2r.
The number **π** (about 3.14) is the circle's built-in ratio: every circle's distance around is π times its diameter. Big or small, that ratio never changes — that's what makes π special.

The **circumference** is the distance around a circle: **C = πd**, or equally **C = 2πr** (since d = 2r). We leave answers as a number times π (exact): a circle with radius 3 has C = 2 × 3 × π = **6π**.
With a **diameter**, skip the doubling: C = πd directly. Diameter 10 gives C = 10π. Given a radius, double it first; given a diameter, use it as-is. The two formulas are the same fact in two outfits.
A circle's **area** — the space inside — is **A = πr²**: square the radius, then multiply by π. Radius 3 gives A = π × 3² = **9π**. This is the very πr² that lives inside the cylinder volume formula.
Circumference and area are the classic mix-up: **C = 2πr doubles**, **A = πr² squares**. A quick sense-check: area answers grow much faster — radius 10 gives C = 20π but A = 100π.
Two angles that fit together into a **square corner** are **complementary**: they add to **90°**. Two angles that fit along a **straight line** are **supplementary**: they add to **180°**.
A memory hook: **C**omplementary makes a **C**orner (90°); **S**upplementary makes a **S**traight line (180°). To find a missing partner, subtract the known angle from the pair's total.

When two lines cross, they make four angles. Angles **across** from each other are **vertical angles** — always **equal**. Angles **next to** each other are **adjacent** — they share a side and add to 180° along each line.
At a crossing, you get everything from one angle. If one angle is 75°: across is 75° (vertical, equal); next to it is 180 − 75 = 105° (adjacent on a line); across from that is 105° again.
Angle facts become **equations**. If x and 2x fit a square corner, then x + 2x = 90, so 3x = 90 and **x = 30**. Write the fact as an equation, combine the x's, divide.
The same recipe works on a straight line. If x and 3x are supplementary: x + 3x = 180, so 4x = 180 and x = 45. The only question is which total to use — 90° for corners, 180° for lines.

Hand three people the same three side lengths — 4, 5 and 6 — and tell them to build a triangle. They will all build the **same** triangle.

It may be flipped or turned, but no one can produce a different shape. Three sides leave nothing to choose, which is what mathematicians mean when they say the conditions **determine a unique triangle**.

The failure case has a rule of its own. Two sides can only meet if together they are **longer** than the third.

2 and 3 cannot bridge a gap of 6: laid end to end they reach 5 and stop short. That is the triangle inequality, and it is why some lists of three lengths describe no triangle at all.

Give two sides and an angle that is **not** between them, and the triangle stops being unique.

The second side swings like a door and can reach the base at two different points. Both landings satisfy every given, so the conditions describe *two* different triangles — this is the ambiguous case, SSA.

Three angles that sum to 180° always describe a real shape — but never a single triangle.

With no length anywhere in the conditions there is nothing to set the scale, so the same shape can be drawn at every size. That is **infinitely many**, and it is a different kind of non-uniqueness from SSA's exactly two.

A compass does one thing: it holds a distance. That single ability is enough to build every construction in this lesson.

Swing equal arcs from each end of a segment and they cross above and below it. Every crossing sits the same distance from both ends, so the line through them is the **perpendicular bisector** — proved, not measured.

The same trick copies an **angle** without ever measuring it.

Swing one arc across the original angle and an identical arc on the new ray. Then step off the distance between the two crossing points. Because every distance was carried by the compass, the copied angle is exactly equal — no protractor, no rounding.

Not every three lengths can form a triangle. The **triangle inequality** decides: the two **shorter** sides together must **beat** the longest side. Sides 3, 4, 5 work because 3 + 4 > 5. Sides 2, 3, 6 fail because 2 + 3 < 6.

Picture why: the longest side is the floor, and the two shorter sides must reach over it to meet. If they're too short to arch over — like 2 and 3 across a floor of 6 — the sides fall flat and never touch.

Slice a 3D solid with a flat cut and the cut face is a 2D shape — a **cross-section**. A cylinder cut **across** (parallel to its base) shows a **circle**; cut straight **down** through the center, it shows a **rectangle**.

The same solid gives different sections depending on the cut. A rectangular box cut parallel to any face shows that face's rectangle. A square pyramid cut parallel to its base shows a smaller **square**; cut down through its tip, a **triangle**.

One chapter left to close Grade 7 geometry: putting it all together. Scale drawings convert, circles measure, angle facts become equations, side lengths decide triangles, and cuts reveal cross-sections.
Skills chain together. That 6 m radius feeds straight into the circle formulas: circumference C = 2π × 6 = 12π meters of fence, area A = π × 6² = 36π square meters of water.

Surface area is a flat question wearing a 3-D costume. Cut a box along its edges and lay it out: what you get is a NET, a flat arrangement of the same faces. Adding up the net's areas is adding up the solid's surface, because they are the same cardboard either way.

So the formula is bookkeeping, not magic: 2(lw + lh + wh). Each product is one face; each 2 is that face's opposite twin. If you ever forget it, unfold the box in your head and add the rectangles — the formula will reassemble itself.

With the net understood, surface area becomes a routine you can trust: find the three distinct face areas, add them, double. The only real hazard is mixing it up with volume — they use the same three numbers and answer completely different questions.

Units settle the question when words do not. Surface area lands in square units because every face is a length times a length. Volume lands in cubic units because it multiplies three lengths. If your answer's units do not match the question's, the wrong measure was computed.

A triangular prism has two triangular ENDS and three rectangular SIDES. The ends match each other, so they still come as a pair; the sides usually do not match at all. Surface area is the same idea as before — add every face — but the bookkeeping has to be done honestly rather than by doubling three products.

The shortcut worth keeping is lateral surface = perimeter of the end × length. Here the perimeter is 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 and the length is 10, giving 120 in one step. Add the two ends and the prism is finished. The same rule works for ANY prism, whatever polygon its end happens to be.

Volume of a right prism is one idea repeated: cover the base once, then stack that layer as many times as the height allows. Base area times height. For a box the base is a rectangle, but the rule never mentions rectangles — it works for a triangular base, a hexagonal base, any base at all.

Because the rule is base-area times height, a triangular prism needs no new formula at all. Compute the triangle's area, multiply by the length, done. The shape of the base changes what you compute FIRST; it never changes the stacking.

Real floor plans are not single rectangles. The move that handles all of them is the same: break the figure into pieces you already know, find each area, then ADD the pieces that are there and SUBTRACT the ones cut away. A ledger, kept honestly, beats any formula.

There is usually more than one correct cut. The same L-shape can be sliced vertically or horizontally, or read as a big rectangle with a bite taken out. Every honest route gives the same total — which makes a second method the fastest way to check the first.

One crate, three questions. How much floor does it stand on? Area. How much paint wraps it? Surface area. How much sand fills it? Volume. The numbers are the same; the question decides which measure answers it — and the units confirm the choice.

The reliable check is units. Floor space and paint are square units. Sand is cubic units. Tape along an edge would be linear units. When an answer's units do not match what the question is asking for, the wrong measure was computed — no matter how clean the arithmetic was.
Counting is a pairing game: touch one toy, say one number. Every toy gets a number, and no toy gets two.
The touch is what keeps the pairing honest — it marks which toys already have their number.
Two mistakes break a count: skipping a toy, and counting a toy twice. Skipping makes the answer too small; repeating makes it too big.
Careful counters go slowly enough that each toy is touched exactly once — speed is the enemy of the pairing.
A line is the friendliest arrangement to count: start at one end, touch each thing in turn, and stop at the other end.
The line does the organising for you — what has been counted sits behind your finger, and what remains sits ahead.
A circle has no ends, so the counter must invent one: remember the starting bead, and stop just before reaching it again.
Forget the start and the count sails past it, counting beads a second time — the circle's only trap.
Pictures on a page cannot move into a line — so mark them instead: each one gets a tick as its number is said.
Marking splits the page the way a line splits a row: ticked things are counted, clean things still wait.
Counting's biggest secret: the last number said is not just the last toy's name — it tells how many are in the WHOLE group.
Count five shells and the word “five” belongs to all of them together. That is what “how many” asks for.
Once a group is counted, its number sticks. Asked again, the counter answers from memory — nothing changed, so the count still holds.
Recounting is only needed when the group itself changes: something added, something taken away.
Count the same toys left-to-right, right-to-left, or hopping about — the answer never moves. Order is the counter's choice; the amount is not.
As long as every toy is counted exactly once, the pairing ends at the same last number from any direction.
Spread five buttons far apart and the group LOOKS bigger — but looking bigger and being more are different. The count ends at five.
Space is not amount. Only adding or removing buttons can change how many there are.
Scattered things are hardest to count — nothing separates counted from uncounted. The oldest trick fixes it: mark each one as its number is said.
With a mark on every counted thing, the mess cannot fool you — the clean ones are exactly the ones still waiting.
Add one more toy and the count does not start over — it simply says the NEXT number. One more than five is six, always.
This is why the counting song matters: each number is exactly one more than the number before it.
A group can grow one toy at a time, and the count grows with it: six, seven, eight — counting ON from where it stood.
Counting on is the fast counter's habit: never start over when you already know where the count stands.
“One more” also compares: if Ben has one more grape than Ana's six, Ben has seven — the very next number.
Pairing the groups one to one shows it: every grape of Ana's matches one of Ben's, and Ben has a single grape left over.
Counting out reverses the game: instead of asking how many, you remove exactly the number asked for — and STOP when the count says so.
The pile's total does not matter. Seven crayons means the count stops at seven, however many remain behind.
Some amounts need no counting at all: a quick look at two dots, or a dice-style four, and the mind names it instantly.
That instant naming is a skill — the eye learns the shapes small numbers make, the way it learns faces.
The ten-frame gives EVERY amount a shape: a full row is five at a glance, so seven reads as five-and-two with no counting.
That is the frame's whole purpose — it turns any number up to ten into a picture the mind can name quickly.

An equation like y = x + 1 draws a line — every point ON it makes the two sides equal. But the line does more: it cuts the whole plane into two halves. Every point not on the line lives on one side or the other, and which side it's on is a fact you can COMPUTE.
So the test is arithmetic, not eyesight: at the point's x, compute the line's y. If the point's y is bigger, it's above; smaller, below; equal, on. Three outcomes, one subtraction.

An inequality like y > 2x − 1 doesn't pick a line — it picks a SIDE. Its solutions are every point whose coordinates make the statement true: a whole half-plane of them. To find which side, you don't need theory. Pick any point not on the boundary and ask it.

Why one witness suffices: crossing the boundary flips the comparison, and NOT crossing it can't. All points on one side vote the same way. So a single test point speaks for its whole side — choose (0, 0) whenever the boundary misses it, because zeros make the arithmetic trivial.

Two inequalities can shade the same side and still disagree — about the boundary itself. y > x + 1 excludes the line: points ON it make the sides equal, and 'equal' isn't 'greater.' y ≥ x + 1 welcomes them. Graphs record the difference in the line's own body: dashed for excluded, solid for included.

Read the symbol, draw the line: > and < mean dashed (the boundary is a fence you can't stand on); ≥ and ≤ mean solid (the fence is part of the yard). The shaded side is decided separately, by the point test — symbol style and side are two independent decisions.

A SYSTEM of inequalities demands both at once: y > x AND y < 4 keeps only points that pass both tests. Each inequality shades a half-plane; the system's solution is where the shadings overlap. Think of two fences — the region is the strip the fences trap between them.

One failed test disqualifies. (5, 2) satisfies y < 4 easily, but 2 > 5 is false — so it's out, no partial credit. When a point fails, it helps to name WHICH fence it hit: that's the difference between being below the strip and being above it.

Where two boundary lines cross, the region gets a CORNER — a vertex. Corners are found by algebra, not squinting: the crossing of y = x and y = 4 is the point satisfying both equations at once. Corners matter because they're where regions are sharpest — and, soon, where best answers hide.

Different pairs, same machine. x + y = 6 crossing y = 2: substitute the known y to get x + 2 = 6, so x = 4 — corner (4, 2). Every corner of every region falls to substitution or elimination, the tools you already own from systems of equations.

Real regions wear several fences: x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0, x + y ≤ 6 is three demands stacked. Membership is still a checklist — run the point through every inequality, and one failure evicts it. The skill is bookkeeping: test each fence, record each verdict, then combine.

When a point fails, say where. (4, 4) passes both sign fences but breaks the cap: 8 > 6. (−1, 2) breaks x ≥ 0 before the cap is even consulted. Diagnosing the broken fence is what lets you FIX a plan, not just reject it.

Rename the picture: in a planning problem, the inequalities are CONSTRAINTS — limits on time, money, materials — and the region they trap is the FEASIBLE region: every plan you could actually run. Nothing new mathematically; the fences just started meaning something.

The feasible region's SHAPE comes from its boundaries: here x = 0, y = 0, and x + y = 6 cut a triangle with corners (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 6). You already know how to find those corners — solve boundary pairs. The corners are about to earn their keep.

Plans differ in value. If profit is P = 2x + y, every feasible point has a score — and we want the highest. Here's the gift: on a straight-fenced region, the maximum of a linear objective always lands ON A CORNER. So don't search the infinite interior; interview the two or three corners.

So the algorithm is short: find the corners (boundary pairs), score each with the objective, keep the best. Different objectives crown different corners — P = x + 3y on the same triangle pays (0, 6) eighteen, dethroning (6, 0). The region sets the menu; the objective picks the meal.

The whole pipeline on one problem. A stall sells trays of cookies (x) and pans of brownies (y). Oven space: cookies take 1 slot, brownies 2, and 8 slots exist: x + 2y ≤ 8. Cookie dough limits x ≤ 4. And x, y ≥ 0. Profit: $3 per tray, $4 per pan.

Now the interview. P = 3x + 4y at each vertex: (0,0) → 0; (4,0) → 12; (4,2) → 12 + 8 = 20; (0,4) → 16. The mixed plan wins — four trays, two pans, twenty dollars. Neither all-in plan beats using BOTH resources fully.
Each rectangle has the same width, h = (b − a)/n. Only its HEIGHT is a choice — and the rule you pick just says where in the strip that height is measured. Left edge, right edge, or middle.

You can find the area of a rectangle. You cannot find the area under a curve — so **cover the curve in rectangles** and add them up.

The answer will be wrong. That is fine: the question is not whether it is wrong but **how** it is wrong, and whether the error can be made as small as you like.

The rules differ only in **where each rectangle takes its height**:

**Left** — the left edge. Undershoots a rising curve.
**Right** — the right edge. Overshoots it.
**Midpoint** — the middle. Usually far better than either.
**Trapezoid** — join the two edges with a slanted top, which is the average of left and right.

The two sums are walls. The true area is between them, and it cannot escape. Raise n and the walls move toward each other — never past the truth, always toward it. Whatever is left when they meet IS the area.

Here is the move that makes calculus possible.

On a rising curve, the left sum is **too small** and the right sum is **too big**. So the true area is caught between them:

**left sum ≤ true area ≤ right sum**

And the gap between the two is [f(b) − f(a)]·h — which shrinks to nothing as n grows. The trap closes.

So the definite integral is **defined** as the number the trap closes on:

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = limit of the Riemann sums as n → ∞.

The elongated S is a stretched-out sum. The dx is the width of a strip that has shrunk to nothing. Every part of the notation is a fossil of the rectangles.
Three facts, and all three come straight from the rectangles. Zero width gives zero area. Sweeping backwards makes every width negative. And two adjacent piles of strips are one bigger pile.

∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is not a formula. It is the **number the trap closes on** — the limit of the Riemann sums.

Three properties fall straight out of the rectangles:

∫ₐᵃ f = 0 (no width, no area).
∫ₐᵇ f = −∫ᵦᵃ f (running backwards flips the sign of every dx).
∫ₐᶜ f + ∫꜀ᵇ f = ∫ₐᵇ f (the strips just join up).

And the integral is **signed**. Where f dips below the axis, the heights are negative — so those strips contribute negative area.

∫ₐᵇ f is not 'the area'. It is the area above the axis **minus** the area below it. If you want the geometric area, you must integrate |f|.
A(x) answers one question: **how much area have I swept out so far?** Move the endpoint and you get a different answer, which is exactly what makes A a function of x.

So far the area has been one fixed number: from a to b.

Now let the far end **move**. Define

**A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt** — the area so far, up to x.

A is a brand-new function, built out of f by sweeping. Feed it an x and it hands you back an area.

The letter inside the integral does not matter.

∫₀ˣ 2t dt and ∫₀ˣ 2u du are the same number. **t is a dummy variable** — it runs across the interval and disappears.

But x, the upper limit, is real. It survives, and it is what A depends on. Writing ∫₀ˣ 2x dx is a genuine error: the x cannot be both the sweeping variable and the endpoint.
Ask only one question at each x: **is area being added, or taken away?** Above the axis, added — A climbs. Below it, taken away — A falls. On the axis, neither — A holds still.

You can describe the accumulation without computing a single area, because the **sign of f decides what A does**:

**f > 0** → A is rising (area is piling on).
**f = 0** → A is momentarily flat (nothing is being added).
**f < 0** → A is falling (area is being subtracted).

If that list sounds familiar, it should. It is the list from `dr-01-02`, with f′ replaced by f.

So the whole shape of A is dictated by f, with no arithmetic at all:

f positive and large → A steeply rising.
f positive and small → A rising gently.
f zero → A flat.
f negative → A falling.

This is the same reading you did in C1 — only now f is playing the part that f′ played then.

Multiply the units. The height of a strip is a RATE — something per something. The width is that something. Multiply and the 'per' cancels, leaving a TOTAL. That cancellation is the entire meaning of the integral.

If f is a **rate**, then the area under it is a **total**.

Velocity (miles per hour) × time (hours) = miles. That is exactly what a strip computes: height × width. Add the strips and you have the total distance.

**∫ₐᵇ (rate) dt = the total change over [a, b].** This is the single most useful sentence in the course.

The pattern is everywhere, and it is always the same shape:

Integrate a **flow rate** → get a **volume**.
Integrate a **birth rate** → get a **population change**.
Integrate a **current** → get a **charge**.
Integrate **marginal cost** → get a **total cost**.

Each one is height × width, summed. Nothing new is happening.
Push the endpoint forward by h and you gain a thin sliver of area — nearly a rectangle, width h and height f(x). So the area grows at the RATE f(x). That is all the theorem says: **A′ = f**.

Push the accumulation forward a hair. From x to x + h you gain a sliver of area — and that sliver is very nearly a rectangle of width h and height f(x).

So A(x + h) − A(x) ≈ f(x)·h. Divide by h and let h → 0:

**A′(x) = f(x).**

Differentiation and integration are inverse operations. That is the Fundamental Theorem, and it is why they are taught together.

With the chain rule, the upper limit can be anything:

**d/dx[∫ₐ^(g(x)) f(t) dt] = f(g(x))·g′(x)**

The accumulation is being swept at a rate g′(x), so the area piles up that much faster. It is the gears again.
Two steps. **One:** find any F with F′ = f — undo the derivative. **Two:** compute F(b) − F(a). The commonest error in the entire chapter is doing step one and forgetting to subtract the lower limit.

Part 1 said A′ = f, so A is **an antiderivative** of f.

But A(x) = ∫ₐˣ f is the area from a, so A(a) = 0 and A(b) = the area you want. And any other antiderivative F differs from A only by a constant — which cancels in a subtraction. Hence:

**∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) − F(a)**, for ANY antiderivative F of f.

No rectangles. No limits. Just: undo the derivative, and subtract.

So the antiderivative is the whole game, and you already have it.

Every derivative rule from C1 runs backwards. **Raise the power by one, then divide by the new power** — that is the power rule reversed, and it is the only antiderivative you need for the rest of this lesson.

Always check by differentiating your answer. It costs ten seconds and catches almost every error.
Ask what you are being asked to DO. Differentiating an accumulation? That is Part 1, and the answer is the integrand. Computing a definite value? That is Part 2: antiderivative, then subtract.

Part 1: **differentiating an accumulation gives back the function.** (A′ = f)
Part 2: **the accumulation can be computed from any antiderivative.** (∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) − F(a))

These are not two facts. They are one fact, read in two directions: **differentiation and integration are inverse operations.** Part 2 is what you get by taking Part 1 seriously.

And now the two courses are one course.

Every derivative rule you learned in C1 is now an **antiderivative rule**, read backwards. The power rule reversed gives xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1). The chain rule reversed is about to give you substitution.

Differentiation was never a separate subject. It was the other half of this one.

Two moves, and then a check. **Raise** the exponent by one. **Divide** by the new exponent. Then **differentiate your answer** — if it does not give back what you started with, you have made an error and you will know instantly.

Differentiation drops the exponent in front and lowers the power. So **run it backwards**: raise the power, then divide by the new power.

∫ xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C, for n ≠ −1.

And check by differentiating. It takes ten seconds and catches nearly every error.

Why the **+ C**?

Because a constant has zero slope, x⁴/4 and x⁴/4 + 7 have the *same* derivative. Antidifferentiating cannot recover information the derivative destroyed.

So an indefinite integral is a whole **family** of parallel curves. For a definite integral, C cancels in the subtraction and you may ignore it.
Three steps. **Integrate**, keeping the + C. **Substitute** the given point. **Solve** for C. Only then answer the question that was actually asked.

∫ 2x dx = x² + C is a **family**: a stack of identical parabolas, one for every C.

They all have the same slope at every x — which is exactly why the derivative could not tell them apart. To choose one, you need a single extra fact: **one point the curve passes through.**

That fact is called an *initial condition*, and it pins C.

That is the shape of every problem in the next course:

**A rate + a starting value = the whole story.**

The rate gives the shape (the antiderivative). The starting value gives the height (the constant). Neither one alone is enough, and together they are always enough.

You are not learning new facts — you are reading old ones backwards. Take each derivative rule from C1, swap the sides, and add a + C. The only one that bites is sin, because its antiderivative carries a minus.

Every derivative from C1 is now an antiderivative, read backwards:

∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C
∫ (1/x) dx = ln|x| + C
∫ cos x dx = sin x + C
∫ sin x dx = **−**cos x + C

The minus on the last one is where nearly every error lives. Check by differentiating: (−cos x)′ = +sin x ✓.

With the chain rule running backwards, each library entry gains a partner:

∫ e^(kx) dx = e^(kx)/k + C
∫ cos(kx) dx = sin(kx)/k + C

The **division by k** is the price of the inner derivative. Differentiating would have MULTIPLIED by k, so antidifferentiating must divide by it.

That single observation is the whole of the next chapter, in embryo.

Look for an **inside function** and its **derivative**, sitting together. Name the inside u, write du = u′ dx, and swap everything over. If a piece of x is left over that is not a constant, the substitution was the wrong one.

The chain rule left a fingerprint: **the derivative of the inside, multiplied on the outside.**

So when an integrand contains an inside function AND its derivative, you are looking at the output of a chain rule — and you can run it backwards.

Call the inside **u**. Then du = u′ dx, and the whole integral collapses into ∫ (something in u) du.

If the inner derivative is present but with the **wrong constant**, fix it with a constant — never with an x.

∫ x(x² + 1)³ dx has an x where a 2x is wanted. Write du = 2x dx, so x dx = du/2, and the ½ comes out front.

Constants may be moved across the integral sign. **Variables may not.** That single rule keeps substitution honest.

The moment you write du, the integral lives in u — so its limits must be u-values. Compute u at the old lower limit and u at the old upper limit, and write those instead. Mixing the two worlds gives a tidy answer that is simply wrong.

A definite integral carries limits, and the limits are values of **x**. Change variable to u and they must change too.

∫ₓ₌ₐ^(x=b) → ∫ᵤ₌ᵤ₍ₐ₎^(u=u(b))

Otherwise you would be feeding x-values into a u-integral, which is a category error — and it silently gives the wrong number.

Substitution also handles the plain **linear inside**, which is the commonest case of all:

∫ cos(3x) dx → u = 3x, du = 3 dx → (1/3)∫ cos u du = sin(3x)/3 + C.

That division by 3 is the same division you met at the end of the last lesson. It is the inner derivative, being paid back.

Write down the candidate u, then immediately write du. Now look at the integrand: **does it contain that du, up to a constant?** If yes, substitute. If a bare x is left over, stop — that substitution is the wrong one.

Nothing labels the inside for you. Two questions decide it:

**What is inside something?** (a bracket, a root, an exponent, a denominator)
**Is its derivative also present, up to a constant?**

If both answers are yes, that thing is u. If the second answer is no, substitution will not save you — and in this course, that means the integral is out of reach.

And that is integration, in this course.

You can **define** an integral (the trap, squeezed shut), **interpret** it (a rate integrated gives a total), **compute** it (an antiderivative, evaluated twice), and **transform** it (substitution, the chain rule reversed).

What remains is not new machinery but new uses: areas between curves, volumes, average values. Those are the next course.

Draw a vertical strip through the region. Its top end sits on one curve and its bottom end on the other. **Height = top − bottom.** That height is what you integrate — and nothing else about the problem matters.

One curve gave you the area under it. **Two curves give you the area between them** — and the only thing that changes is the height of a strip.

Each strip runs from the **bottom** curve to the **top** one, so its height is **top − bottom**. Add the strips:

**Area = ∫ₐᵇ (top − bottom) dx**

That is the entire idea, and everything in this course is a variation on it.

Get the order wrong and the integral comes out **negative**. Area cannot be negative — so a negative answer is the integral telling you that you subtracted the wrong way round.

And if the curves **cross inside** the interval, the top and bottom SWAP. Split the integral at the crossing and do each piece separately, or you will silently subtract one region from the other.
One strip, spun about the axis, sweeps out a coin. The coin's RADIUS is the height of the curve, f(x). Its FACE is πr². Its thickness is dx. Add up the coins and you have the solid.

Take the region under a curve and **spin it around the x-axis**. It sweeps out a solid.

Now take one thin strip of that region. What does IT sweep out? A **disc** — a coin of radius f(x) and thickness dx.

Its volume is **πr²·dx = π[f(x)]²·dx**. Add up the coins:

**V = π∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx**

The integral has not changed. Only what you measure on the slice.

Notice how little actually changed.

**Area** — slice, measure the HEIGHT, add: ∫f dx.
**Volume** — slice, measure the DISC, add: ∫πf² dx.

Same slicing. Same summing. The only difference is what you measure on one slice. That single sentence is the whole of this course, and it is worth carrying into every problem you meet.

Two circles, one inside the other. Work out the BIG face, work out the HOLE, and subtract: π R² − π r². Squaring comes first and subtracting comes second — reversing them gives a different (and wrong) number.

Revolve the region **between two curves** and each strip sweeps out not a disc but a **washer** — a coin with a hole punched through it.

Outer radius R = the top curve. Inner radius r = the bottom one. The face is the big circle minus the small one:

**π(R² − r²)**

And once again: slice, measure the slice, add them up. Only the measurement changed.

So the whole course is one sentence, repeated:

**Slice the region. Measure ONE slice. Add them up.**

An area measures a slice's **height**. A disc measures **πr²**. A washer measures **π(R² − r²)**. The slicing never changes; the summing never changes. Only the measurement does — and that is the only thing you ever have to work out.
What shape is standing on the slice, and what is its AREA? Write that in terms of x, then integrate it. The calculus does not care whether the shape is a circle, a square or a triangle — only you do.

A solid does not have to be made by revolving anything. Stand a **square** on every slice of a flat region and you get a solid just as real — and just as easy.

The slice's area is whatever the cross-section's area is. If the side is s = f(x), a square slice is **s²**, and

**V = ∫ₐᵇ [f(x)]² dx.**

And notice: **no π anywhere.** π only appeared because a disc is a circle.

So the recipe is completely general:

**Work out the area of ONE cross-section, in terms of x.** Then integrate it.

Square → s². Equilateral triangle → (√3/4)s². Semicircle → (π/8)s². Circle → πr².

The calculus never notices which. It only ever adds up slices — and the geometry of the slice is your job, not the integral's.
Add up all the heights (that is the integral) and divide by how many there were (that is the width). The result is the height of the flat rectangle holding the same amount.

What is the average height of a curve? You cannot add up infinitely many heights and divide.

But you CAN: add them with an integral, then divide by the width.

**f_avg = (1/(b − a)) ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx**

Geometrically: it is the height of the **rectangle with the same area** as the region. Flatten the curve without spilling anything, and the level you end up at is the average.

So this is the **Mean Value Theorem for Integrals**, and it is the same theorem you already met, one level up.

**C3:** somewhere, the tangent's slope equals the secant's slope.
**Here:** somewhere, the function's value equals its average value.

Both say the same thing: *a continuous quantity must actually attain its own average at some instant.*
Two questions, two integrals. **Where did it end up?** — integrate v, signs and all. **How far did it travel?** — integrate |v|, which means splitting at the sign changes and adding the magnitudes.

In C2 you split a journey into legs by hand, measured each one, and added the lengths as positive numbers. That was hard work.

Here is the machine that does it:

**Displacement = ∫ₐᵇ v dt** — where you ended up.
**Total distance = ∫ₐᵇ |v| dt** — every metre you actually covered.

The absolute value does *exactly* the leg-splitting you did by hand. It was never a different idea; it was the same idea, automated.

So the recipe for total distance is exactly the hand method, written down:

**Find where v = 0 and changes sign.** (the turns)
**Integrate v on each piece.**
**Add the ABSOLUTE VALUES.**

And that is why ∫|v| is not a strange new integral — it is three ordinary integrals with the minus signs stripped off.
'How much longer' is a gap question: line both objects up at the same start and the overhang IS the answer.
The gap you can see equals the difference you can compute — subtracting the shorter from the longer names the overhang.
With several measurements, comparing means ranking: scan every number before naming the longest or the shortest.
The middle numbers are the traps — an item can beat two others and still lose the crown.
A ruler measures by marks: an object from the 3 cm mark to the 11 cm mark is 11 − 3 = 8 cm — the END mark is not the length.
Starting away from zero is fine; the ruler just asks you to subtract the start back out.
Joining lengths end to end ADDS them: a 34 cm piece and a 25 cm piece make one 59 cm stretch.
The joined length has no seams — where one piece stops the next begins, and the far end reads the sum.
A journey's total distance collects every leg: add them one at a time and let the running total walk with you.
Three legs of 34, 21, and 20 meters total 75 — staged exactly like any long sum, because that is what it is.
A missing length hides inside a whole: whole minus the known part reveals it, because the parts must rebuild the whole.
If the trail is 75 m and the first stretch is 40, the rest can only be 35 — nothing else re-assembles to 75.
A bar drawing turns a length story into geometry: one bar per quantity, aligned starts, and the picture asks its own question.
Equal ends say 'these match'; a gap says 'find me'; stacked bars say 'add us' — the drawing does the translating.
The number line is a ruler that never ends: lengths become jumps from zero, joins chain forward, and differences appear as gaps.
Everything from the number-line course carries over — length was the line's first job all along.
Some stories take two steps: ribbon is used AND bought, trail is walked AND backtracked. Handle one step at a time and carry the total between them.
'Had 60, used 25, bought 30' is 60 − 25 + 30 — two moves, one running answer.
Before trusting an answer, test it against the story: totals must outgrow their parts, gaps must fit inside the longer piece, and ruler spans cannot beat their end marks.
Sense-checking costs seconds and catches the classic slips — added marks, skipped legs, reversed steps — before they ever leave your page.

A **limit** asks a simple question: as x gets closer and closer to some value, what does f(x) head toward? We write lim(x→a) f(x) = L. The key idea is **approach** — we care where the function is GOING near a, not necessarily its value AT a.

Crucially, the limit can exist even where the function has a **hole**. For f(x) = (x² − 4)/(x − 2), plugging in x = 2 gives 0/0 — undefined. But everywhere else f(x) = x + 2, so as x → 2 the outputs approach 4. The limit is 4 even though f(2) doesn't exist.

A **numerical table** estimates a limit: evaluate f at x-values creeping toward a from both sides and watch the outputs settle. If both columns close in on the same number, that's the limit. Tables are how you probe a limit you can't yet solve by algebra.

On a **graph**, trace the curve toward x = a with your finger from each side. The limit is the y-height both fingers approach — even if there's an open circle (hole) there. A filled dot ON the curve gives the function's value; the limit is about the trend leading INTO the point.

A limit **fails to exist** when the two sides disagree. If f approaches one value from the left and a DIFFERENT value from the right, there's no single number it heads toward — the limit does not exist (DNE). This is the story at a **jump**.

Two more ways limits fail: **unbounded** behavior (f shoots to +∞ or −∞ near a, as with 1/x² at 0) and wild **oscillation** that never settles. In each case there's no single finite value the function approaches, so the limit does not exist.

For most functions the limit is easy: if f is **continuous** at a (no hole, jump, or blow-up), then lim(x→a) f(x) = f(a). Just **substitute**. Polynomials are continuous everywhere, so lim(x→2)(3x + 1) = 3(2) + 1 = 7. Substitution is always the first thing to try.

The **limit laws** let you break a complicated limit into pieces:

lim(f + g) = lim f + lim g,  lim(f·g) = (lim f)(lim g),  lim(f/g) = lim f / lim g (if lim g ≠ 0).

Limits of sums, products, and quotients are the sums, products, and quotients of the limits — algebra distributes cleanly across the limit.

When substitution gives **0/0**, that's the **indeterminate form** — it doesn't mean the limit is 0 or undefined; it means 'more work needed.' The fix for rational functions: **factor** the numerator and denominator, **cancel** the shared factor causing the 0/0, then substitute into what remains.

Why cancelling is legal: for a limit, x approaches 2 but never EQUALS 2, so x − 2 ≠ 0 the whole time and dividing it out is valid. The cancelled expression matches the original everywhere near 2 — exactly where the limit lives. The removed factor was just the hole.

When a **square root** causes the 0/0, factoring won't help — but **multiplying by the conjugate** does. For (√(x + 4) − 2)/x, multiply top and bottom by (√(x + 4) + 2). The numerator becomes a difference of squares, (x + 4) − 4 = x, which cancels the x below.

The trick works because (√A − B)(√A + B) = A − B² erases the root. That difference-of-squares in the numerator cancels the troublesome factor in the denominator, converting an indeterminate 0/0 into something you can finally substitute into.

Sometimes a function behaves differently on each side of a. A **one-sided limit** looks at just one direction: lim(x→a⁻) approaches from the LEFT (smaller x), lim(x→a⁺) from the RIGHT. The two-sided limit exists **only if both one-sided limits agree**.

When the two one-sided limits DO agree, the two-sided limit exists and equals their shared value. This is the precise rule: **lim(x→a) exists ⟺ lim(x→a⁻) = lim(x→a⁺)**. One-sided limits are the building blocks that decide whether the full limit lives.

A **limit at infinity** asks where f(x) heads as x grows without bound. For a rational function, compare the **degrees** of top and bottom. When they're **equal**, the limit is the ratio of leading coefficients — and that value is the **horizontal asymptote** (recall pra). The end behavior IS a limit.

The degree comparison has three cases:
• **top degree < bottom degree** → limit **0** (asymptote y = 0),
• **degrees equal** → ratio of leading coefficients,
• **top degree > bottom degree** → **±∞** (no horizontal asymptote; it grows without bound).

When the numerator's degree is **larger**, the fraction grows without bound: lim(x→∞) = +∞ or −∞, and there's **no horizontal asymptote**. The top overwhelms the bottom. Intuitively, the fastest-growing term wins the tug-of-war as x races off.

So the full menu, as x → ∞ for a rational function: a **horizontal asymptote** (degrees equal or top smaller) OR **unbounded growth** to ±∞ (top larger). The single tool — compare degrees, then leading coefficients — settles every case at both +∞ and −∞.

A function is **continuous at x = a** if you can draw through that point without lifting your pen. Precisely, three things must ALL hold: (1) f(a) is defined, (2) the limit lim_{x→a} f(x) exists, and (3) they're **equal**: lim_{x→a} f(x) = f(a). Break any one and continuity fails.

For 'nice' functions — polynomials, and rational/root/trig functions where they're defined — continuity is automatic, so the limit is just **f(a)** by direct substitution (recall Ch2). Continuity is what MAKES substitution legal. The interesting points are exactly where one of the three conditions breaks.

Discontinuities come in three flavors. A **removable** discontinuity is a single hole — the limit exists, but f(a) is missing or misplaced; you could 'fill it in.' A **jump** has the left and right limits disagree. An **infinite** discontinuity has the function blowing up to ±∞ (a vertical asymptote).

A **jump** occurs when the one-sided limits exist but differ (recall Ch3): the graph leaps from one height to another, so no single limit exists. Common in piecewise functions and step functions — think of a price that jumps at a threshold.

The **Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)**: if f is continuous on [a, b] and N is any value between f(a) and f(b), then f hits N somewhere in between — there's a c in (a, b) with f(c) = N. Continuity means the graph can't skip a value; it must pass through everything on the way.

The most common use is **root-finding**: if a continuous f changes sign on [a, b] — that is, f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs — then f must cross zero, so a root lives in (a, b). A sign change is a guarantee of a solution, even without solving.

The **average rate of change** of f over [a, b] is the slope of the **secant line** joining (a, f(a)) and (b, f(b)):

(f(b) − f(a)) / (b − a).

It's the familiar rise-over-run (recall slope), now measuring how fast f changes on average across an interval — like average speed over a trip.

Notice the average rate DEPENDS on the interval: x² averaged 4 on [1, 3] but 7 on [2, 5] — steeper further right. A secant only reports the overall change between two points; it can't tell you the rate at a single instant. That gap is what the next lesson closes.

Let the step h shrink to zero. The secant pivots into the **tangent line**, and the difference quotient's LIMIT is the **instantaneous rate of change** — the **derivative**:

f′(a) = lim_{h→0} (f(a + h) − f(a)) / h.

This is the whole course's payoff: a single-point slope, defined by a limit.

The derivative reads as an **instantaneous** rate: the exact speed at one instant, the tangent's steepness at one point. Average rate needed two points; the derivative needs a limit to capture just one. This limit — the same tool from all of Chapter 1 — is the gateway to calculus.

One idea has run through this whole course — the **limit** — and it reaches beyond derivatives. An **infinite sum** is itself a limit: the value of the **partial sums** as you add more and more terms. Adding forever is really asking, 'what limit do the running totals approach?'

This is exactly the infinite geometric series from earlier (recall the sum a/(1 − r) for |r| < 1). What that formula computes IS a limit of partial sums. For 1/2 + 1/4 + ⋯: a = 1/2, r = 1/2, so a/(1 − r) = (1/2)/(1/2) = 1 — the same 1 the totals crept toward.
An equation is a **balance**: the two sides are equal, and any move you make must be done to BOTH sides to keep them equal. To solve, undo the operations around x one at a time until x stands alone.
Undo in REVERSE order: the last thing done to x is undone first. In 4x + 8, x was multiplied by 4, then 8 was added — so subtract 8 first, then divide by 4. Each undo peels one layer.
When x sits on BOTH sides, like 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, first collect the x-terms on one side. Take 3x off both sides — the balance stays level — leaving 2x + 2 = 10. Then solve as usual.
Subtract the SMALLER x-term to keep the coefficient positive. For 7x + 3 = 4x + 15, take 4x from both sides, giving 3x + 3 = 15 — easier than ending up with a negative x-term.

Clear parentheses FIRST using the distributive property: 3(x + 4) means the 3 multiplies BOTH parts, giving 3x + 12. Then solve the equation that remains. The 3 reaches every term inside the parentheses.
The classic slip is distributing to only the FIRST term: 3(x + 4) is NOT 3x + 4 — it's 3x + 12. The 3 must hit the 4 as well. Miss this and every later step is off.
Not every equation has an answer. When you solve and the variable DISAPPEARS, leaving a FALSE statement like 3 = 5, the equation has NO solution — no value of x could ever make it true.
This happens when both sides have the SAME x-coefficient but DIFFERENT constants — like two parallel lines that never meet. The x-terms cancel, and the leftover numbers can't be equal.
The opposite case: when the variable cancels and leaves a TRUE statement like 3 = 3, EVERY value of x works — there are INFINITELY MANY solutions. Both sides are secretly the same expression.
This happens when both sides are the SAME after simplifying — same x-coefficient AND same constant. It's like two lines drawn exactly on top of each other: they share every point.

Any linear equation falls into exactly three cases. Simplify both sides, then look: if x survives with a real value, ONE solution; if x cancels leaving a true statement, INFINITELY MANY; if x cancels leaving a false statement, NONE.

A quick shortcut: compare the simplified x-coefficients. DIFFERENT coefficients always give one solution (the lines cross). SAME coefficients give either none or infinitely many, decided by whether the constants match.

A **system** is two equations you solve at the same time. Its **solution** is the single point (x, y) that makes BOTH equations true at once — not just one of them. It's the point the two lines share.
To CHECK a proposed solution, substitute it into BOTH equations. The point counts only if it makes every equation true. A point on just one line is not a solution of the system.
To solve a system BY GRAPHING: draw each line (start at its y-intercept, then step by its slope), and read off where they CROSS. That crossing point is the solution — the (x, y) that works in both.
You can also find the crossing without a perfect graph: set the two expressions for y EQUAL. For y = 2x and y = x + 3, solve 2x = x + 3 → x = 3, then y = 2(3) = 6. The crossing is (3, 6).
Just like single equations, systems have three cases — and you can tell WHICH before solving by comparing the lines. DIFFERENT slopes → the lines cross → ONE solution. Same slope needs a closer look.

When the slopes are EQUAL, the lines are parallel. If their y-intercepts DIFFER, they never meet — NO solution. If the y-intercepts are the SAME too, they're the same line — INFINITELY many solutions.

Graphing is slow and imprecise. **Substitution** is exact. When one equation already says y = (something), replace y in the OTHER equation with that expression — now there's just one variable to solve.
Worked all the way: y = 2x − 1 and 3x + y = 9. Substitute: 3x + (2x − 1) = 9 → 5x − 1 = 9 → 5x = 10 → x = 2. One variable, solved exactly — no graph needed.
Substitution gives you x — but a system's solution is a POINT (x, y). To find y, **back-substitute**: plug your x back into the isolated equation (the easy y = one). Then the full solution is (x, y).

Always back-substitute into the ISOLATED equation — it's already solved for y, so it's the easy one. Then CONFIRM the point in both equations to be sure. For x = 2 in y = 3x: y = 6, and (2, 6) checks in both.

Real problems often hide a system. When two quantities are related two different ways — like a total AND a difference — write one equation for each, then solve with substitution. Two facts, two equations, one solution.
Once you have one unknown, back-substitute for the other, then answer the actual question. For x = 2 in y = 4x, the larger number is y = 8 — and 2 + 8 = 10 ✓, 8 = 4(2) ✓. Both facts check out.

Slope measures a line's **steepness** as **rise ÷ run**: how far it climbs (rise) for how far it moves across (run). A gentle ramp has a small slope; a steep stair has a large one. Count the rise, count the run, and divide.

Slope is a **rate of change**: it says how much y changes each time x increases by 1. A slope of 3 means y climbs 3 for every 1 step right. That steady rate is exactly what makes the graph a straight line.
The **bigger** the slope, the **steeper** the climb. Slope 5 rises five units per step across; slope 2 rises only two. Same run, more rise means a steeper line.

Given two points, you don't need a grid to find slope. The **rise** is the change in y, and the **run** is the change in x. So slope = **(y₂ − y₁) ÷ (x₂ − x₁)**. Subtract the y's on top, the matching x's on the bottom, and divide.
**Keep the order matched.** If you start with the second point's y on top, start with the second point's x on the bottom too. Mixing the orders flips the sign and gives the wrong slope.
A slope can be a **fraction**. If a line rises 2 over a run of 3, its slope is 2/3 — a real, valid slope, just shallower than 1. Leave it as a reduced fraction; don't round it away.

Read the slope's **sign** from the line's direction. Going **uphill** left to right — y rising as x grows — gives a **positive** slope. Going **downhill** — y falling as x grows — gives a **negative** slope.
A **horizontal** line never rises: the y-values stay equal, so the rise is 0 and the slope is **0 ÷ run = 0**. Flat means a slope of zero — not 'no slope'.
A **vertical** line never runs: the x-values stay equal, so the run is 0. Dividing by 0 is impossible, so a vertical line's slope is **undefined** — a different thing from zero.

Most lines can be written in one tidy form: **y = mx + b**. The **m** is the **slope** — the number multiplied by x. The **b** is the **y-intercept** — the number added on, where the line crosses the y-axis. Read a line's equation and you already know how steep it is and where it starts.
Why is b the y-intercept? Set **x = 0**. Then y = m·0 + b = b. Every line hits the y-axis at x = 0, so the y-value there is always b. That's why b tells you where the line starts on the y-axis.

Both m and b can be **negative** or **fractional**. In y = (1/2)x - 3, the slope is the fraction 1/2 and the y-intercept is -3. Read the coefficient of x for m, and the constant (with its sign) for b.

You can graph **y = mx + b** without a table. **Step 1:** plot b on the y-axis — that's the point (0, b), where the line starts. **Step 2:** from there, use the slope as **rise over run** to step to the next point. **Step 3:** connect them into a line.

The slope is your **step**. Slope 2 means **up 2, right 1**. Slope 1/3 means **up 1, right 3**. From the y-intercept, take that step to land on a second point — then a third. Same step each time keeps you on the line.
A **negative** slope steps **down**. For y = -x + 6, start at (0, 6), then go down 1, right 1 to each next point. Positive slopes climb left-to-right; negative slopes descend.

A slanted line crosses **both** axes. The **y-intercept** is where it crosses the y-axis — there **x = 0**, and the height is b. The **x-intercept** is where it crosses the x-axis — there **y = 0**. Two crossings, two different questions.
To find the **x-intercept**, set **y = 0** and solve for x. Take y = 2x - 8. Set 0 = 2x - 8, add 8 to get 2x = 8, divide by 2 to get x = 4. So the line crosses the x-axis at (4, 0).
You can also **build** a line's equation. Put the slope m in front of x, and the y-intercept b at the end. Slope 3 and intercept -2 give **y = 3x - 2**. Slope first, intercept last.

There's a form built for **one point and a slope**: **y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)**. Here (x₁, y₁) is a point the line passes through, and m is the slope. Know a point and a slope, and you can write the line straight away — the point's numbers slot into the blanks.
**Building it:** copy the point in with the same subtractions the form shows. A point (2, 5) with slope 3 becomes **y − 5 = 3(x − 2)**. The 5 and 2 are the point; the 3 is the slope out front.
So watch the inside signs. **y + 2** is really y − (−2), so **y₁ = −2**. **x + 3** is x − (−3), so **x₁ = −3**. A plus sign inside the form is hiding a negative coordinate.

Point-slope and y = mx + b describe the **same line** in different clothes. To convert, **distribute** the slope, then **add y₁** to both sides. The slope m never changes; only the constant becomes b. Shortcut: **b = y₁ − m·x₁**.
The shortcut in action: for y − 5 = 2(x − 1), the slope stays 2 and **b = 5 − 2·1 = 3**. So the slope-intercept form is **y = 2x + 3** — no distributing needed once you trust the formula.
You can go **backward** too. Given y = mx + b and any point the line passes through, write y − y₁ = m(x − x₁) with that point. The y-intercept point (0, b) always works, but any known point does.

A third way to write a line is **standard form: Ax + By = C**, with A, B, C whole numbers and A not negative. Both variables sit on the left. It hides the slope, but it makes the **intercepts** especially quick to find.

The trick: to find an intercept, **zero the other variable**. Set y = 0 for the x-intercept (x = C/A); set x = 0 for the y-intercept (y = C/B). For 3x + 2y = 12: x-intercept 12/3 = 4, y-intercept 12/2 = 6.

To convert **y = mx + b into standard form**, move the x-term left and make A positive. From y = 2x − 5: subtract 2x → −2x + y = −5, then multiply by −1 → **2x − y = 5**. Clear any fractions so A, B, C are whole numbers.

Give me one point and a slope, and I can write the whole line. The slope you're handed is already **m**. The only missing piece is **b**, and you get it from **b = y₁ − m·x₁**. Then write **y = mx + b**.
b can come out negative. For (2, 3) with slope 4: **b = 3 − 4·2 = −5**, so the line is **y = 4x − 5**. Check it — 4·2 − 5 = 3, which is the point's height. The point always lands back on the line.
One special case: **slope 0** makes a **horizontal line**. Then b = y₁ − 0 = y₁, so the line is simply **y = y₁**. A line through (2, 5) with slope 0 is just **y = 5** — the same height everywhere.
Two points also fix a line. Work in order: first the **slope**, m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁). Then use **either point** to get b = y₁ − m·x₁. Then write **y = mx + b**, and confirm both points fit.
Full example with (1, 1) and (4, 10): slope = (10 − 1)/(4 − 1) = **9/3 = 3**; then b = 1 − 3·1 = **−2**; so **y = 3x − 2**. Check the other point: 3·4 − 2 = 10. Both fit — the line is right.

Watch for a **vertical line**: if the two points share the same x, the run is 0 and the slope is **undefined** — you can't divide by zero. The line is just **x = that value**, e.g. (3, 1) and (3, 6) give **x = 3**.

Slope decides how two lines relate. **Parallel** lines never meet — they have the **same slope**. **Perpendicular** lines cross at a right angle — their slopes are **negative reciprocals** (flip the fraction, change the sign), so **m₁·m₂ = −1**.

"Negative reciprocal" is two moves: **flip**, then **change the sign**. Slope 2 → flip to 1/2 → negate → **−1/2**. It works both ways: slope −1/2 → flip to −2 → negate → **2**. The product is always −1.

To **write** a parallel or perpendicular line through a point: pick the right slope (same for parallel, negative reciprocal for perpendicular), then find **b = y₁ − m·x₁** exactly as before. The point and the new slope give the full equation.

Four building blocks of geometry. A **point** is an exact location — no size, just a spot, named with a capital letter. A **line** stretches forever in both directions. A **line segment** is a piece of a line with two definite endpoints. A **ray** starts at one point and shoots forever in a single direction.
The endpoint count is the whole trick: **0 endpoints = line, 1 endpoint = ray, 2 endpoints = line segment.** Every shape's edge, every fence line, every beam of light fits one of these three.

You already measured angles in degrees. Now name their parts: an angle forms where two rays share a starting point, called the **vertex.** The two rays themselves are the angle's **sides.** Every angle you measured was really two rays meeting at a vertex.

Angles get precise names using three points: one on each ray, with the **vertex always in the middle.** Angle ABC means a ray toward A, the vertex at B, and a ray toward C. Swap the outer letters and it's still the same angle — but the vertex letter never moves from the middle.

Real figures mix every term you've learned: points, rays, angles, all at once. Reading one means checking each piece against what you know — how many endpoints, is there a shared vertex, what's the angle's name.
A figure can hide several angles at once. If three rays share vertex P, going toward Q, R, and S, that's actually THREE separate angles: QPR, RPS, and QPS (the two smaller ones combined).

**Parallel lines** stay exactly the same distance apart, forever — no matter how far you extend them, they never touch. Railroad tracks are the classic example: the two rails never get closer or farther apart, and never cross.

Diagrams mark parallel lines with matching arrow symbols — a single arrowhead (›) on each line in one parallel pair, double arrowheads (››) on a different pair. The matching arrows tell you which lines belong together.

**Perpendicular lines** cross at exactly 90° — a right angle, the same benchmark from Course 9. Diagrams mark the crossing with a small square symbol, not an arrow. A plus sign (+) is the classic perpendicular shape.

The word **'exactly'** matters, just like Course 9's angle boundaries. Two lines crossing at 89° are close, but not perpendicular — only a true 90° crossing counts. 'Almost perpendicular' isn't a real category.

Real figures often hide BOTH relationships at once. A rectangle's **opposite sides are parallel** (top-bottom, left-right); its **adjacent sides are perpendicular** (each corner is a 90° crossing). One shape, two relationships.

A tic-tac-toe grid hides the same idea at a bigger scale: the 2 horizontal lines are parallel to each other, the 2 vertical lines are parallel to each other, and every horizontal-vertical crossing is perpendicular.

A triangle's **largest angle** names its family, reusing the acute/right/obtuse vocabulary you already know. **Acute triangle:** every angle under 90°. **Right triangle:** one angle exactly 90°. **Obtuse triangle:** one angle over 90°.

A triangle can have **at most one** angle of 90° or more. Why? All three angles must add to 180° — if two angles were each 90° or more, they alone would total 180° or beyond, leaving nothing (or less) for the third.

Every triangle, no matter its shape, has three angles that add up to exactly **180°** — the same total as angles on a straight line. Tear off a triangle's three corners and line them up, and they form a straight line.
This works for **every** triangle — tiny or huge, acute, right, or obtuse. The 180° total never changes, even though the individual angles can be almost anything, as long as they add up right.

Remember shapes as members-only clubs with entry rules? A **rectangle's** entry rule is angle-based: **all four angles must be exactly 90°.** A quadrilateral missing that rule — even by one angle — doesn't get into the rectangle club, though it's still a quadrilateral.

A quadrilateral can have **any number** of right angles — zero, one, two, or four (never exactly three, since the fourth would then be forced to also equal 90° by the shape's angle total). Fewer than four just means a different family, not a failed shape.

A shape has a **line of symmetry** if folding along that line makes both halves land exactly on top of each other — like a mirror. A square folded straight down the middle matches perfectly. A random scribbled shape usually doesn't.

Not every line through a shape works. A square has SOME lines that produce a match (straight down the middle, or corner to corner) and infinitely many that don't (any random slanted line off-center). Only the special ones count as symmetry lines.

A **regular shape** (every side and angle equal) has exactly as many symmetry lines as it has sides. An equilateral triangle: 3 sides, 3 symmetry lines. A square: 4 sides, 4 symmetry lines. A regular pentagon: 5 sides, 5 symmetry lines.

Shapes that AREN'T regular can have fewer symmetry lines. A rectangle (unequal sides) has only **2** — the horizontal and vertical center lines. Its diagonals do NOT produce a match, since folding along one would need the two different side lengths to line up, which they can't.

Symmetry hides in everyday letters too. Using standard block capital letters: **A** has a vertical line of symmetry (left-right mirror). **H** has both a vertical AND a horizontal line. **F** has none at all.

Watch out for a trap: the letter **N** looks like it might have symmetry because spinning it 180° looks the same. But that's **rotational** symmetry (a spin), a completely different idea from **line** symmetry (a fold). No single fold line makes N's two halves match.

You can solve 2^x = 8 by matching bases. But 2^x = 10? No power of 2 matches. Math's answer is a new function: **log₂ 10 means 'the exponent that turns 2 into 10.'** In general: **log_b x = y  ⟺  b^y = x**. A logarithm IS an exponent — nothing more exotic.

Every log statement has a twin exponential statement, and converting between them is the core skill. log₅ 25 = 2 twins with 5² = 25. Going the other way: 3⁴ = 81 twins with log₃ 81 = 4. **Base stays the base; the log's output is the exponent.**

Three instant values every log shares. **log_b 1 = 0** (anything to the 0 is 1). **log_b b = 1** (b¹ = b). And **log_b of a fraction can go negative**: log₂ (1/8) = −3 because 2⁻³ = 1/8. The log's output ranges over ALL real numbers — negatives included.

Two more families. **Base 10** is so common it hides its subscript: log 1000 = 3 (it's log₁₀). And fractional INSIDES pair with negative exponents: log₃ (1/9) = −2 since 3⁻² = 1/9. Fractional ANSWERS appear too: log₉ 3 = 1/2, because 9^(1/2) = √9 = 3 — rational exponents, straight from Radical Functions.

Because log₂ x undoes 2^x, its graph is the exponential's **mirror image across the line y = x** — inputs and outputs trade places. (1, 2) on the exponential becomes (2, 1) on the log. The mirror flips the exponential's horizontal asymptote into a **vertical asymptote at x = 0**.

The swap dictates everything. The exponential's domain (all reals) becomes the log's **range** (all reals); the exponential's range (y > 0) becomes the log's **domain: x > 0**. Zero and negatives have no logarithm — no exponent turns 2 into −4 or into 0. The graph hugs its wall at x = 0, exactly like last course's vertical asymptotes.

Exponent rules become log rules — because logs ARE exponents. Multiplying powers ADDS exponents (2³ · 2⁴ = 2⁷), so logs of products split into sums: **log_b (MN) = log_b M + log_b N**. Check: log₂ (8 · 4) = log₂ 32 = 5, and log₂ 8 + log₂ 4 = 3 + 2 = 5. ✓

The property runs both directions. **Expand:** log₂ (8x) = log₂ 8 + log₂ x = 3 + log₂ x. **Condense:** log 5 + log 20 = log (5 · 20) = log 100 = 2. Condensing often turns ugly pieces into a clean whole — 5 and 20 alone have messy logs; their product doesn't.

Two more exponent rules translate. Division subtracts exponents, so **log_b (M/N) = log_b M − log_b N**. And a power multiplies its exponent, so **log_b (Mᵖ) = p · log_b M** — the exponent inside marches out front. Check: log₂ (8²) = log₂ 64 = 6 = 2 · 3. ✓

The power property is the workhorse of the whole subject: it drags an unknown **down from the exponent**. log₂ (x⁵) = 5 log₂ x — and later, taking log of both sides of 2^x = 10 will pull the x down where algebra can reach it. Special case: roots. log₉ (√9) = log₉ (9^(1/2)) = **1/2**.

**Expanding** unpacks one log into a sum/difference of simple logs — outside-in: quotient first, then products, then powers. **Condensing** reverses it — coefficients become powers FIRST, then sums merge into products and differences into quotients. Two directions, opposite orders.

Order matters when condensing: **coefficients become exponents before anything merges**. 3 log₂ x − log₂ y: first 3 log₂ x = log₂ (x³), then the difference divides: **log₂ (x³/y)**. Merging first (log₂(x/y) then cubing everything) would wrongly cube the y too.

Calculators usually offer only log (base 10) and ln. The **change-of-base formula** unlocks every other base: **log_b x = (log x)/(log b)** — any base upstairs and downstairs, as long as they match. So log₂ 10 = (log 10)/(log 2) = 1/0.301 ≈ **3.32**.

Why does it work? Let y = log_b x, so bʸ = x. Take log (base 10) of both sides: y · log b = log x — the power property drags y down. Divide: y = (log x)/(log b). The formula is just the power property doing equation work — a preview of this whole chapter.

Base-matching solved 2^x = 8. For 2^x = 10, the tool is **take the log of both sides**: log(2^x) = log 10, and the power property pulls x down — x · log 2 = log 10, so x = (log 10)/(log 2) ≈ **3.32**. Notice: that's exactly log₂ 10 by change of base. Same answer, two roads.

Full pipeline with a coefficient: 5 · 2^x = 80. **Isolate the power first** (divide by 5): 2^x = 16 — oh, that one matches bases: x = 4. But 5 · 2^x = 90 → 2^x = 18 → x = (log 18)/(log 2) ≈ 4.17. Isolate, then match if you can, log if you can't.

When the LOG holds the unknown, **convert to exponential form**: log₂(x − 3) = 4 means x − 3 = 2⁴ = 16, so x = **19**. Check in the original: log₂ 16 = 4. ✓ One conversion, then ordinary algebra — the definition from Chapter 1 doing equation work.

Logs on **both sides** with the same base? Equal logs mean equal insides: log₅(2x − 1) = log₅(x + 4) forces 2x − 1 = x + 4, so x = 5. But logs bring their **domain**: every inside must end up **positive**. Candidates that leave any inside ≤ 0 are extraneous — the radical-equations discipline, back again.

Compound $1 at 100% interest: once a year gives $2. Twice a year: (1 + 1/2)² = $2.25. Monthly: ≈ $2.613. Daily: ≈ $2.7146. Compounding **continuously** — infinitely often — the value stops climbing at a specific number: **e ≈ 2.71828**, the natural base of growth.

Why care about one weird constant? Because e is the base of **smooth, continuous change** — populations, radioactive decay, cooling coffee, interest compounding every instant. The function f(x) = eˣ is an ordinary exponential (base ≈ 2.718 > 1: growth), sitting between 2ˣ and 3ˣ.

Every base gets a log; e's is famous enough to earn its own name: **ln x = log_e x**, the natural log. Same machine as Chapter 1 — ln x asks 'e to what power gives x?' So **ln 1 = 0**, **ln e = 1**, and ln(e⁵) = 5. On calculators, ln sits right beside log.

ln and eˣ **undo each other in both directions**: ln(eˣ) = x and e^(ln x) = x (for x > 0). And every property from Chapter 2 carries over unchanged: ln(ab) = ln a + ln b, ln(a/b) = ln a − ln b, ln(aⁿ) = n ln a. Nothing new to memorize — just a new base wearing a short name.

Chapter 3's playbook, natural edition. Unknown in the **exponent**? Take ln of both sides: eˣ = 10 → x = **ln 10** (≈ 2.303). Unknown inside a **log**? Exponentiate: ln x = 2 → x = **e²** (≈ 7.389). Each tool summons its inverse.

With structure around the power, **isolate first** — the standing rule. 5e^(2x) = 20: divide by 5 → e^(2x) = 4 → take ln → 2x = ln 4 → x = (ln 4)/2. And since ln 4 = 2 ln 2, that's exactly **ln 2 ≈ 0.693**. The properties keep simplifying after the solve.

The all-purpose continuous model: **A = P·e^(rt)** — P the start, r the continuous rate (negative for decay), t the time. $500 at 6% for 10 years: A = 500·e^0.6 ≈ 500 · 1.822 = **$911**. Algebra 1's a·bˣ models, upgraded to compound every instant.

Read the anatomy: in A = 300·e^(0.08t), the start is **300** (t = 0 makes e⁰ = 1) and the continuous rate is **8%**. A negative rate flips it to decay: A = P·e^(−0.10t) shrinks continuously at 10%. Same skeleton either way — the exponent's sign tells the story.

Radioactive decay runs on a **half-life** h: every h units of time, half the sample survives. The model: **N = N₀ · (1/2)^(t/h)**. Iodine-131's half-life is 8 days; 160 mg after 24 days is 3 half-lives: 160 → 80 → 40 → **20 mg**. The exponent t/h counts the halvings.

Fractional half-lives run through the formula's exponent. After 4 days with h = 8: N = 160·(1/2)^(4/8) = 160·(1/2)^(1/2) ≈ 160 · 0.707 ≈ 113 mg — about **71% survives** at the halfway mark, not 75%, because decay compounds. And 'how long?' questions fall to ln, exactly like every exponential equation.

Some quantities span such vast ranges that scientists measure their **logarithms** instead. On a log scale, **each step of 1 means ×10 underneath**: a magnitude-6 earthquake shakes 10 times harder than a magnitude 5, and 100 times harder than a magnitude 4. Equal steps, equal multiplications.

pH runs the same way (each pH step = ×10 in acidity, downward: pH 3 is 10× more acidic than pH 4), and decibels use steps of 10 dB per ×10 of intensity. Converting is always the same move: **factor = 10^(difference in scale readings)** — and backwards, **difference = log(factor)**.
Before dividing by a two-digit number, size the answer with compatible numbers: 552 ÷ 24 is near 600 ÷ 25, which is 24.
Compatible numbers are chosen because they divide CLEANLY, not merely because they are round. That is what makes the estimate instant.
A divisor that is a multiple of ten splits into two easy steps: dividing by 30 is dividing by 3 and then by 10.
This is place value doing the work again — the same shortcut that makes multiplying by tens easy runs in reverse.
Partial quotients counts the groups in whatever batches are convenient: take 20 groups of 24, then 3 more, and total them.
The batches need not be equal or tidy. All that matters is that they are all counted, because the quotient is simply how many groups came out.
The standard algorithm counts the same groups, but fixes the batches by place value — one digit at a time, largest place first.
That makes it compact and quick, and also less forgiving: a digit placed one column out is wrong by a factor of ten.
Trial digits with a two-digit divisor are guesses, and guessing too high is routine: if 4 × 24 = 96 exceeds the 88 available, lower the digit to 3.
Adjusting is part of the method, not a sign of failure. The algorithm never leaves a negative remainder.
The check has two halves: quotient times divisor plus remainder must rebuild the dividend, and the remainder must be smaller than the divisor.
If the remainder reaches the divisor, another whole group fits and the quotient was too small — the second half of the check catches exactly that.
Objects hide many amounts at once: how LONG, how HEAVY, how MUCH they hold. Each amount is an attribute, and each can be measured.
Pick the attribute first, then the tool: a ruler for length, a seesaw for weight, a scoop for what fits inside.
Length wears many words: a snake is LONG, a tower TALL, a pencil stub SHORT. All describe one attribute — distance end to end.
Tall is length standing up; long is length lying down. Turn the tower sideways and tall becomes long.
Weight has its own words: HEAVY presses down hard, LIGHT barely presses at all. The seesaw turns that pressing into something you can see.
Down means heavier, up means lighter, level means equal — the seesaw's three answers.
Containers hold different amounts. HOLDS MORE and HOLDS LESS compare capacity — the room inside — which eyes alone often misjudge.
The fair test is filling: one same scoop, count the scoops each container swallows, compare the counts.
To compare two lengths, put them side by side from ONE start line, then read the far ends: the one reaching farther is longer.
The unit ticks let you say by HOW MUCH: count each length in cubes and compare the counts.
To compare two weights, load one on each pan and read the tilt: the sinking side is heavier, the rising side lighter.
A level beam is an answer too — it says the weights are EQUAL, neither side winning.
The oldest length trick: give one ribbon a head start and it LOOKS longer. Fair comparing means lining the starting ends up first.
Align first, judge second. Once the starts agree, the far ends tell the truth.
Standing things compare by the same rule turned upright: same floor as the start line, and the top that reaches higher is TALLER.
The floor does the aligning for you — which is why towers are easy to compare and ribbons are not.
Sorting asks ONE question of every object — red or not? round or not? — and the answers build the groups.
Change the rule and the groups change: a red sock joins the red pile under a color rule, the clothing pile under a kind rule.
Size is a sorting rule too: BIG in one group, SMALL in the other. The rule must say where big begins before sorting.
Size-sorting is not length-measuring — it asks a yes-or-no question, not a how-many question.
After the sort, count each group: touch and count the reds, then the blues. Each group earns its own number.
The counts turn piles into data — three groups become three numbers, ready for comparing.
With every group counted, the last question answers itself: the group with the greatest count has the MOST; the least count, the FEWEST.
Sort, count, compare — the full chain. The counts do the comparing; the shapes' sizes never vote.

Remember the kilo-badge from big numbers? A kilogram works exactly the same way: **kilo means ×1000.** 1 kilogram = 1,000 grams. The same badge that turned a thousand into 'kilo' on a big number now turns a thousand grams into one kilogram.

Here's the useful part: the badge works **no matter what you're measuring.** Kilo means ×1000 whether it's attached to grams (mass), meters (length), or anything else. One badge system, many quantities — that's the whole point of the metric system.

The length ladder: 10 mm = 1 cm, 100 cm = 1 m, 1,000 m = 1 km. Each step is its own badge. To convert, multiply when going from a bigger unit to a smaller one, and divide when going from smaller to bigger.

Some conversions need **two hops.** To go from meters to millimeters directly, combine both badges: 100 cm/m × 10 mm/cm = 1,000 mm per meter. So 1 km to cm hops through meters: 1 km = 1,000 m = 1,000×100 = 100,000 cm.

The same kilo badge you just used for length works for mass and volume too. **1,000 grams = 1 kilogram. 1,000 milliliters = 1 liter.** Same ×1000 rule, just measuring weight and liquid instead of distance.

Picking the right unit matters in real life. You'd measure an elephant's weight in **kilograms**, not grams (the number would be absurdly huge) — and a raindrop in **milliliters**, not liters (the number would be a tiny fraction). Choose the unit that keeps the number reasonable.

You already know area from counting unit squares tiled inside a rectangle. That counting has a name: the **AREA FORMULA — length × width.** An 8-by-6 rectangle has 8×6=48 unit squares, no counting required.
For bigger rectangles, reuse the break-apart trick from Course 6: split one side into tens and ones, multiply each piece, then add. 23×14 splits into 23×10 + 23×4 = 230+92 = **322.**

Remember walking the fence — tracing every side and adding the distances? That has a formula name too: **PERIMETER = 2 × (length + width).** For a 6-by-4 rectangle: 2×(6+4)=2×10=**20.** Two lengths, two widths, walked all the way around.

Area and perimeter move **independently.** A 3-by-8 rectangle and a 5-by-6 rectangle both have perimeter 22 — but their areas are 24 and 30. Same fence length, different amount of grass inside. One never tells you the other.

Word problems hide the formula in their verbs. **Covering, tiling, carpeting, painting** — that's surface, so it's **area.** **Fencing, framing, bordering, trimming** — that's the distance around, so it's **perimeter.** Spot the verb, pick the formula.

Fencing and framing signal perimeter instead. And for bigger dimensions, area calculations may need the break-apart trick from Course 6 — the story decides the formula, and the numbers decide whether you need to split them apart.

An angle's size is measured in **degrees.** A full turn all the way around is **360°.** Cut that turn exactly in half, and you get a **straight angle: 180°.** Cut it in half again, and you get a **right angle: 90°** — the same halving idea from fractions, now measuring a turn instead of a pizza.
The halving keeps going. Half of a right angle (90°) is **45°** — the diagonal angle you'd see cutting a square corner exactly in two. Same fraction-halving move, one more step down.

A protractor counts the exact degrees between two rays. Here's a tool you already own: a **clock face.** A full trip around the clock is 360°, split into 12 equal hours — so each hour mark is 360÷12=**30°.** The angle from 12 to 3 o'clock spans 3 hours: 3×30=90°.

A real protractor just measures more precisely than whole clock-hours — counting single degrees instead of 30° jumps. But the idea is identical: count how many degree-units fit between the two rays, whatever size those units are.
Every angle sorts into one of four families, compared to two benchmarks — 90° and 180°. **Acute:** less than 90°. **Right:** exactly 90°. **Obtuse:** between 90° and 180°. **Straight:** exactly 180°.
The boundaries are **exact**, not approximate. 90° is always right — never 'almost right.' 89° and 91° are both a full family away from 90°: acute and obtuse. One degree can flip the classification.
