The **midsegment** you met earlier is just the side-splitter's most famous special case: the parallel line hits the MIDPOINTS, so the ratio is 1 : 1 and each piece is half. Every midsegment is a side-splitter; not every side-splitter is a midsegment.

The side-splitter runs **both ways**. Forward: parallel ⇒ proportional split. **Converse**: if a line splits two sides of a triangle **proportionally**, then it must be **parallel** to the third side. This is how proportional measurements PROVE two lines parallel — the mirror of the corresponding-angles converse.

The idea extends beyond one triangle: **three (or more) parallel lines** cut across two transversals in **proportional** segments. Whatever ratio the parallels carve on one transversal, they carve the same ratio on the other. It's the side-splitter's logic stretched across a ladder of parallels.

A close cousin: the **Angle Bisector Theorem**. The bisector of a triangle's angle splits the opposite side in the ratio of the two **adjacent sides**: BD/DC = AB/AC. Same proportional flavor, different trigger — an angle bisector instead of a parallel line.

Real figures stack these ideas. The skill is **spotting which proportion applies**: a parallel line means side-splitter; a shared angle with proportional sides means SAS~; an angle bisector means the bisector ratio. Read the figure's marks — parallel arrows, angle ticks — to choose the right tool, then set up ONE proportion.

When two similar triangles overlap, corresponding sides may be hard to pair. Anchor on the **equal angles** first — matching angle marks reveal which vertices correspond, and therefore which sides. Get the correspondence right, and the proportion writes itself.

The master strategy for any proportion problem: (1) identify the configuration (parallel, bisector, or shared-angle similarity); (2) name the theorem; (3) write ONE proportion with corresponding parts aligned; (4) cross-multiply and solve. Same four steps, whatever the figure throws at you.

Drop the **altitude from the right angle** to the hypotenuse of a right triangle, and something remarkable happens: the two smaller triangles you create are each **similar to the whole** — and to each other. Three nested similar triangles from one line. Every angle is shared around, so AA does all the work.

Matching the corresponding parts is the tricky bit. Line up each small triangle with the whole by their equal angles: the right angle maps to the right angle, and the shared acute angle to itself. Once aligned, the proportional sides give you the powerful **geometric mean** relationships coming next.

This one configuration secretly proves the **Pythagorean theorem**. Writing the leg geometric-mean relationships and adding them recovers a² + b² = c². The altitude-on-hypotenuse picture isn't just a curiosity — it's one of the cleanest routes to the most famous theorem in geometry.

The **geometric mean** of two numbers a and b is √(ab) — the value x where a/x = x/b. It's the 'multiplicative middle,' the way the average is the additive middle. In the altitude picture, the equal ratios between similar triangles turn directly into geometric means.

Each **leg** is a geometric mean too — of the whole hypotenuse and the segment ADJACENT to that leg: leg = √(hypotenuse × adjacent segment). Two flavors: the altitude is the geometric mean of the two SEGMENTS; a leg is the geometric mean of the HYPOTENUSE and its adjacent segment. Keep them straight.

With the geometric-mean toolkit you can solve a right triangle from surprisingly little. Given the two hypotenuse segments, the altitude and both legs all follow. The trick is choosing the RIGHT relationship: altitude from the two segments, each leg from the hypotenuse and its adjacent segment.

Choosing wrong is the classic mistake, so anchor on WHICH segments the mean connects. Altitude ↔ the two little segments. Leg ↔ the whole hypotenuse and the one segment touching that leg. Sketch the picture and label p, q, and the hypotenuse before reaching for a square root.

It all ties back to Pythagoras as a check. Once you have both legs and the hypotenuse, confirm a² + b² = c². The geometric-mean relationships and the Pythagorean theorem describe the same right triangle from two angles — they must always agree.

How do you measure a tree you can't climb? **Similar triangles.** At the same moment, a tree and a person cast shadows; the sun's rays strike both at the same angle, and both stand at 90° to the ground. Two equal angles — AA — so the triangles are similar, and one proportion reveals the height.

The **mirror method** works even in shade. Place a mirror on the ground and step back until you see the treetop in it. Light reflects at equal angles, so your eye-to-mirror triangle is similar to the mirror-to-tree triangle. Measure your height, your distance to the mirror, and the mirror's distance to the tree.

Both methods share one recipe: identify the two similar triangles, match corresponding parts (height ↔ height, near-distance ↔ far-distance), write ONE proportion, and solve. The power of indirect measurement is reaching the unreachable with nothing but a shadow, a mirror, and a ratio.

A **scale drawing** is a similar copy at a stated ratio — a map, a blueprint, a model car. The **scale** tells you the ratio between drawing and reality, like 1 cm : 50 cm or 1 in : 8 ft. Multiply a drawing length by the scale to get the real length; divide to go the other way.

Maps work the same way. A scale of **1 cm : 2 km** means each centimeter on the map is 2 km on the ground. Measure the map distance, multiply by the scale, and you have the real distance — the reason a ruler and a map can plan a road trip.

One subtlety trips people up: scale applies to **lengths**, but AREA scales by the square of the ratio. A 1 : 50 model has parts 1/50 the length — but its surface area is 1/50² = 1/2500 of the real thing. Length uses the scale; area uses the scale squared; volume, the cube.

Similar figures scale predictably: **perimeter scales by k** (the same ratio as the sides), but **area scales by k²**. Double every side and the perimeter doubles while the area quadruples. This gap between k and k² is behind everything from pizza pricing to why big animals aren't just scaled-up small ones.

This is why 'twice the size' can mislead. A 16-inch pizza isn't twice a 8-inch pizza — the diameter doubles (k = 2), so the AREA quadruples (k² = 4). You get four times the pizza, not two. Reasoning with k² instead of k is the difference between a good deal and a bad one.

A dilation stretches everything away from (or toward) one fixed **centre**, by the scale factor k. When a line segment does NOT pass through the centre, dilating it produces a new segment that is longer or shorter — but always running exactly **parallel** to the original. That parallelism is not a coincidence; it is what a dilation always does to a line it doesn't touch.

The parallel-line property doesn't depend on stretching versus shrinking, or on where exactly the centre sits. Whether k is greater than 1 (enlarging) or between 0 and 1 (reducing), any segment that misses the centre comes out parallel to where it started — the theorem holds across the whole range of scale factors.

Grade 7 sliced prisms and pyramids; now the round solids join. A **cross-section** is still the flat face where a plane slices a solid — and for a cylinder the catalog is tidy: slice **parallel to the base** and you get a circle congruent to it; slice **parallel to the axis** and you get a rectangle; slice at a slant and an ellipse appears.

The sphere is the aristocrat: **every** planar slice of a sphere is a circle. Through the center, the slice is as large as possible — the **great circle**, radius equal to the sphere's own. Slice at distance d from the center and the disk's radius obeys chapter-friendly Pythagoras: r²ₛₗᵢᶜₑ = R² − d².

Slicing has a reverse gear: **revolution**. Spin a flat region about an axis and it sweeps a solid — the figure's rectangle (one side ON the axis) sweeps a cylinder whose radius is the rectangle's width and whose height is its length along the axis. Spin therefore MANUFACTURES the solids whose sections you just cataloged.

Sections are evidence. A solid's slice pattern identifies it (all circles ⇒ sphere; constant congruent circles ⇒ cylinder; shrinking-to-a-point circles ⇒ cone), sizes it (a great circle exposes the true radius), and — next chapter — will price its volume. Reading slices IS reading solids.

Push a stack of coins sideways: it leans, but nothing about any coin changed. **Cavalieri's principle** captures this: if two solids have the same height and their cross-sections at EVERY level have equal areas, their volumes are equal. Volume lives in the slices — how the slices are stacked (straight, sheared, curved) is irrelevant.

Cavalieri also compares UNLIKE solids. Chapter 1 found the circle-in-square section ratio: π/4 at every height. Promote it: if one solid's sections are always k times another's (same height), its volume is k times as large — the equal-slices principle, run through a constant multiplier.

The comparison move generalizes beautifully: any solid squeezed slice-for-slice between two others inherits their verdicts, and any solid whose sections COPY a known solid's (however the stacking bends) copies its volume. Next chapter this becomes an engine: the sphere's volume will fall out of a cylinder-minus-cone comparison, slice by slice.

A principle is defined by its edges. Cavalieri certifies VOLUME only — shear a stack and the volume holds, but the leaning stack's outside gets LONGER: lateral surface grows with slant. And the converse fails: two solids can share a volume while their slices disagree at every single level.

Grade 5 counted unit cubes into V = Bh for prisms. The cylinder inherits the formula by Cavalieri: stand it next to ANY prism with the same base AREA and height — every level of both shows that same area — so their volumes agree, and the cylinder's is Bh = πr²h. The formula Grade 8 recalled is now JUSTIFIED, not just remembered.

Where does ⅓ come from? Take a cube of side 6: it splits into **three congruent square pyramids**, each with a face of the cube as base and the same far corner as apex. Three identical pieces filling Bh exactly ⇒ each pyramid is ⅓Bh. The third is a TILING fact, before it is a formula.

The masterpiece. Set a hemisphere (radius r) beside a cylinder of radius r and height r with a CONE drilled out (apex down, at the base's center). Slice both at height h: the hemisphere shows a disk of radius √(r² − h²) — area π(r² − h²); the drilled cylinder shows a RING: πr² − πh². Identical, at every height.

Real objects are compounds: a silo is a cylinder wearing a hemisphere; a capsule is a cylinder with hemispherical caps. Volume ADDS across a clean joint — decompose, price each piece with the justified formulas, sum. The only skill is seeing the seam.

Hollows price by SUBTRACTION: outer solid minus the removed one. Chapter 1's offset sweep — the tube — finally gets its bill: outer cylinder minus inner cylinder, π(R² − r²)h. Every ring-sectioned solid works this way, and the drilled cylinder that priced the sphere already showed the pattern.

Surface needs two new prices and one discipline. Prices: a sphere's surface is **4πr²** (so a hemisphere's curved dome is 2πr²), and a cylinder's curved wall is its unrolled rectangle: **2πrh**. Discipline: at a seam, the shared circle is INTERIOR — count it zero times. Surface bills only what's exposed.

The similarity course showed a 1:50 model's AREAS shrink by 50². Volume completes the trilogy: scale every length by k and **lengths go ×k, areas ×k², volumes ×k³** — the figure's k = 2 cube holds 2×2×2 = 8 unit cells because scaling stretched all THREE directions at once.

Volume meets matter through **density = mass ÷ volume**. A material's density is its identity card — steel ≈ 7.8 g/cm³, water 1, pine 0.6 — so mass = density × volume turns every formula this course justified into a WEIGHT prediction, and density < 1 predicts floating.

Modeling assigns each COST to its law: paint, sheet metal, and cooling bill by SURFACE (k²); capacity, concrete, and weight bill by VOLUME (k³). The tension between the two — volume outrunning surface as things grow — is the deepest design fact in this course.

An equation like **3x + 5 = 20** is a two-step machine: x was multiplied by 3, then 5 was added. To find x, run the machine in **reverse**, undoing the *last* step first: subtract 5 (leaving 15), then divide by 3. So x = 5.
Whatever you do, do it to **both sides** — that keeps the equation true. Each undo peels one layer off the x until it stands alone.

When x sits on **both sides**, like 5x + 2 = 3x + 10, collect it on one side first. Take 3x off both pans — the balance stays level — leaving 2x + 2 = 10, a two-step equation you already know. So x = 4.
Subtract the **smaller** x-term to keep the coefficient positive: for 7x + 3 = 4x + 15, take 4x from both sides, giving 3x + 3 = 15.

Parentheses first: **3(x + 4)** is a 3-by-(x + 4) rectangle, so the 3 reaches BOTH parts — 3x + 12. To solve 3(x + 4) = 27, distribute (3x + 12 = 27) or divide both sides by 3 first (x + 4 = 9). Either road gives x = 5.
The classic slip is distributing to only the **first** term: 3(x + 4) is NOT 3x + 4. The area picture shows why — the 4-wide strip is also 3 tall.
A fraction is just division: **x/3 + 2 = 7** means x was divided by 3, then 2 was added. Undo in reverse: subtract 2 (x/3 = 5), then **multiply** by 3 — undoing division. So x = 15.
Undoing division means **multiplying** — and whatever multiplies one term must multiply **every** term if you clear the fraction first.
Two fractions? Clear them both at once. For **x/2 + x/3 = 5**, multiply EVERY term by the LCD 6: the fractions become whole — **3x + 2x = 30** — so 5x = 30 and x = 6.
The LCD stamp hits **both sides** — scaling only the left breaks the balance, just like removing weight from one pan.
Decimals clear like fractions: for **0.5x + 1.2 = 3.7**, multiply EVERY term by 10 — each decimal point slides one place — giving **5x + 12 = 37**. Then the familiar two-step: 5x = 25, x = 5.
The classic slip: shifting the decimals but leaving a **whole number** unshifted. In 0.2x + 3 = 4, the ×10 turns 3 into 30 and 4 into 40 — zeros for everyone.

A **literal equation** has more than one letter, like the perimeter **P = 2L + 2W**. To solve for W, use the exact same moves as with numbers: subtract 2L (P − 2L = 2W), then divide by 2. So W = (P − 2L) / 2 — the letters just stay letters.
The goal is the same as always: get your chosen letter **alone**. Whatever surrounds it — added terms, multipliers — gets undone in reverse, onto both sides.
The triangle area **A = bh/2** hides h inside a division. Clear it first: multiply both sides by 2 (2A = bh), then divide by b. So **h = 2A/b** — clear the fraction, then isolate.
The line **y = mx + b** solved for x needs two undos: subtract b (y − b = mx), then divide by m. So **x = (y − b)/m** — subtract, then divide.
Temperature ties them together: **C = (F − 32)·5/9**. To solve for F, undo each layer in reverse: multiply by 9, divide by 5, then add 32. The result is **F = 9C/5 + 32** — the everyday conversion.
Assembling a solved formula, order matters: the whole **(y − b)** rides over m. Parentheses keep the subtraction together before the division.
An inequality like **2x + 3 < 11** solves just like an equation: subtract 3 (2x < 8), divide by 2 (x < 4). The difference is the answer — not a single number but a whole **range**: every x below 4.

The range draws as a **ray** on a number line. For x > 5, an **open circle** sits at 5 (5 itself isn't included) and the arrow runs right through every larger number. A `<` or `>` uses an open circle; `≤` or `≥` fills it in.

One move breaks the pattern: **multiplying or dividing by a negative flips the inequality**. Solve −2x < 6 by dividing by −2 — and the `<` becomes `>`: **x > −3**. The number line mirrors across zero, so the direction reverses.
The trap is forgetting to flip. Adding or subtracting a negative number does **not** flip — only ×/÷ by a negative coefficient does. Check: is the number multiplying x negative?
Everything comes together: **2x + 5 > 5x − 4**. Collect x-terms as with equations, but watch the sign. Subtract 5x: −3x + 5 > −4. Subtract 5: −3x > −9. Divide by −3 and **flip**: x < 3.
A slicker route dodges the flip: collect x on the side that keeps it **positive**. Moving 2x right gives 9 > 3x, then x < 3 — same answer, no flip. Either path works if you track signs.

Before accepting "A causes B", try to invent a third thing that would move both. If you can, and nobody randomised A, the study cannot rule it out. Watching finds companions; only assigning finds causes.

Before you trust a number, ask how it was **made**. Three designs, three ceilings on what may be claimed:

**Survey** — sample at random, describe a population.
**Observational study** — watch, and report what goes together.
**Experiment** — assign at random, and only then say *cause*.

The design sets the ceiling. No amount of data raises it.

When you only watch, a **lurking variable** can drive both columns of your table. Ice cream sales and drownings rise together; heat drives both.

Random assignment defeats this because the coin, not the person or the weather, decides who gets the treatment. Anything that could confound the comparison is dealt evenly into both arms.
Picture a dartboard. Random error scatters the darts around the bullseye. Bias moves the whole cluster off it. Throwing more darts tightens the cluster — it never re-aims it.

A **biased** method misses the truth *systematically* — it leans the same way every time. Ask only people who answer the phone at noon, and you will keep landing in the same wrong place.

Collecting more data does not fix a lean. It just plants your estimate more firmly in the wrong spot: a more precise wrong answer.

Three ways a sample tilts:

**Undercoverage** — some of the population can never be picked (landline-only lists).
**Nonresponse** — the picked ones who refuse differ from those who answer.
**Voluntary response** — the people who show up feel strongest.

All three change *who* is in the sample. None of them is a small-sample problem.

Run the checklist. Is there a comparison arm? Did a coin decide who went where? Is anyone who could tilt the result kept in the dark? Are there enough subjects that chance alone could not fake the gap? Each answer plugs one specific leak.

A usable experiment needs four parts:

**Control** — a comparison arm, so you know what would have happened anyway.
**Random assignment** — the coin decides the arm, not the person.
**Blinding** — nobody who could tilt the result knows which arm they are in.
**Replication** — enough subjects per arm that chance alone cannot fake the gap.

Drop any one and the causal claim leaks.

**Random assignment ≠ random sampling.** They are two different coins doing two different jobs.

Sample at random from a population → your finding **generalises** to that population.
Assign at random within your subjects → your finding is **causal** for them.

A drug trial on volunteers can prove cause without generalising. A random survey can generalise without proving cause.

Ask where the number came from. From every member of the population? Then it is a parameter — fixed, and usually unknowable. From the people you happened to ask? Then it is a statistic — knowable, and different every time you ask again.

The population has one fixed number — the **parameter**, p. You never see it.

What you see is a **statistic**, p̂: the answer your particular sample happened to give. Draw a new sample and you get a new p̂.

The truth stands still. The estimate moves. Every idea in this course is about how much it moves.

So a single poll is not "the answer". It is **one draw** from a whole spread of answers your method could have produced.

That spread is the thing worth studying. It has a shape, a centre, and a width — and each of those tells you something you can act on.

Precision tracks the SQUARE ROOT of the sample size. So the useful question is never "how many more people?" but "how many TIMES more people?". Four times as many people halve the wobble; nine times as many divide it by three.

Collect every answer your method could give, and you have the **sampling distribution** — the pile.

It has two features worth knowing:

**Centre** — sits on the truth, if the method is unbiased.
**Width** — shrinks as the sample grows. That is the only lever you control.

The width does not fall in step with n. It falls with **√n**.

Quadruple the sample and you halve the wobble. Go from 400 people to 1600 and the spread halves — from 1600 to 6400 it halves again.

That is why national polls stop at about a thousand people: the next halving costs four times as much.

Work the formula in order. First p(1−p). Then divide by n. Then take the square root — that is one SE. Then double it for the 95% band. Skipping the square root is the most common slip, and it inflates the answer enormously.

The width of the pile has a formula. For a proportion, the **standard error** is

SE = √( p(1−p) / n ).

It is the typical distance between a poll and the truth. And about 95% of the pile sits within **two** standard errors of the centre — the fact the rest of this course is built on.

Two practical facts fall out of the formula.

**p(1−p) is largest at p = 0.5.** A 50/50 split is the hardest to pin down, so pollsters quote the worst case to be safe.

**n is under the square root.** The wobble depends on the SIZE of the sample, not on the size of the population — polling 1,000 people works as well for a city as for a country.

Take the estimate, subtract the margin, add the margin — that is the band. Report the band, not the point. And remember what the band was built from: sampling wobble only, assuming the method itself was sound.

You know the poll lands within about 2 SE of the truth, 95% of the time. Turn that around and the truth lies within about 2 SE of the poll.

That distance is the **margin of error**, and it turns a number into a band:

48% ± 3 → every value from 45% to 51% is plausible.

The margin is honest about exactly one thing: **random sampling wobble**.

It assumes your sample was random and everyone answered truthfully. It cannot see undercoverage, nonresponse, or a leading question.

So ± 3 means *if the method is sound*, the truth is within 3 points. If the method leans, the ± is measuring the wrong thing.

Think of a machine that stamps out intervals. About 19 in 20 of its intervals contain the truth. You pull one out of the machine. You cannot say your interval has a 95% chance of being right — you can say the machine is right 95% of the time, and you trust the machine.

Here is the sentence almost everyone gets wrong:

*"There is a 95% chance the truth is inside this interval."*

The truth is a fixed number. It is either inside your interval or it is not — there is no chance about it. The 95% describes the **method**: run it many times and about 95% of the intervals it makes will capture the truth.

Raising the confidence level widens the interval. There is no free lunch:

**99%** — catches the truth almost always, but the band may be so wide it rules nothing out.
**80%** — a tight, decisive-looking band that misses one time in five.

95% is a convention, not a law of nature. It is a chosen trade between being right often and saying something useful.
Draw both bands before you say anything. If they share any ground, the poll cannot tell you which one is really higher. If they are cleanly apart, it can.

"A leads B, 48% to 45%." With a margin of ±3, A's band runs 45–51 and B's runs 42–48. They overlap.

So a truth of 47% for both is perfectly consistent with this poll. The lead is **inside the wobble** — which is what commentators mean, when they are careful, by a statistical tie.

Three questions to ask any poll, in order:

**Who was asked, and how were they chosen?** (bias — the margin cannot see it)
**How many?** (the margin — how much wobble)
**Is the effect bigger than the margin?** (whether the finding survives its own uncertainty)

Skip the first and the other two are decoration.

The scores never change. Only the labels move. If the treatment truly did nothing, then the labels are just stickers — and any gap you see is an accident of which scores happened to get which sticker. Shuffling shows you every accident that was available.

Two groups differ. Before you celebrate, ask the only question that matters:

**Could chance alone have produced a gap this big?**

To answer it, you need to know what gaps chance *does* produce. So build them: shuffle the labels at random, keeping the same scores, and record the gap. Do it hundreds of times.

Now compare. The real gap was **4**. In the pile of chance gaps, almost nothing reaches out that far — in the exact count, 6 of the 252 possible splits, about **2%**.

So either something unusual happened by luck (about a 1-in-50 event), or the method really did something. That comparison is the whole logic of a significance test.

Read the p-value in one direction only: given no effect, how often would chance hand me data this extreme? It never tells you the probability that there is no effect. Swapping those two is the same reversal error as confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A).

Count the tail. Of all the gaps chance produced, what fraction reached as far as the one you actually saw?

That fraction is the **p-value**: the chance of data at least this extreme *if the no-effect story were true*.

Small p-value → the no-effect story explains your data badly.

How small is small enough? By convention, **p < 0.05** — a result that chance would produce less than 1 time in 20 gets called *statistically significant*.

That 5% is a custom, not a discovery. It buys you a mistake rate: even when nothing is going on, about 1 study in 20 will clear the bar by luck alone.

Ask two questions of every finding, never one. **Is it real?** — that is the p-value's job. **Is it big?** — that is the effect size's job, measured in the units of the problem. A yes to the first and a no to the second means: real, and not worth doing.

"Significant" answers exactly one question: **could chance alone have done this?**

It does not answer:

– Is the effect **big**?
– Does it **matter**?
– Is it **true**?

With a large enough sample, an effect of 0.3 points on a 100-point test becomes significant. It is real, and it is worthless.

Three more things a significant result does not give you:

**Proof.** About 1 significant result in 20 is a fluke when nothing is going on.
**Generalisation.** It applies to the population you sampled, not to everyone.
**Cause** — unless the treatment was randomly assigned. Significance and causation are different questions with different guardians.

Run two checks on any headline. Was the treatment assigned by a coin? If not, delete every causal verb from the sentence. Was the sample drawn at random from the population being talked about? If not, shrink the sentence to the people who were actually studied.

Every claim has a design underneath it, and the design is a ceiling.

A voluntary online poll supports almost nothing. An observational study supports association. A random sample supports a population estimate. A randomised experiment supports cause.

A claim can travel **down** this ladder. It can never climb it.

Two more questions the design answers, and the headline usually hides:

**Who was in it?** A drug tested only on men aged 20–35 is a drug tested only on men aged 20–35.
**Compared with what?** "Improves memory" — compared with a placebo? With nothing? With a rival product?

A claim with no comparison group is not a weak claim. It is not a claim at all.

Ask two questions of any conclusion. **Who does it speak for?** Only the people who could have been sampled. **Where does it apply?** Only inside the range of the data. A conclusion that leaves either boundary is no longer supported by the study.

The arithmetic can be perfect while the sentence is false. Three ways it happens:

**Reach** — the claim covers people the sample never included.
**Extrapolation** — the claim runs past the range of the data.
**Swapped conditional** — P(A | B) reported as P(B | A).

Each one is a failure of *interpretation*, not of computation.

The third failure is the reversal you met in probability.

"95% of people with the disease test positive" is P(positive | disease).
"95% of positive tests mean disease" is P(disease | positive).

When the disease is rare, these two numbers are wildly different — and the second one is usually the false claim in the headline.

Take the questions in order and stop at the first failure. A claim that fails question 1 cannot be rescued by a beautiful p-value at question 4 — the later answers are only meaningful once the earlier ones pass.

You now have five questions, and in this order they catch almost everything:

1. **How was the data made?** (design → ceiling)
2. **Who was left out?** (bias — the margin cannot see it)
3. **How much wobble?** (margin of error)
4. **Is the effect bigger than the wobble?** (significance)
5. **Is it big enough to matter?** (effect size)

Two habits worth keeping for life:

**Ask what was randomised** before you read anything else. It is one question and it settles what the claim may say.

**Read the band, not the number.** Every estimate is a range, every gap has its own wobble, and every "significant" finding still owes you an effect size.

Chapter 2 showed the statistic wobbling from sample to sample. Now stack those wobbles up: draw sample after sample and pile each proportion on a line. The pile that grows has a shape — and it is always the same shape.

This mound has a name: the normal distribution. It appears whenever many small chances add up — sample proportions, measurement errors, heights. Same curve, different rulers: what changes is only its center (the mean) and its width (the standard deviation).

Every normal curve keeps the same promise, whatever its center μ and width σ: about 68% of values land within one σ of μ, about 95% within two, about 99.7% within three. Scores on a test with μ = 100, σ = 10 will be our running example.

Notice what just happened: symmetry let you split the leftover. Outside two σ is 5%; each tail takes exactly half. Every region under the bell is reachable from the three memorized numbers plus halving.

'Within two σ' keeps coming up — so give the idea its own number. z = (x − μ) / σ asks: how many widths is x from the center? z = 0 is the mean itself; z = 2 is the edge of the 95% country; the sign says which side.

A **system** is two equations you solve at the same time. Its **solution** is the single point (x, y) that makes **both** equations true at once. On a graph, that's exactly where the two lines **cross**.
To **check** a proposed solution, substitute it into **both** equations. For (2, 3) with y = x + 1: 3 = 2 + 1 ✓. With y = −x + 5: 3 = −2 + 5 ✓. Both come out true, so (2, 3) really is the solution.

That's the heart of it: a solution must satisfy **every** equation at once, not just one. A point can sit on one line and still miss the system entirely. Only the shared point — the crossing — counts.

To solve a system **by graphing**: draw each line (start at its y-intercept, then step by its slope), and find where they **cross**. That crossing point is the solution — read off its x and y, then confirm by substitution.

Worked example: **y = 2x** and **y = x + 3**. Plot both and they cross at **(3, 6)**. Check by substituting: 2·3 = 6 ✓ and 3 + 3 = 6 ✓. When the crossing lands on grid lines, graphing reads the solution right off the page.

Always **check the crossing** by substituting into both equations. A graph read by eye can land a little off, especially between grid lines; the substitution is what proves the point is exactly right.

You can tell how many solutions a system has **before** solving, by comparing the lines. **Different slopes** → they cross once → **one solution**. **Same slope, different intercept** → parallel → **no solution**. **Same slope and intercept** → the same line → **infinitely many**.

**Parallel** is the no-solution case. Equal slopes tilt the lines the same way; different y-intercepts start them at different heights. They march alongside each other forever and never cross — so there's no point that satisfies both.

When both equations describe the **same line**, every point on it satisfies both — **infinitely many** solutions. Watch for equations that look different but are the same line in disguise; comparing slope and intercept settles it.

Graphing is slow and imprecise. **Substitution** is exact. When one equation already says **y = (something)**, replace y in the *other* equation with that something. Now it has only x — solve it, then use y = (something) to find y.
Worked all the way: **y = 2x − 1** and **3x + y = 9**. Substitute: 3x + (2x − 1) = 9 → 5x − 1 = 9 → 5x = 10 → **x = 2**. Then back-substitute: y = 2·2 − 1 = **3**. Solution **(2, 3)**.

Back-substitute into the **isolated** equation — it's already solved for y, so it's the easy one. Then confirm the point in **both** equations. If either fails, a sign slipped during the substitution.

Often nothing is isolated yet. Then **solve one equation for a variable first** — pick one with a coefficient of 1 so you avoid fractions. From x + y = 7 you get **y = 7 − x**. Now substitute that into the other equation, exactly as before.
Worked: **x + y = 8** and **3x − y = 4**. From the first, y = 8 − x. Substitute: 3x − (8 − x) = 4 → 4x − 8 = 4 → **x = 3**, then y = 8 − 3 = **5**. Solution **(3, 5)** — check both to be sure.

Guard the **sign**. When you substitute into a **−y** term, wrap the expression in parentheses: −(8 − x) = −8 + x. Skip the parentheses and you'll flip the sign of the second piece — the most common substitution mistake.

Substitution solves **any** system, whether or not the graph is clear. The full method: isolate a variable if needed, substitute into the other equation, solve for one variable, back-substitute for the other, and check the point in both equations.

The check into **both** equations isn't a formality. If the point fails one equation, a sign slipped during substitution — most often forgetting to distribute a minus into a substituted expression. Re-check that step first.

**Elimination** combines the two equations so one variable disappears. If a variable has **opposite** coefficients (+y in one, −y in the other), **add** the equations — it cancels. If it has **matching** coefficients, **subtract**. Either way you're left with one variable to solve.
Worked: **x + y = 8** and **x − y = 2**. The y-coefficients are opposite, so add: (x + y) + (x − y) = 8 + 2 → 2x = 10 → **x = 5**. Back-substitute: 5 + y = 8 → **y = 3**. Solution **(5, 3)**.

Matching coefficients → **subtract**. But subtract carefully: the minus applies to **every** term of the second equation. (2x + y) − (x + y) = 2x + y − x − y = x. A sign dropped here is the usual elimination mistake.

When no coefficients line up, **multiply one whole equation** by a number so a coefficient matches the other. Then add or subtract as usual. Multiplying every term of an equation by a nonzero number keeps it the same line — it just rescales it.
Worked: **2x + y = 7** and **x + 3y = 11**. Multiply the second by 2 → 2x + 6y = 22. Subtract the first: (2x + 6y) − (2x + y) = 22 − 7 → 5y = 15 → **y = 3**, then **x = 2**. Solution **(2, 3)**.

Pick the variable that's easiest to match — usually one with a coefficient of 1, since you just multiply by the other equation's coefficient. Scale only the equation that needs it; leave the other alone.

Sometimes **both** equations need scaling. Multiply each by its own number so one variable's coefficients match, then subtract (or add). It's the same method with one extra multiplication — aim for the least common multiple of the two coefficients you're matching.

Worked: **2x + 3y = 13** and **3x + 2y = 12**. First×3 → 6x + 9y = 39. Second×2 → 6x + 4y = 24. Subtract: 5y = 15 → **y = 3**, then **x = 2**. The 6 is the LCM of 2 and 3 — the smallest match to aim for.

Elimination also exposes the **special cases**. If both variables cancel and you're left with a **false** statement like 0 = 7, the lines are parallel — **no solution**. If you're left with a **true** one like 0 = 0, they're the same line — **infinitely many**.

Word problems become systems: **name each unknown**, then write **one equation per fact**. A total gives x + y = (sum). A difference — "x is k more than y" — gives x − y = k. Two facts, two equations, one solvable system.

Worked: two numbers sum to 20, and one is 6 more than the other. Let x be the larger: **x + y = 20** and **x − y = 6**. Add: 2x = 26 → **x = 13**, then **y = 7**. Check: 13 + 7 = 20 and 13 − 7 = 6. Both facts hold.

Mind the **direction** of "more than": "x is 6 more than y" means **x − y = 6**, not y − x = 6. Assign x to the larger quantity so the difference stays positive and the equation reads the way the sentence does.

Two-category problems give two equations: a **count** equation (how many of each — x + y = total) and a **value** equation (what they're worth — price·x + price·y = total worth). Coins, tickets, and stamps all follow this pattern.
Worked: x adult tickets at $8, y child tickets at $5, **9 tickets** for **$57**. Count: x + y = 9. Value: 8x + 5y = 57. Substitute y = 9 − x: 8x + 5(9 − x) = 57 → 3x + 45 = 57 → **x = 4**, **y = 5**.

Keep the two equations distinct. The **count** equation just adds the items, so its coefficients are 1. The **value** equation weights each item by its price. Mixing a price into the count equation (or vice versa) is the usual slip.

With three methods available, pick the easiest: **substitution** when a variable is already isolated (or easy to isolate), **elimination** when coefficients line up or scale cleanly, graphing only for a rough read. Then do the last step everyone forgets — **answer the question actually asked**.

Elimination shines when a variable cancels directly. For **3x + 2y = 12** and **3x − y = 3**, both have 3x — subtract to cancel it: (3x + 2y) − (3x − y) = 12 − 3 → 3y = 9 → **y = 3**, then **x = 2**. Choosing the fitting method saves steps.

Then **interpret**. The solution is a pair of numbers, but the question asks for one specific thing. If x = adult tickets and the question asks how many children, report **y**. Re-read the question before writing the final answer.
Eleven is not a brand-new thing — it is ten and one more. The ten is finished; a single extra rides on top.
Say it as a walk: land on ten, take one more step. That step's name is eleven.
Twelve works the same way: ten and two more. The ten never gets recounted — only the two extras are new.
Every teen will follow this pattern: one finished ten, plus some ones you can count on your fingers.
The ten-frame turns any teen into a picture: the full frame is the ten, and the dots outside are the ones.
Reading the picture is instant — nobody counts a full frame. Ten at a glance, then count only the extras.
Eleven, twelve, thirteen — the odd-sounding teens. Their names hide it, but each is still ten and some: 10+1, 10+2, 10+3.
Trust the numeral over the name: the left digit is the ten, the right digit counts the ones.
Fourteen, fifteen, sixteen say their secret out loud: FOUR-teen, FIF-teen, SIX-teen — the ones first, then “teen” for the ten.
Hear a -teen name and you already know the split: the front of the word counts the ones.
Seventeen, eighteen, nineteen fill the frame's neighbourhood almost to twenty. Nineteen is ten and nine — one dot shy of two full tens.
The pattern holds to the very edge: left digit one ten, right digit the ones, all the way to 19.
Building runs backwards too: any teen BREAKS into its ten and its ones. Sixteen splits into 10 and 6, always.
The split is not one choice among many — the ten-and-ones split is written into the numeral itself.
The split can be WRITTEN: 15 = 10 + 5. The equals sign says both sides name one amount: teen, and ten-and-ones.
One little equation carries the whole idea: whole on one side, ten and ones on the other.
Fill a frame from a teen-sized pile and some dots will not fit. Those LEFTOVERS are exactly the ones digit, sorted out for you.
Seventeen dots: ten vanish into the frame, seven remain outside. The 7 of 17 stands there in plain sight.
On the number line the teens are the stretch between 10 and 20 — every teen sits its ones-count of steps past the ten.
Thirteen lives three steps past ten; eighteen, eight steps past. The line and the frame tell one story.
Now run it in reverse: shown a frame-and-extras picture, NAME the teen. Count the extras, put “ten and” in front, and the numeral appears.
Full frame plus 6 outside? Ten and six — sixteen — 16. Picture to name to numeral, one straight path.
Teens hide everywhere: an egg tray of 10 with 2 beside it, a pack plus spares. Spot the ready ten; the count is nearly done.
That is the teen habit for life: find the ten, count the extras, and read the number whole.
Ten single ones bundle together to make one ten. A "ten" is just 10 ones grouped into a rod. So 3 tens is the same as 30 ones — three groups of ten.
Going the other way, 40 ones make 4 tens, because 40 is 4 groups of ten. To find how many tens, count the groups of ten.
A bundle keeps its size: 1 ten is always 10 ones, whether you see a rod or ten loose cubes. Bundling into tens makes big counts quick to read.
A two-digit number is made of tens and ones. In 46, the 4 means 4 tens and the 6 means 6 ones. The left digit counts the tens; the right digit counts the ones.
You can build a number from its parts: 4 tens and 6 ones make 46. Put the tens count on the left and the ones count on the right.
The same works for any two-digit number. In 72 there are 7 tens and 2 ones. In 30 there are 3 tens and 0 ones — the 0 means no extra ones.
Base-ten blocks show a number: each rod is a ten and each cube is a one. So 3 rods and 5 cubes means 3 tens and 5 ones, which is 35. Count the rods, then the cubes.
Count the tens first, then the ones. 5 rods and 0 cubes is 5 tens and 0 ones, which is 50 — no cubes means the ones digit is 0.
Rods always come first because tens are worth more. 6 rods and 4 cubes is 6 tens and 4 ones, which is 64.
Expanded form breaks a number into its tens value and ones value. 46 = 40 + 6: the 4 tens are worth 40 and the 6 ones are worth 6. Add them back to get 46.
The tens part is the tens digit times ten. In 72, the 7 tens are worth 7 × 10 = 70. The digit is 7, but its value is 70 because it sits in the tens place.
Put the parts back together to check: 70 + 2 = 72. Expanded form and the number are just two ways to write the same amount.
Read expanded form by adding the parts. 40 + 6 = 46. The tens part tells you the left digit, and the ones part tells you the right digit.
The tens part is always a multiple of ten. 80 + 5 = 85. If the ones part is 0, the number ends in 0: 60 + 0 = 60.
Expanded form can be written in either order, but the value is the same: 6 + 40 still makes 46. Add the tens and ones however they appear.
A digit's value depends on its place. In 52, the 5 is worth 50 (5 tens) but the 2 is worth just 2 (2 ones). The same digit means more when it sits in the tens place.
In 33 both digits are 3, but they're worth different amounts: the left 3 is worth 30 and the right 3 is worth 3. The place, not the digit, decides the value.
This is why 40 is bigger than 4: the 4 sits in the tens place in 40, worth 40, but stands alone as 4 ones in 4. Place is everything.
Adding 10 adds one ten, so only the tens digit goes up by 1. 34 + 10 = 44 — the 4 ones stay the same. Subtracting 10 takes one ten away: 34 − 10 = 24.
The ones digit never changes when you add or subtract ten. In 34 + 10, the 4 ones stay; only the tens move. That's why the answer ends in the same digit.
So for one ten, just move the tens digit by one: up for plus, down for minus. The ones ride along unchanged.
Adding 20 adds two tens, so the tens digit goes up by 2. 40 + 30 = 70: 4 tens plus 3 tens is 7 tens. The ones stay the same.
Count the tens you're adding. 26 + 40 adds four tens: 2 tens + 4 tens = 6 tens, so 66. The ones digit (6) rides along unchanged.
The tens add just like small numbers: 5 tens + 3 tens = 8 tens, so 55 + 30 = 85. Add the tens, keep the ones.
Subtracting tens takes whole tens away. 65 − 30 = 35: 6 tens minus 3 tens is 3 tens, and the 5 ones stay. The tens digit drops by the number of tens removed.
The ones digit stays put. In 90 − 40, the 0 ones stay 0; 9 tens minus 4 tens is 5 tens, so 50.
You can count down by tens if it helps: 65, 55, 45, 35 is minus three tens. Or just drop the tens digit by 3. Same result.
To compare two-digit numbers, look at the tens first. 45 vs 52: 4 tens is less than 5 tens, so 45 < 52. More tens means a bigger number. The sign < points to the smaller one.
The number with more tens is greater, even if its ones are smaller. 40 has more tens than 39, so 40 > 39 — even though 0 ones is less than 9 ones.
The symbol opens toward the bigger number: > means the left is greater, < means the left is smaller. 28 < 71 because 2 tens is less than 7 tens.
When two numbers have the same tens, compare the ones. 63 vs 67: both have 6 tens, so look at the ones — 3 is less than 7, so 63 < 67.
Always check the tens first; only when they match do the ones decide. 71 and 76 both have 7 tens, so 1 < 6 means 71 < 76.
If the tens and the ones are both the same, the numbers are equal. 45 = 45. That's when you use the = sign.
To compare any two two-digit numbers: check the tens. If they differ, more tens wins. If they're equal, more ones wins. That one rule handles every pair.
Watch out: a bigger ones digit doesn't win if the tens are smaller. 39 vs 41: 9 ones looks big, but 3 tens is less than 4 tens, so 39 < 41.
Equal numbers have the same tens and ones. Otherwise, the first place that differs decides it — always starting from the tens.

A **rational number** is any number that can be written as a fraction a/b of two integers (b ≠ 0). That includes whole numbers (5 = 5/1), negatives (-2 = -2/1), and familiar decimals (0.5 = 1/2). Every rational number, in decimal form, either stops or repeats forever.

Why do rational decimals always stop or repeat? Long division only ever produces remainders smaller than the divisor — so dividing by 3, the only possible remainders are 0, 1, or 2. Eventually a remainder must repeat, and once it does, the digits after it repeat too.

You can predict the pattern before dividing: a fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator's only prime factors are 2 and/or 5 (since our number system is base ten = 2×5). 1/4 terminates because 4 = 2². 1/3 repeats because 3 is neither a 2 nor a 5.
Always simplify first! 3/6 looks like it has a factor of 3 in the denominator, but 3/6 = 1/2 — after simplifying, the 3 cancels away and only a 2 remains, so it terminates.

To turn a repeating decimal into a fraction: let x equal the decimal, multiply by a power of 10 that shifts one full repeating block to the left of the decimal point, then subtract the original x. The repeating parts cancel, leaving a simple equation to solve for x.

For a TWO-digit repeating block, multiply by 100 instead of 10, so the whole block shifts past the decimal point. Example: x = 0.454545…, so 100x = 45.4545…, and 100x − x = 45, giving 99x = 45, so x = 45/99 = 5/11 once simplified.

Draw a square with side length 1. Its diagonal has length c, where 1² + 1² = c² (the Pythagorean theorem), so c² = 2. No fraction, when squared, lands on exactly 2 — this diagonal's length is called an **irrational number**, written √2.
Compare with √4: since 4 = 2², √4 = 2 exactly — a whole number, so it's rational. But √2, √3, √5, and √7 are irrational, because none of 1, 4, 9, 16, 25, … (the perfect squares) equals 2, 3, 5, or 7.

Every real number is either rational (a fraction a/b — its decimal terminates or repeats a block forever) or irrational (its decimal never terminates and never settles into a repeating block — π, √2, and √3 are classic examples).

A repeating decimal like 0.4545… IS rational (it equals 5/11) — it just looks messy. What makes π different is that its digits never lock into ANY repeating block, no matter how far you go — 3.14159265358979…, forever unpatterned.

Between ANY two different numbers on the number line — no matter how close together — there's always another number hiding in between. Rational and irrational numbers are mixed together everywhere on the line; there are no empty patches.

This matters for locating √2: since 1.4² = 1.96 and 1.5² = 2.25, √2 must be trapped between 1.4 and 1.5. We can keep narrowing forever without ever landing on a clean decimal, because √2 truly never terminates or repeats.
To estimate √n, find the two perfect squares n sits between. For √50: 49 < 50 < 64, and 49 = 7², 64 = 8², so 7 < √50 < 8 — √50 is trapped between the whole numbers 7 and 8.
Once you know the two whole numbers, decide which one it's closer to by comparing how far n is from each perfect square. Since 50 is very close to 49, √50 is much closer to 7 than to 8.
Once √n sits between two whole numbers, narrow further with decimals — testing 7.0², 7.1², 7.2²… — the same squeezing idea, one decimal place at a time.
The same idea applies to π: since π ≈ 3.14159…, at one decimal place π ≈ 3.1. We could keep narrowing to as many decimal places as we want — the digits just never stop or repeat.

To compare irrationals and rationals fairly, convert everything to decimals first. Notation (radicals, fractions, decimals) can trick the eye — decimals put every number on equal footing for comparison.

To estimate an expression like π², use a rational approximation for π — like 3.14 — and compute: 3.14² ≈ 9.86, so π² ≈ 9.86. That estimate is close to, but never exactly, the true (irrational) value of π² itself.

A **translation** slides every point of a shape the same distance in the same direction — no turning, no flipping. On the grid, add the slide to each point: sliding right 4 and down 1 sends (x, y) to (x + 4, y − 1).

Right and up are POSITIVE moves; left and down are NEGATIVE. Sliding left 3 subtracts 3 from x; sliding down 2 subtracts 2 from y. Apply the same shift to every point, and the shape arrives unchanged in size and shape.

A **reflection** flips a shape across a line, like a mirror. Reflecting across the **x-axis** keeps x and flips the sign of y: (x, y) → (x, −y). Reflecting across the **y-axis** flips x: (x, y) → (−x, y).
The mirror line is what you flip ACROSS. Points keep their distance from the line but land on the opposite side. Across the x-axis, a point 5 above lands 5 below. The shape's size never changes.
A **rotation** turns a shape around a center point by an angle. Around the origin, a **180° turn** flips both signs: (x, y) → (−x, −y). A point and its 180° image sit on opposite sides of the center.
A **90° turn counterclockwise** around the origin sends (x, y) → (−y, x): swap the coordinates, then flip the sign of the new first one. For (2, 3): swap to (3, 2), flip the first to get (−3, 2).

You have slid shapes around already. Now write down exactly what a slide **does to the numbers**.

Move three right and two up and every point obeys the same instruction: (x, y) → (x + 3, y + 2). Not the vertices you happen to notice — every point, the same shift. That sentence is the whole transformation.

Because a translation is just addition, two of them in a row simply add up.

Slide (+2, −5) and then (−7, +1) and the net effect is (−5, −4) — one slide doing the work of two. No shape has changed at any stage, which is the deeper point: translations preserve every distance and every angle.

A flip changes exactly one coordinate's sign, and which one depends on the mirror.

Across the **y-axis**, left and right swap: (x, y) → (−x, y). Across the **x-axis**, up and down swap: (x, y) → (x, −y). The coordinate that changes is the one measured *perpendicular* to the mirror line.

Reflections are rigid, and that has a consequence worth noticing: they preserve every length and every angle, yet they reverse **orientation**.

Trace the vertices of the original in order and then trace the image. What ran clockwise now runs anticlockwise. That is the one thing a translation can never do, and it is what distinguishes a flip from a slide.

Translations and reflections are rigid: they move a shape without resizing it. A **dilation** is the one that changes size.

From the origin with scale factor k, the rule is (x, y) → (kx, ky). Every distance from the centre is multiplied by k, so the shape is preserved exactly while the size is not.

A dilation is **not** rigid, and that is exactly its job: it produces a **similar** figure — same angles, all lengths multiplied by k.

That is the difference the whole chapter turns on. Translations, reflections and rotations give congruence; dilations give similarity. And an area does not scale by k, but by k² — doubling the lengths quadruples the space inside.

Two shapes are **congruent** when one can be moved onto the other using only rigid motions — translations, reflections, and rotations. Since those never change size or shape, congruent shapes are identical: same side lengths, same angles.
To show two shapes are congruent, describe a SEQUENCE of rigid motions that maps one exactly onto the other — for example, 'translate, then rotate.' If such a sequence exists, they're congruent.

A **dilation** resizes a shape by a **scale factor** from a center point. From the origin, multiply each coordinate by the scale factor: factor 2 sends (x, y) → (2x, 2y). The shape keeps its proportions but changes size.
A scale factor bigger than 1 enlarges; a factor between 0 and 1 shrinks. Factor ½ sends (6, 8) → (3, 4), shrinking to half. Whatever the factor, the shape's angles and proportions stay the same.

Two shapes are **similar** when one maps onto the other by a dilation, possibly combined with rigid motions. Similar shapes have the SAME ANGLES but PROPORTIONAL side lengths — same shape, possibly different size.

In similar shapes, the ratio between matching sides is the same everywhere — that's the scale factor. If a 3-side matches a 6-side (ratio 2), then a 4-side matches an 8-side, and a 5-side matches a 10-side.

When a line (a **transversal**) crosses two **parallel** lines, it makes eight angles — but only two different sizes. **Corresponding angles** (same position at each crossing) are equal, and **alternate interior angles** (opposite sides, between the lines) are equal too.

Angles that sit together on a straight line are **supplementary** — they add to 180°. So next to a 70° angle, the angle completing the straight line is 110°. Co-interior angles (same side, between the lines) are supplementary this way.
The three angles inside ANY triangle always add up to **180°**. Know two of them and you can find the third by subtracting from 180. This holds for every triangle, no matter its shape.
This works even for right triangles. A right triangle has one 90° angle, so the other two must add to 90°. If one of them is 35°, the last is 90 − 35 = 55°.

Two triangles are **similar** if just TWO pairs of their angles match. Since all three angles of any triangle sum to 180°, matching two forces the third to match too — so the triangles have the same shape. This is the **angle-angle (AA)** rule.

Why does two force the third? Because the three must total 180°. If two triangles share two angles, their third angles are both 180 minus the same sum — so those match automatically. Equal angles mean the same shape.

In a right triangle, name the two short sides (the **legs**) a and b, and the long side opposite the right angle (the **hypotenuse**) c. The **Pythagorean theorem** says a² + b² = c². Build a square on each side to see why.

That area picture is the proof: for ANY right triangle, the squares built on the two legs have areas a² and b², and together they exactly fill the square built on the hypotenuse, whose area is c². So a² + b² = c² always holds.
To find the hypotenuse, add the leg-squares and take the square root: c = √(a² + b²). For legs 3 and 4: c = √(9 + 16) = √25 = 5. Here every answer comes out a whole number.
To find a missing LEG instead, subtract: a = √(c² − b²). If the hypotenuse is 13 and one leg is 5, then a = √(169 − 25) = √144 = 12. Subtract because the hypotenuse-square is the biggest.

The theorem runs backward too — the **converse**: if a triangle's sides satisfy a² + b² = c² (with c the longest), then it's a RIGHT triangle. Test any triangle by checking whether the two smaller squares add to the biggest.
If the two smaller squares DON'T add to the biggest, the triangle is NOT right. For 5, 6, 7: 25 + 36 = 61, but 7² = 49. Since 61 ≠ 49, it fails the test — not a right triangle.

A **cylinder** is a can: a circle stacked into a column. Its volume is the base circle's area times the height: **V = πr²h**. Because answers involve π, we leave them as a number times π (exact) unless asked to round.
The key is squaring the radius FIRST, then multiplying by the height. For r = 5, h = 2: r² = 25, then 25 × 2 = 50, so V = 50π. Squaring the radius is the step most people rush.

A **cone** with the same base and height as a cylinder holds exactly **one-third** as much. So its volume is **V = ⅓πr²h** — the cylinder formula times a third. Three cones fill one matching cylinder.
The reliable method: find the matching cylinder's volume (πr²h) first, then divide by 3. For r = 6, h = 5: cylinder is 36 × 5 = 180, and the cone is 180 ÷ 3 = 60, so V = 60π.
A **sphere** is a perfect ball. Its volume uses the radius cubed: **V = 4⁄3 πr³**. Cube the radius first (r × r × r), multiply by 4, then divide by 3 — leaving the answer as a number times π.

The order that avoids mistakes: cube the radius, multiply by 4, then divide by 3. For r = 6: r³ = 216, times 4 = 864, divided by 3 = 288, so V = 288π. Cubing (not squaring) is the key difference from cylinders and cones.

Congruence means a rigid motion maps one triangle onto another — but checking all **six** parts (three sides, three angles) is a lot. The good news: a triangle is rigid, so a few parts LOCK the rest. A **congruence criterion** is a shortcut — a small set of equal parts that GUARANTEES the motion exists, no need to check the other three.

**SAS** works too: two sides with the **included** angle (the one BETWEEN them). Fix two sticks and the hinge angle between them, and the third side has nowhere to go — it snaps to one length. Included is the key word: the angle must sit between the two sides you're using.

**ASA** flips it: two angles with the **included** side between them. Fix two angles and the side joining their vertices, and the other two sides must meet at exactly one point — one triangle. And because a triangle's angles sum to 180°, knowing two angles gives the third for free.

Not every arrangement locks a triangle. **SSA** — two sides and a NON-included angle — can leave TWO different triangles. Swing the second side from its fixed angle and, for the right lengths, it can reach the base line at two different points. Both fit the given parts; both are legal. So SSA is NOT a congruence criterion.

The same logic exposes **AAA**: three equal angles fix the SHAPE but not the SIZE. A triangle and a scaled-up copy have identical angles yet different side lengths — they're **similar**, not congruent. Angles alone never guarantee congruence; you always need at least one side.

So the valid criteria are exactly **SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS** — each with at least one side, each locking size AND shape. The two impostors are **SSA** (ambiguous — two triangles) and **AAA** (similar — any size). Memorize the winners; recognize the two traps.

Now put criteria to work. A congruence proof has two acts: FIRST prove the triangles congruent by a criterion (SSS/SAS/ASA/AAS); THEN, because congruent triangles match in every part, read off whatever equal side or angle you need. That second act has a name: **CPCTC** — Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent.

Choosing the criterion is a matching game: inventory what you're GIVEN (and what's free — shared sides are reflexive, vertical angles are equal), then pick the criterion whose pattern you can complete. Given two sides and the angle between? SAS. Two angles and a side? ASA or AAS. Three sides? SSS.

One caution graders love: **letter order encodes correspondence.** In △ABC ≅ △DEF, A↔D, B↔E, C↔F. So AB corresponds to DE — not to EF. When you apply CPCTC, match parts by POSITION in the statement, never by how the triangle happens to look.

Right triangles get a fifth criterion the others don't: **HL** — hypotenuse and one leg. Given a right angle, an equal hypotenuse, and one equal leg, the triangles are congruent. It looks like the forbidden SSA (two sides + a non-included angle), but the right angle rescues it — the second leg is forced by the Pythagorean theorem.

HL is really SAS-in-disguise once you compute. Fix the right angle and the two legs (one given, one recovered by Pythagoras) and you have two sides plus the included right angle — the very pattern of SAS. So HL isn't a loophole; it's SAS wearing the right angle as its included angle.

One guardrail: HL needs the **hypotenuse** specifically, plus a leg. Two legs and the right angle would just be SAS. A leg and the hypotenuse with the right angle is HL. But a NON-right angle with two sides is back to ambiguous SSA — the right angle is non-negotiable for HL.

CPCTC is the workhorse for proving parts equal that you can't measure directly. The strategy never changes: find two triangles containing the target parts, prove those triangles congruent by a criterion, then release the part you want with CPCTC. The art is spotting WHICH two triangles hold your target.

Watch for the hidden free parts, they turn a two-given problem into a full criterion. **Shared sides** are reflexively equal. **Vertical angles** at a crossing are equal. **Right angles** are all equal to each other. Each is a part you didn't have to be handed — spot them before declaring a criterion incomplete.

A subtle rule: you may use CPCTC only for parts NOT already used to prove the congruence. You prove the triangles congruent with SOME parts, then CPCTC unlocks the REMAINING ones. It never re-proves a part you already assumed — that would be circular.

The trickiest proofs hide the triangles: they **overlap**, sharing a side or angle. The move is to mentally pull them apart into two separate triangles, then look for the shared part — which is reflexively equal. Once separated, the usual criteria apply as normal.

Some conclusions need **two congruences in sequence**. First prove one pair of triangles congruent to get an intermediate equal part by CPCTC; then USE that part to prove a SECOND pair congruent, and CPCTC again for the final goal. Each CPCTC feeds the next proof — a relay.

A planning tip for these: work BACKWARD from the goal. Ask 'which two triangles contain my target part?' Then 'what do I need to prove those congruent?' If a needed part isn't given, ask 'which earlier congruence could CPCTC it?' Backward planning turns a maze into a checklist.

An **isosceles** triangle has two equal sides — the **legs** — and the angles opposite them, the **base angles**, turn out equal too. This is the Base Angles Theorem: equal legs force equal base angles. It's not obvious from looking; it earns its certainty from a congruence proof.

The bisector does triple duty. In an isosceles triangle, the segment from the apex is at once the **angle bisector**, the **perpendicular bisector of the base**, the **median**, and the **altitude** — all the same line. That coincidence is special to isosceles (and equilateral) triangles.

Equal legs guarantee equal base angles — a one-way street for now. The reverse question (do equal base angles guarantee equal legs?) is the CONVERSE, and it deserves its own proof. That's the next lesson. For now: whenever you see two equal sides, you may immediately mark the base angles equal.

The **converse** of the Base Angles Theorem: if two base angles are equal, then the sides opposite them are equal — the triangle is isosceles. Unlike some converses, this one is TRUE, and it's the tool you use to PROVE a triangle isosceles from its angles.

Push both theorems to the limit with the **equilateral** triangle. All three sides equal means (by the Base Angles Theorem, applied to each pair) all three angles equal — **equiangular**. And each angle is 180 ÷ 3 = **60°**. The converse runs backward: three equal angles ⇒ three equal sides.

So for triangles, **equilateral and equiangular are the same thing** — each implies the other. This tidy equivalence is special to triangles; for polygons with more sides (like a rectangle: equiangular but not equilateral), the two properties can part ways.

Join the **midpoints** of two sides of a triangle and you get a **midsegment** with two striking properties: it's **parallel** to the third side, and it's exactly **half** its length. One little segment, two guarantees — proved with congruent triangles or coordinates.

Why half and parallel? Coordinates make it clean: place the base on the x-axis and compute the two midpoints. Their difference is exactly half the base vector, and its y-component is zero — so the midsegment is parallel and half-length. A congruence proof reaches the same conclusion.

The three midsegments split a triangle into **four** smaller triangles, all congruent to each other and each **similar** to the original at half scale. The middle one is flipped; the three corner ones are translates. It's a tidy self-similar tiling that the midsegment properties guarantee.

Three lines of the same type in a triangle often meet at a single point — they're **concurrent**. The **circumcenter** is where the three **perpendicular bisectors** of the sides meet. Because every point on a side's perpendicular bisector is equidistant from that side's two endpoints, the meeting point is equidistant from all three vertices.

The **incenter** is the other equidistance center: where the three **angle bisectors** meet. Every point on an angle's bisector is equidistant from the two SIDES forming that angle, so the common point is equidistant from all three sides — the center of the inscribed circle that just touches each side.

A tale of two centers: **circumcenter** = perpendicular bisectors = equidistant from VERTICES = circle AROUND. **Incenter** = angle bisectors = equidistant from SIDES = circle INSIDE. The incenter always sits inside the triangle; the circumcenter can fall outside (for an obtuse triangle) since it only cares about vertex distances.

The **centroid** is where the three **medians** meet — a median joins a vertex to the midpoint of the opposite side. It's the triangle's balance point (center of mass), and it always lands inside. Its coordinates are just the **average** of the three vertices' coordinates.

The **orthocenter** is where the three **altitudes** meet — an altitude drops from a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side. Unlike the balance-point centroid, the orthocenter has no averaging or equidistance property; it's purely the altitudes' intersection, and it can land outside an obtuse triangle.

A beautiful bonus: for ANY triangle the **circumcenter, centroid, and orthocenter are collinear** — they lie on one line, the **Euler line**, with the centroid always between, twice as close to the circumcenter as to the orthocenter. (The incenter generally sits off this line.)

Four centers, four jobs. **Circumcenter** (perpendicular bisectors) — equidistant from vertices. **Incenter** (angle bisectors) — equidistant from sides. **Centroid** (medians) — balance point. **Orthocenter** (altitudes) — altitudes' meeting. Knowing the defining LINES and PROPERTY of each is the whole chapter.

A quick memory hook by the LINES: **perpendicular bisectors → circumcenter**, **angle bisectors → incenter**, **medians → centroid**, **altitudes → orthocenter**. And by PROPERTY: two are equidistance centers (circum from vertices, in from sides), the centroid is the balance point, and the orthocenter is the odd one out with no special distance property.

Only two centers are guaranteed to stay INSIDE every triangle: the **centroid** and the **incenter**. The **circumcenter** and **orthocenter** slip outside when the triangle is obtuse. For a right triangle, the circumcenter lands exactly on the hypotenuse's midpoint — a handy special case.

Not every trio of lengths makes a triangle. The **Triangle Inequality** says the sum of any two sides must **exceed** the third. If two sides can't reach across the gap left by the third, they never meet — the triangle collapses flat or fails entirely. Check all three pairings to be safe.

The inequality also **bounds the third side**. Given two sides, the third must be more than their **difference** and less than their **sum**: |a − b| < third < a + b. Too short and the sides overlap; too long and they can't close. That window is exactly the buildable range.

Sides and angles line up in order: the **largest angle sits opposite the largest side**, the smallest opposite the smallest. So in a 5-6-7 triangle, the biggest angle faces the 7. This side-angle ranking lets you order a triangle's angles just by glancing at its sides.

Picture a door hinge with two fixed arms. Open it wider and the gap between the arm-ends grows. That's the **Hinge Theorem**: if two triangles share two pairs of equal sides, the one with the **larger included angle** has the **longer third side**. Same two sides, bigger angle, bigger opposite side.

The Hinge Theorem is really the **SAS inequality** — a cousin of SAS congruence. SAS congruence: equal sides AND equal included angle ⇒ equal third sides (congruent). The hinge: equal sides but a BIGGER included angle ⇒ a bigger third side. Equal angle gives equal; bigger angle gives bigger.

A neat door analogy seals it: the two door edges are the fixed sides; the hinge is the included angle; the gap you'd measure between the door's free edge and the frame is the third side. Swing the door open wider, the gap widens. Close it, the gap shrinks toward zero.

Congruence proofs conclude parts are EQUAL; inequality proofs conclude one part is GREATER. The tools mirror each other: instead of SAS congruence you reach for the **hinge theorem**, instead of the base-angles theorem you use **bigger side ⇒ bigger opposite angle**. The proof shape is the same; only the relation changes from = to >.

The **Exterior Angle Inequality** adds another tool: an exterior angle of a triangle is **greater than either** of the two remote interior angles. (In fact it EQUALS their sum, so it must exceed each.) It's handy for proving one angle bigger than another across a figure.

Putting it together: to prove one segment or angle bigger than another, find the triangle (or two triangles) linking them, then apply the matching inequality — hinge for two triangles sharing sides, side-angle ordering within one triangle, or the exterior-angle inequality across a vertex. Same detective work as congruence, aimed at > instead of =.

Stand at an acute angle θ of a right triangle. The side across from you is the **opposite**; the side touching you (not the hypotenuse) is the **adjacent**; the longest side, across from the right angle, is the **hypotenuse**. Three ratios of these sides get names: **sin θ = opp/hyp, cos θ = adj/hyp, tan θ = opp/adj** — SOH-CAH-TOA.

Move to the OTHER acute angle and the legs swap jobs: what was opposite becomes adjacent and vice versa — the hypotenuse never moves. That swap is why **sin θ = cos(90° − θ)**: one angle's opposite is its complement's adjacent.

Why do the ratios deserve names? **Scale the triangle and they don't change.** Double 3-4-5 into 6-8-10: the sides all doubled, but opp/adj is still 6/8 = 3/4. Similar triangles share every ratio — so sin, cos, and tan depend only on the ANGLE. Tan even has a physical reading: rise over run, the steepness.

Know an angle and one side? A ratio hands you the others. Pick the ratio that links the side you KNOW to the side you WANT. Hypotenuse 20, θ = 30°, want the opposite: sine links them — sin 30° = opp/20, so opp = 20 · sin 30° = 20 · 0.5 = 10. Known hypotenuse ⇒ multiply.

Flip the knowns and the operation flips. If the OPPOSITE is known and the hypotenuse is wanted, sin θ = opp/hyp rearranges to **hyp = opp / sin θ** — divide. Sanity check every answer: the hypotenuse is the longest side, so it must come out BIGGER than the known leg.

Choosing the ratio is a matching game: **which two sides are in play?** Opposite-and-hypotenuse → sine. Adjacent-and-hypotenuse → cosine. Opposite-and-adjacent → tangent — the go-to whenever the hypotenuse isn't part of the story at all.

Sides known, angle missing — run the ratio BACKWARD. If sin θ = 0.5, then θ = sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30°: the inverse function asks “which angle has this sine?” One notation warning: **sin⁻¹ is NOT 1/sin** — the −1 marks an inverse function, not a reciprocal.

Which inverse? Same matching game as before: identify WHICH two sides you hold, and take that ratio's inverse. Opposite-and-hypotenuse → sin⁻¹. Adjacent-and-hypotenuse → cos⁻¹. The two legs → tan⁻¹. The sides choose the function for you.

Built-in check: a right triangle's two acute angles always total 90°. Find one with an inverse and the other is 90° minus it — 36.9° pairs with 53.1°. If your two inverses don't add to 90°, a ratio got flipped somewhere.

Degrees are a human invention — 360 slices because ancient astronomers liked the number. The circle offers its own unit: bend one RADIUS along the rim, and the angle it spans is **one radian**. Since the full rim is 2π radii long, a full turn holds 2π ≈ 6.28 radians.

Why bother? Because radians are the circle's NATIVE unit: they're a pure ratio (arc length ÷ radius), no unit attached — and every clean circle formula, starting with arc length s = rθ next lesson, works **only** when θ is in radians. Degrees always need converting first.

Converting hinges on one anchor: **180° = π radians**. Degrees to radians: multiply by π/180. Radians to degrees: multiply by 180/π. Keep the anchor in view and the factor's direction is never in doubt — the 180 sits opposite the π.

The angles you'll meet constantly are clean fractions of the anchor: **30° = π/6, 45° = π/4, 60° = π/3, 90° = π/2**. The pattern: the denominator tells how many copies fit in 180°. Six 30s, four 45s, three 60s, two 90s — the smaller the angle, the BIGGER the denominator.

Reading π-fractions BACK is the same skill reversed: treat the denominator as a step size and count. π/6 steps are 30° each, so 5π/6 is five 30° steps: 150°. No formula grinding — just steps of a known size.

Angles don't stop at one lap. A negative angle turns CLOCKWISE, and an angle past 2π keeps spinning — a full turn plus a quarter turn lands exactly where the quarter turn does. The landing spot repeats every 2π; the total rotation is what the number records.

Here's what radians buy you. Since 1 radian of angle spans 1 radius of arc, **θ radians span θ radii**: arc length **s = rθ**. One multiplication, no circumference fractions, no 360s — provided θ is in radians.

The classic wreck: feeding DEGREES into s = rθ. Radius 4, angle 90° — plugging 90 straight in claims a 360-unit arc on a circle whose whole rim is only about 25. Convert first: 90° = π/2, then s = 4 · π/2 = 2π ≈ 6.28.
s = rθ is also the **rolling** law. A wheel of radius r that turns through θ radians rolls exactly s = rθ along the ground — the rim unspools onto the road. Every odometer is quietly computing rθ.

Right triangles cap θ below 90° — the unit circle removes the cap. Draw a circle of radius 1 and rotate a point θ from the positive x-axis: **cos θ is the point's x-coordinate, sin θ is its y-coordinate.** For acute θ this reproduces the old ratios (hypotenuse 1) — but now EVERY angle, any size, any sign, has a sine and cosine.

Signs now come free from the QUADRANT. Q1: x and y both positive — everything positive. Q2: x < 0 — only sine positive. Q3: both negative — only tangent (y/x) positive. Q4: y < 0 — only cosine positive. The classic mnemonic, counterclockwise from Q1: **A-S-T-C** — All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine.

Tangent rides along: **tan θ = sin θ / cos θ = y/x** — the SLOPE of the radius line. Its sign follows the quadrant rules, and it has a failure mode the others don't: wherever x = 0 (straight up at 90°, straight down at 270°), the division breaks.

Every angle on the circle leans on Quadrant I. The **reference angle** is the acute angle between the terminal side and the X-AXIS — and the point at any angle has the SAME coordinates as its reference point, up to sign. Size from the reference, sign from the quadrant: that's the whole system.

Three rules, one per outer quadrant — all measuring the gap to the nearest x-axis crossing. **Q2: 180 − θ. Q3: θ − 180. Q4: 360 − θ.** In radians the same shapes: π − θ, θ − π, 2π − θ. Locate the quadrant first; the rule follows.

Now compute anything: **magnitude from the reference angle, sign from A-S-T-C.** cos 150°: reference 30° gives magnitude cos 30° = √3/2 ≈ 0.87; Quadrant II makes cosine negative. Answer: −0.87. Two lookups, one sign check — the whole circle from one quadrant's table.

Two special triangles hand you exact values forever. The half-equilateral (30-60-90) and half-square (45-45-90) give: **sin 30° = 1/2, sin 45° = √2/2, sin 60° = √3/2** — and cosines run the same list BACKWARD. Memory device: √1/2, √2/2, √3/2 — sine climbs the roots as the angle grows.

Combine the table with reference angles and the WHOLE circle is exact. cos 300°: quadrant IV (the C quadrant — cosine positive), reference 360 − 300 = 60°, magnitude cos 60° = 1/2. So cos 300° = **+0.5**. Reference for size, A-S-T-C for sign, table for the number.

Radians change nothing but the labels: **sin(π/6) = 1/2, sin(π/4) = √2/2, sin(π/3) = √3/2.** The denominator names the family — 6 for the 30s, 4 for the 45s, 3 for the 60s — and reference-angle rules run in π-form exactly as before.

Let θ run and track sin θ — the unit circle's HEIGHT. It climbs 0 → 1 (top), falls back through 0, dips to −1 (bottom), and returns: one full lap, one full **wave**. And because lap θ + 2π revisits the same point, the wave repeats forever: sine is **periodic with period 2π**.

Cosine draws the SAME wave from the x-coordinate — identical shape, different starting pose. At θ = 0 the point is (1, 0): so **cosine starts at its peak** (cos 0 = 1) while **sine starts at the midline, rising** (sin 0 = 0). One wave, two entrances.

Real waves rarely swing between ±1 — but two reads recover any wave's anatomy. **Midline = (max + min)/2** — the horizontal center the wave oscillates around. **Amplitude = (max − min)/2** — how far it swings from that center. Average for the center, half-the-span for the swing.

You already own these moves from function transformations: in **y = a sin x + d**, the a is a vertical STRETCH and the d a vertical SHIFT. Trig gives them names: |a| is the **amplitude**, y = d the **midline**. The figure's y = 2 sin x + 1 swings 2 around a center of 1: top 3, bottom −1.
