Reading runs backward, too: a graph hands you the rule. Read the **midline** off the center — that's d. Read the **amplitude** off the swing — that's a. A wave oscillating between 10 and 2 centers on (10+2)/2 = 6 and swings (10−2)/2 = 4: y = 4 sin x + 6.

A negative a is the transformation you'd expect: a **reflection over the midline** (the vertical flip). y = −3 sin x starts at the midline heading DOWN instead of up. The amplitude stays |a| = 3 — amplitude is a distance, and distances don't carry signs.

The last dial sits INSIDE: y = sin(bx). The b is a horizontal squeeze — at b = 2 the input races twice as fast, finishing a full lap in half the room. The rule: **period = 2π/b**. Bigger b, faster wave, SHORTER period.
Designing a wave runs the rule backward: **b = 2π/period**. Want a wave that repeats every π/2? Then b = 2π ÷ (π/2) = 4. The check never lies: b × period must equal 2π, always.

All three dials assemble into **y = a sin(bx) + d**: amplitude → a, midline → d, period → b = 2π/period. Given any wave description, fill the three slots in that order — each read is independent of the others.

Circular motion IS a wave — watch a rider's HEIGHT. A wheel of radius 20 ft with its axle 25 ft up, boarding at the bottom, gives **h(t) = 25 − 20 cos t**: axle height as the midline, radius as the amplitude, and −cos because the ride STARTS at its lowest point.

Every part of the formula is a part of the wheel. **Midline = axle height** (the center of the motion). **Amplitude = radius** (how far the rider swings from it). And the entrance: boarding at the BOTTOM means starting at the minimum — exactly what −cos does (it opens at −1).

Any oscillating data fits the same anatomy from last chapter: **midline = (max + min)/2, amplitude = (max − min)/2**. A tide running between 8 ft and 2 ft centers on 5 ft and swings 3 — the wheel's logic, without the wheel.

Temperatures, tides, daylight hours — anything that cycles fits y = a sin(bt) + d (or its −cos twin). The data hands you two of the dials immediately: a day running from 10° up to 30° has **amplitude (30 − 10)/2 = 10** and **midline (30 + 10)/2 = 20**.

The third dial comes from the real-world REPEAT time: **b = 2π/period**, exactly as in the graphs chapter — except now the period arrives in hours or seconds. A tide repeating every 12 hours takes b = 2π/12 = π/6 ≈ 0.52.

Assembled, the model PREDICTS: plug in a time, get a value. h(t) = 3 sin(πt/6) + 5 models the tide — at t = 3 hours the inside is π/2, sine hits its peak 1, and the tide reads 3 · 1 + 5 = 8 ft: high tide, right on schedule.

One last gift from the unit circle. Every point on it satisfies x² + y² = 1 — that's the Pythagorean theorem on a radius-1 triangle. But x = cos θ and y = sin θ, so for EVERY angle: **sin²θ + cos²θ = 1**. Not an equation to solve — an identity, true always.

The procedure has one subtlety. **cos²θ = 1 − sin²θ** hands you a square, and the root offers TWO candidates: ±. The identity can't tell them apart — the QUADRANT does. Chapter 3's sign rules return: locate θ, then pick.

Fractions run the same machine — and old friends surface. cos θ = 5/13 gives sin²θ = 1 − 25/169 = 144/169, so sin θ = ±12/13: the 5-12-13 triple, living inside the identity. Every Pythagorean triple is a (cos, sin) pair in disguise.

You already move waves UP (midline) and STRETCH them (amplitude, period). The last motion is SIDEWAYS: y = sin(x − C) slides the whole wave **C to the right** — the **phase shift**. Inside the parentheses, minus means right (the same inside-flip as every function shift).

With a period change, read the shift ONLY after factoring: y = sin(2x − π/3) = sin(2(x − **π/6**)) — the shift is π/6, not π/3. The B multiplies the whole inside, so the raw constant overstates the slide by a factor of B.

Every sinusoid is y = **A** sin(**B**(x − **C**)) + **D**: amplitude A (recall), period 2π/B (recall), phase shift C (new), midline D (recall). Four independent dials. To graph: draw the midline, mark the amplitude band, start a sine shape at x = C, and fit one period of length 2π/B.

Going the other way — **reading a graph** — use the landmarks in this order: midline D = (max + min)/2; amplitude A = (max − min)/2; period from repeat-distance, then B = 2π/period; finally C = where a rising midline-crossing sits.

To sketch y = A sin(B(x − C)) + D cleanly, plot the **five key points** of one period: start (midline, rising) at x = C, then quarter-period steps — peak, midline falling, trough, midline rising again. Five dots, one smooth wave through them.

A **negative A** flips the pattern: y = −A sin(…) starts at the midline heading **down** — the five points run start, trough, midline, peak, close. Same dots' x-positions, swapped heights. (Recall reflections: the minus mirrors across the midline.)

Cosine draws the SAME wave shape as sine with one difference: it **starts at the peak**. cos 0 = 1 (recall the unit circle: the point starts at (1, 0), and cosine reads the x-coordinate). Five key points for cos x: peak, midline falling, trough, midline rising, peak.

All four dials work identically on cosine: y = A cos(B(x − C)) + D has amplitude A, period 2π/B, shift C, midline D. Only the **starting posture** differs — cos begins at the top of its band instead of mid-climb.

Slide the sine wave LEFT by π/2 and it starts at a peak — exactly cosine's posture. That's an identity:

**cos x = sin(x + π/2)**  and equally  **sin x = cos(x − π/2)**

Every sinusoid can wear either name; only the phase constant changes.

Choosing a name is about **convenience**: if a graph's rising midline-crossing is easiest to spot, write it as sine from there; if a **peak** is the clean landmark, write cosine with C at the peak. Same curve, cheaper bookkeeping.

A HALF-period slide flips a wave upside down: **sin(x + π) = −sin x** and **cos(x + π) = −cos x**. So reflection (the outside minus, recall) and a π-slide are the SAME motion for sinusoids — one graph can wear rules that look wildly different.

Equivalence is testable: two rules name the same wave iff they agree on the **landmarks** — same midline, amplitude, period, and same value-and-direction at one x. Checking a single well-chosen point (plus the dials) beats expanding identities.

Tangent is a QUOTIENT: tan x = sin x / cos x. Wherever **cos x = 0**, the quotient blows up — a **vertical asymptote** (recall the portrait rule: bottom's zeros build walls). Between walls, tangent sweeps from −∞ up through 0 to +∞: a climbing branch, repeated forever.

Tangent's period is **π**, not 2π: after half a turn, BOTH sin and cos flip sign (recall sin(x + π) = −sin x, cos(x + π) = −cos x), and the two minuses cancel in the quotient. So walls stand at π/2 + kπ, and each branch is one π-wide copy.

Tangent's exact values come straight from the ratio of the exact sin/cos values you know: tan(π/6) = (1/2)/(√3/2) = **1/√3 ≈ 0.58**, tan(π/4) = 1, tan(π/3) = (√3/2)/(1/2) = **√3 ≈ 1.73**. The trio 0.58, 1, 1.73 climbs — as every tangent branch does.

Pressed against a wall, tangent is one-sided: approaching π/2 **from the left**, cos shrinks through tiny POSITIVE values while sin ≈ 1, so tan → **+∞**; from the right, cos is tiny and NEGATIVE, so tan → **−∞**. Each branch exits its wall at opposite infinities.

Tangent takes the same dials with two twists. **Period:** y = tan(Bx) has period **π/B** (the base period is π, not 2π). **No amplitude:** a branch already spans −∞ to +∞, so A in y = A tan x only steepens the climb — there is no max to scale.

Slides work unchanged: y = tan(x − C) moves every zero and every wall right by C, spacing intact. To find any wall of a transformed tangent, set the whole **inside equal to π/2 + kπ** and solve — one equation covers stretch and slide at once.

sin x fails the horizontal line test spectacularly — every output is hit infinitely often — so, recall the rescue: **restrict the domain**. Keep only **[−π/2, π/2]**, one clean climb from −1 to 1. THAT piece is one-to-one, and its inverse is **arcsin** (also written sin⁻¹).

Domain and range swap (recall): sin on the branch has domain [−π/2, π/2] and range [−1, 1], so **arcsin has domain [−1, 1] and range [−π/2, π/2]**. Inputs beyond ±1 are meaningless — no angle has sine 2.

Cosine can't use sine's branch: on [−π/2, π/2] cosine rises then falls — it repeats outputs (cos(−π/3) = cos(π/3)), failing the line test. Cosine's clean one-to-one run is **[0, π]**, a pure descent from 1 to −1. So **arccos has range [0, π]** — never negative.

Tangent's turn: one full climbing branch, **(−π/2, π/2)** — OPEN, because the walls are excluded values. **arctan** inverts it: domain ALL reals (each branch spans −∞ to +∞), range (−π/2, π/2), and the walls become **horizontal asymptotes** of arctan: y → ±π/2 as x → ±∞. (Recall: inverses swap domain and range — so vertical walls swap into horizontal ones.)

Each inverse graph is its branch **reflected across y = x** (recall the mirror). Arcsine: an S-shaped climb from (−1, −π/2) to (1, π/2). Arccosine: a descent from (−1, π) to (1, 0). Arctangent: a flattening climb pinched between the lines y = ±π/2.

Arctangent's mirror inherits tangent's landmarks: the branch's center (0, 0) stays put, its steepness flattens (steep sections mirror into flat ones), and the vertical walls x = ±π/2 mirror into the **horizontal fences y = ±π/2** that arctan approaches forever.

One composition direction is always safe: **sin(arcsin v) = v** for every v in [−1, 1] — arcsin outputs a branch angle, and sine happily eats it. The reverse, **arcsin(sin x)**, equals x ONLY when x already lies in the branch [−π/2, π/2]. Outside it, the round trip returns a different angle (recall the same one-way trap from verifying inverses).

The general rule: **arcsin(sin x)** answers *"which BRANCH angle has the same sine as x?"* For second-quadrant x, that's the mirror **π − x**; the same logic gives arccos(cos x) = the [0, π] angle sharing x's cosine. Compositions of DIFFERENT functions, like cos(arcsin v), come next.

What is cos(arcsin(3/5))? Name the hidden angle: θ = arcsin(3/5) means **sin θ = 3/5 with θ in the branch**. Draw the helper right triangle — opposite 3, hypotenuse 5 — and the missing leg is 4 (recall 3-4-5). So cos θ = **4/5**, no calculator, exactly.

The identity route (recall sin²θ + cos²θ = 1) gives the same answer: cos θ = ±√(1 − v²), and the **branch chooses the sign** — arcsin's outputs in [−π/2, π/2] always have cos θ ≥ 0, so cos(arcsin v) = **+√(1 − v²)** for every valid v, even negative ones.

sin x = 1/2 has infinitely many solutions, but **arcsin hands you exactly one**: x₁ = arcsin(1/2) = π/6. The rest come from the circle (recall reference angles): sine repeats its value at the **supplement π − x₁**, and everything recurs every 2π. On [0, 2π): x = π/6 and 5π/6.

Tangent is easiest: period π means solutions come **one per branch** — x₁ = arctan(v), then x₁ + π, x₁ + 2π, … On [0, 2π), tan x = 1 gives π/4 and π/4 + π = 5π/4. The pairing rule depends on the FUNCTION: supplement for sine, reflection for cosine, +π for tangent.

On [0, 2π), sin x = 1/2 gave two solutions (recall the twins π/6 and 5π/6). But sine repeats every 2π forever, so EVERY solution is one of those two **plus any whole number of turns**:

x = π/6 + 2πk or x = 5π/6 + 2πk, k any integer.

Two families capture infinitely many answers.

Why two families and not one? Because 2π-stepping from π/6 never reaches 5π/6 (they differ by 2π/3, not a multiple of 2π). The complete answer is always: **each [0, 2π) solution founds its own +2πk family**. Same recipe for cosine with its twins x₁ and 2π − x₁.

Tangent's period is **π** (recall), so its general solution needs only **one family with a π step**: tan x = 1 gives x = π/4 + **πk** — no twin required, because the twin (5π/4) is just the k = 1 rung. A denser ladder from a shorter period.

Sine and cosine families can ALSO merge when the twins are exactly π apart. cos x = 0 has base solutions π/2 and 3π/2 — a π gap — so the two 2πk families collapse into the single dense family **x = π/2 + πk**. Always check the twin gap before writing two ladders.

For sin(2x) = 1/2, solve for the INSIDE first: 2x = π/6 + 2πk or 2x = 5π/6 + 2πk. Then divide EVERYTHING — including the 2πk — by 2:

x = π/12 + **πk** or x = 5π/12 + **πk**.

The ladder step shrinks with the period: dividing by B compresses the spacing too.

The full recipe for A·trig(B(x − C)) = v: **(1)** isolate the trig; **(2)** write the inside's general ladder from the base twins; **(3)** solve the linear equation inside = ladder for x — dividing or shifting the ENTIRE expression, k-term included.

Every trig function is built from sine and cosine. The **quotient** identity (recall the ratio observation): tan θ = sin θ / cos θ. The three **reciprocals** name the flips: **sec θ = 1/cos θ**, **csc θ = 1/sin θ**, **cot θ = 1/tan θ = cos θ/sin θ**. Learn the pairings, not six separate objects.

These identities also **simplify** expressions. sin θ · sec θ = sin θ · (1/cos θ) = sin θ/cos θ = **tan θ**. The trick is always the same: rewrite everything in sines and cosines, then cancel. Complicated-looking products collapse.

From the one identity you know — **sin²θ + cos²θ = 1** (recall) — two more appear by division. Divide every term by **cos²θ**:

tan²θ + 1 = **sec²θ**.

Divide instead by **sin²θ**:

1 + cot²θ = **csc²θ**.

Three identities, one parent.

These shine when **simplifying**: sec²θ − 1 collapses straight to **tan²θ**, and 1 − sin²θ becomes **cos²θ**. Spotting a Pythagorean pair inside a messy expression is the single most useful move in identity work.

To PROVE an identity, transform **one side** until it matches the other — never move terms across the equals sign (that assumes what you're proving). The reliable strategy: pick the messier side, **convert to sines and cosines**, and simplify using the toolkit.

A harder pattern: combine fractions over a common denominator, then look for a Pythagorean collapse. To prove **(1 − cos²θ)/sin θ = sin θ**: the numerator 1 − cos²θ is sin²θ, so the fraction is sin²θ/sin θ = sin θ. Recognizing the identity BEFORE grinding saves all the algebra.

You know exact values at 30°, 45°, 60°. The **sum and difference formulas** unlock their combinations — 75° = 45° + 30°, 15° = 45° − 30°:

sin(A ± B) = sin A cos B ± cos A sin B
cos(A ± B) = cos A cos B ∓ sin A sin B

Note cosine's sign **flips**: plus-angle uses minus in the formula.

Cosine's sign flip is the classic trap: cos(A + B) = cos A cos B **−** sin A sin B. The plus-angle takes a minus. So cos 75° = cos45°cos30° − sin45°sin30° = (√6 − √2)/4 ≈ 0.2588 — a small positive, as a 75° cosine should be.

Tangent has its own formula, all tangents:

tan(A ± B) = (tan A ± tan B) / (1 ∓ tan A tan B).

The denominator's sign is OPPOSITE the numerator's. For tan 75° = tan(45° + 30°): (1 + 1/√3)/(1 − 1·1/√3), which simplifies to **2 + √3 ≈ 3.732**.

**Cofunctions**: sin and cos are the SAME wave a quarter-turn apart (recall cos x = sin(x + π/2)), which means **sin(90° − θ) = cos θ** and cos(90° − θ) = sin θ. 'Co' literally means *complementary*: each function of an angle equals its cofunction of the complement.

Read backwards, the formulas COMPRESS. Spot the pattern sin A cos B + cos A sin B and rewrite it as the single **sin(A + B)**. This collapses scary expressions: sin 40° cos 10° + cos 40° sin 10° is just **sin 50° ≈ 0.766** — no evaluation of the parts needed.

A recurring simplification: **sin(x + π) = −sin x** falls right out of the sum formula (sin x cos π + cos x sin π = sin x·(−1) + 0 = −sin x). Every reflection and shift identity from the graphing chapter is really a sum formula in disguise.

Set A = B = θ in the sum formulas and the **double-angle** identities fall out:

sin 2θ = **2 sin θ cos θ**
cos 2θ = **cos²θ − sin²θ**

These turn a doubled angle into single-angle pieces — the key to both evaluating and later un-doubling.

**Sign warning:** cos 2θ can be negative even when θ is acute — it flips once θ passes 45°. And sin 2θ depends on θ's quadrant through cos θ: if θ sits in Quadrant II with sin θ = 3/5, then cos θ = −4/5 and sin 2θ = 2·(3/5)·(−4/5) = **−24/25**.

Using sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, cos 2θ wears **three equal forms**:

cos 2θ = cos²θ − sin²θ = **1 − 2sin²θ** = **2cos²θ − 1**.

Each is best in a different situation: pick the one matching what you're GIVEN or what you want to CANCEL.

Read backwards, these give the crucial **power-reduction** formulas — the way to lower an exponent:

sin²θ = (1 − cos 2θ)/2,  cos²θ = (1 + cos 2θ)/2.

They trade a squared single-angle for a first-power double-angle — indispensable in calculus and for solving certain equations.

Double-angle identities SOLVE and PROVE. To prove sin 2θ/sin θ = 2 cos θ: expand the top — 2 sinθ cosθ/sinθ = 2 cos θ. The sin θ cancels. Whenever a '2θ' meets a 'θ', expand the double angle so everything speaks one angle.

For EQUATIONS, expanding turns a mixed-angle equation into one solvable angle. sin 2x = sin x becomes 2 sinx cosx = sinx, then **2 sinx cosx − sinx = 0**, factor **sinx(2cosx − 1) = 0** — two simple equations (recall zero-product).

Many trig equations are **quadratics wearing a trig coat**: 2sin²x − sin x − 1 = 0 is just 2u² − u − 1 = 0 with u = sin x. Factor as usual — (2sin x + 1)(sin x − 1) = 0 — then solve each simple trig equation with the twin/ladder rules (recall).
Watch for branches with **no solution**: if a factor gives sin x = 2, discard it — sine never exceeds 1 (recall arcsin's domain). Only real, in-range values survive to the twin/ladder step.

When an equation mixes sin AND cos with different powers, **convert to one function** using an identity. For 2cos²x + 3sin x − 3 = 0, replace cos²x with 1 − sin²x (Pythagorean): the equation becomes all-sine, then factors as a quadratic in sin x.

Choose the substitution that leaves the LOWEST power: if the equation has sin²x and cos x, replace **sin²x = 1 − cos²x** to get an all-cosine quadratic. Converting toward the linear term's function keeps the algebra a clean quadratic.

Two operations create traps. **Squaring** both sides can invent **extraneous** roots — always substitute back and discard failures. **Dividing** by a trig factor can DELETE roots — factor instead of dividing (recall). Both traps come from operations that aren't reversible.

The dividing trap: solving sin x cos x = sin x by DIVIDING by sin x gives only cos x = 1 — losing every solution where sin x = 0. Factor instead: sin x(cos x − 1) = 0 keeps BOTH branches. Never divide away a factor that can equal zero.
Distributing works the same way with a **negative** multiplier — every term still gets multiplied, sign included. -3(x + 2) = -3x + (-3)(2) = -3x − 6.
Check any distribution by evaluating both the original and expanded form at the same x — they must match at EVERY value, not just one.
Two negatives multiply to a positive — the same sign rule from the last course applies here too. -2(x − 6) = -2x + 12.
Combining like terms works the same with negative coefficients — add the coefficients using the signed-number rules you already know. -3x + 5x: different signs, so 5-3=2, keep positive: 2x.
Constants (plain numbers) stay separate from x-terms. Simplify each group on its own: 4n + 3 + 2n = (4n+2n) + 3 = 6n + 3.
You can distribute first, then combine — 2(x+3)+4x becomes 2x+6+4x, and combining the x-terms gives 6x+6.
You now have every tool for simplifying linear expressions: distribute using the sign rule, then combine like terms using the signed-number rules.
The order of operations always matters: distribute (multiply into the parentheses) before you combine (add matching terms together).
Practice noticing which pattern you're facing — pure distribution, pure combining, or both together — before you start computing.

Distributing takes 3(x + 4) apart into 3x + 12. **Factoring** runs the same road the other way: it takes 3x + 12 and finds the equal groups hiding inside it.

The question factoring asks is always the same — *what does every term share?* Here both 3x and 12 are divisible by 3, so three equal rows of (x + 4) can be built.

A common factor is not always **the** common factor. 12x + 18 really does equal 2(6x + 9) — but a 3 is still hiding inside that bracket, so the job is half done.

Taking out the *greatest* common factor, 6, leaves 6(2x + 3) with nothing left to pull. That is what "fully factored" means.

Raise a price *a* by 5% and the natural way to write it is two moves: the price, plus 5% of the price. That is a + 0.05a.

But a is really 1a, so a + 0.05a is 1a + 0.05a — like terms. Combined, they are **1.05a**. Same value, one move instead of two.

The multiplier form is not merely shorter — it is more **useful**. Two increases in a row become 1.05 × 1.05 instead of a two-line calculation done twice, and a decrease of 20% becomes × 0.80.

That is what the standard means by rewriting an expression to shed light: the second form makes the rate visible as a single number.

8n + 8 and 8(n + 1) are the same number for every n. They are not equally **useful**.

If you want the total cost, 8n + 8 is already arithmetic you can do. If you want to know how many things were bought at $8 each, 8(n + 1) says it outright: n + 1 of them. The question picks the form.

There is a test, and it is not opinion: two forms are equivalent when they agree for **every** value of the variable, not just the one you tried.

One substitution can fool you — 2x and x² both give 4 at x = 2. Distributing or factoring is what proves equivalence; substitution only ever disproves it.
A two-step equation like 3x + 4 = 19 needs two undo-moves: first subtract 4 from both sides (3x = 15), then divide both sides by 3 (x = 5).
The order matters: undo addition/subtraction FIRST (it's outside the multiplication), then undo the multiplication last.
Always check your answer by substituting it back into the ORIGINAL equation — if both sides match, you solved it correctly.
When the x-coefficient is negative, the same two steps work — undo addition/subtraction, then divide by the negative coefficient, using the signed-number rules you already know.
The result can also come out negative — different signs give a negative quotient, exactly as you learned before.
Always check your work carefully with negative coefficients — a sign slip anywhere gives a completely wrong answer.
Real problems translate into two-step equations. A cab charges $3 plus $4 per mile; a $19 fare means 4m + 3 = 19, so m = 4 miles.
A temperature-drop story can involve a negative coefficient — the same two-step method still applies, using the sign rules you know.
Whatever the story — fares, temperatures, savings — translate it into px+q=r, then solve with the same two steps.

An equation is a balanced scale: 2x + 3 = 11 says the two pans weigh the same. You can take tiles away — but only if you take the SAME amount off BOTH pans. Take from one side only and the beam tips: the two sides stop being equal, and the equation you're holding is no longer the one you started with.

Notice the order the balance forces on you. You can't share the pans into equal groups while loose unit tiles sit next to the x-tiles — so the units must be cleared FIRST, and the splitting comes LAST. That is exactly why, on paper, you subtract before you divide.

An equation like 5x + 3 = 28 is a machine: x goes in, the machine multiplies by 5, then adds 3, and 28 comes out. Solving it means UNDOING the machine. And undoing has a rule: the LAST thing the machine did is the FIRST thing you undo. The + 3 happened last, so it goes first — subtract 3, then divide by 5.

Once the undo machine is built, solving is just feeding it the answer-side number. For 6x − 5 = 25: send 25 through the undo track — add 5 to get 30, divide by 6 to get x = 5. Every two-step equation you've solved was secretly this: build the undo, run the number through it.
An equation like 3(x + 2) = 18 has parentheses first — distribute across them before solving. 3(x+2)=18 becomes 3x+6=18, then solve the usual way: x=4.
The parentheses can hold a subtraction too — distribute the same way, watching the signs carefully.
After distributing, the equation looks exactly like the two-step equations from the last chapter — the same undo-moves apply.
When the multiplier outside the parentheses is negative, distribute using the sign rule, then solve as usual. -2(x + 5) = -6: distribute to -2x-10=-6, then solve: x=-2.
A negative multiplier with a subtraction inside gives a positive constant when distributed — same signs multiply to positive.
Always double-check the distribution step first — a sign error there carries through the entire solve.
You now handle any parenthesized equation: distribute using the sign rule, then solve the two-step equation that results — whatever the multiplier's sign.
The very first move is always the same: identify the multiplier outside the parentheses, and distribute it across every term inside.
Practice catching your own errors: if your final answer doesn't satisfy the ORIGINAL equation when substituted back, retrace your distribution step.
Solving a two-step inequality uses the same undo-moves as an equation — with a POSITIVE coefficient, the direction never changes. 3x + 2 > 14: subtract 2, divide by 3: x > 4.
Check a solved inequality by testing a number from the solution set — plug it into the ORIGINAL inequality and confirm it holds true.
The comparator (>, <, ≥, ≤) stays exactly the same throughout, as long as you never multiply or divide by a negative number.
Dividing an inequality by a NEGATIVE number flips the direction. -2x + 5 > -3: subtract 5 (-2x>-8), divide by -2 — and FLIP: x < 4.
The rule only triggers when you multiply or divide by a negative — adding or subtracting a negative number never flips anything.
A useful check: pick a number in your solution set and test it in the ORIGINAL inequality — if it works, you flipped correctly.
Real problems translate into inequalities too. A budget story: saving $5 a week plus $20 already saved, wanting at least $50 — 5x + 20 >= 50 — solves to x >= 6 weeks.
The first move for any story problem is the same: identify the constant fee, the per-unit rate, and the target — then write px+q [comparator] r.
Whatever the story — savings, cost limits, temperature — the same two rules apply: undo addition/subtraction first, then divide, flipping only for a negative.
Fractions add by counting pieces — but only when the pieces are the same size. Halves and thirds cannot be counted together any more than metres and inches can.
This is why 1/2 + 1/3 is not 2/5. Adding across ignores the piece sizes entirely, and produces an answer smaller than one of the parts.
A common denominator is a piece size both fractions can be cut into. Any shared multiple of the two denominators will do.
Renaming does not change either fraction — it re-cuts the same amount into finer pieces, which is exactly what scaling top and bottom accomplishes.
Any common multiple works, but the LEAST one keeps the numbers smallest and the simplifying lightest.
For fourths and sixths, both 24 and 12 are shared sizes. Twelve is the least, so it is the one worth choosing.
Both fractions must be renamed, not just one. Each gets its own scaling factor, chosen so that both land on the shared denominator.
1/4 and 1/6 into twelfths: the first scales by 3, the second by 2. Different factors, same destination.
Once both fractions wear the same denominator, addition is pure counting: the pieces match, so the totals simply combine.
The denominator does not add. It names the piece size, and the pieces stayed the same size throughout.
Subtraction runs the same course: rename to a shared size, then take one count from the other.
The demand is identical — matching pieces — because you cannot remove thirds from halves any more than you can add them.
Mixed numbers carry wholes and parts at once. Add the fraction parts and the whole parts separately, then reassemble.
If the fraction parts pass one whole, the extra whole moves across — the same carrying that whole-number addition uses.
Subtracting mixed numbers works the same way — provided the top fraction is big enough to subtract from.
Converting both to improper fractions sidesteps the question entirely: with everything in pieces, there are no wholes to trade.
When the top fraction is smaller than the bottom one, trade a whole: 4 1/8 becomes 3 9/8, because one whole is eight eighths.
This is the fraction version of borrowing, and it obeys the same law — the amount is unchanged, only its packaging moves.
Simplifying divides top and bottom by their greatest common factor. The value does not move; the numbers just get smaller.
It is the exact inverse of renaming: one scales up to make pieces match, the other scales down once counting is done.
Benchmark estimation rounds each fraction to 0, 1/2 or 1 before any renaming happens. 7/8 + 1/12 is about 1 + 0.
It costs one glance and rules out most wrong answers, including every result of adding across.
A reasonable answer sits where the parts put it: a sum must exceed each part it was built from, and two proper fractions cannot exceed two.
That single comparison rejects 2/5 as the sum of 1/2 and 1/3 without any calculation at all.
Word problems hide the denominators in the words: read for the quantities, find the shared piece size, then count.
The mathematics is unchanged. Only the job of spotting which fractions are being combined, and in which direction, is new.
Multi-step fraction problems rename ONCE, to a denominator all the fractions share, and then run the steps in the story's order.
Renaming at every step wastes work and invites mistakes. One shared size carries the whole chain.

A **vector** carries two facts at once: a **magnitude** (how much) and a **direction** (which way). In components, v = ⟨a, b⟩ means 'go a right and b up.' Unlike a plain number — a scalar — a vector points somewhere. Velocity, force, and displacement are all vectors.

Magnitude is pure Pythagoras: |⟨a, b⟩| = √(a² + b²). The components are the legs of a right triangle; the vector is the hypotenuse. That's why ⟨3, 4⟩, ⟨5, 12⟩, and ⟨6, 8⟩ have the clean lengths 5, 13, and 10 — they're the Pythagorean triples.

A vector's **direction angle** θ is measured counterclockwise from the positive x-axis. Find it from the components: θ is the angle whose tangent is b/a — **with a quadrant check** (recall the arctan trap from polar). For ⟨1, √3⟩: |v| = 2 and tan θ = √3, so θ = 60° in Quadrant I.

Reverse the process to BUILD a vector from its size and angle — the polar→rectangular formulas (recall):

a = |v| cos θ,  b = |v| sin θ.

A vector of magnitude 10 at 30° is ⟨10cos30°, 10sin30°⟩ = ⟨5√3, 5⟩ ≈ ⟨8.66, 5⟩.

A vector from point A to point B is the **displacement** — subtract tail from tip, coordinate by coordinate:

AB = ⟨x_B − x_A, y_B − y_A⟩.

From A(1, 2) to B(4, 6): ⟨4 − 1, 6 − 2⟩ = ⟨3, 4⟩. The vector records the trip, not the starting spot.

Two vectors are **equal** if they have the same components — regardless of where they're drawn. The displacement ⟨3, 4⟩ starting at the origin and the same ⟨3, 4⟩ starting at (10, 10) are the SAME vector: identical magnitude and direction. Position is not part of a vector's identity.

To **add** vectors, add matching components:

⟨a, b⟩ + ⟨c, d⟩ = ⟨a + c, b + d⟩.

Geometrically, place the second vector's tail at the first's tip — the sum runs from the very start to the very end. This **tip-to-tail** picture is why forces and displacements combine the way they do.

**Subtraction** is adding the opposite: ⟨a, b⟩ − ⟨c, d⟩ = ⟨a − c, b − d⟩. Geometrically, u − v points **from the tip of v to the tip of u** — exactly the displacement idea (recall). Order matters: u − v and v − u are opposites.

Multiplying a vector by a **scalar** k scales every component: k⟨a, b⟩ = ⟨ka, kb⟩. This **stretches** the vector's length by |k| and keeps its direction — unless k is negative, which **flips** it to point the opposite way. The direction is preserved (k > 0) or reversed (k < 0), never rotated.

A **unit vector** has length 1. To build one pointing along v, divide by the magnitude: **û = v/|v|**. For ⟨6, 8⟩ (length 10): û = ⟨6/10, 8/10⟩ = ⟨0.6, 0.8⟩ — same direction, length exactly 1. Unit vectors capture pure direction.

Any vector splits into **length × direction**: v = |v|·û. This lets you REBUILD a vector at a chosen length: to get a vector of length 15 along ⟨3, 4⟩, take 15·û = 15·⟨0.6, 0.8⟩ = ⟨9, 12⟩. Unit vectors are the 'pure direction' you scale to any size.

Vectors shine for **combining motions**. A boat heads across a river at ⟨0, 4⟩ (m/s) while the current pushes ⟨3, 0⟩. Its true velocity is the sum ⟨3, 4⟩ — speed 5 m/s, angled downstream. The components handle each direction independently, then combine.

The **dot product** multiplies two vectors into a single NUMBER (a scalar):

⟨a, b⟩ · ⟨c, d⟩ = ac + bd.

Multiply matching components, then add. ⟨3, 4⟩ · ⟨1, 2⟩ = 3·1 + 4·2 = 11. The result isn't a vector — it measures how much the two vectors point the same way.

The sign of the dot product reveals the rough angle: **positive** if the vectors point generally the same way (< 90° apart), **zero** if perpendicular, **negative** if generally opposite (> 90°). This is the dot product's superpower — it detects alignment.

The dot product also encodes the exact **angle** between vectors:

cos θ = (u · v) / (|u| |v|).

Divide the dot product by the product of magnitudes to get the cosine, then take arccos (recall). This one formula turns component arithmetic into geometry.

When cos θ = 1 the vectors are **parallel** (same direction, 0°); when cos θ = −1 they're **antiparallel** (opposite, 180°). Parallel vectors are scalar multiples of each other, so their dot product equals the full product of magnitudes — no 'wasted' perpendicular part.

In physics, **work** = force · displacement — literally the dot product:

W = F · d.

Only the part of the force ALONG the motion does work. A force ⟨6, 8⟩ N moving an object ⟨10, 0⟩ m does W = 6·10 + 8·0 = **60 joules** — the vertical 8 contributes nothing to horizontal motion.

The **projection** idea underlies this: u · v = |u| |v| cos θ picks out the shadow of one vector on the other. When they align (θ = 0°), the dot product is maximal (full |u||v|); at 90° it's zero. Work measures exactly the force's shadow along the path.

A **2×2 matrix** is a square of four numbers, [[a, b], [c, d]]. Add matrices entry by entry, and scale by multiplying every entry. The real power is the **matrix-vector product**, which sends a vector to a new vector:

[[a, b], [c, d]]·⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨ax + by, cx + dy⟩.

Each output component is a **row of the matrix dotted with the vector** (recall the dot product). The top row makes the new x; the bottom row makes the new y. A matrix is a machine that recombines a vector's coordinates by fixed recipes — the rows.

The **determinant** of [[a, b], [c, d]] is **ad − bc** — a single number measuring how the matrix scales area (recall the unit square). det[[1, 2], [3, 4]] = 1·4 − 2·3 = −2. Its sign tells orientation; its size tells the area factor; **zero means the matrix collapses the plane** (no inverse).

When det ≠ 0, the **inverse** exists:

[[a, b], [c, d]]⁻¹ = (1/det)·[[d, −b], [−c, a]].

Swap the diagonal, negate the off-diagonal, divide by the determinant. The inverse UNDOES the matrix: M⁻¹(M·v) = v.

A linear system is a matrix equation. The system 2x + y = 5, x + 3y = 10 becomes [[2, 1], [1, 3]]·⟨x, y⟩ = ⟨5, 10⟩ — recall solving these by elimination (se). Now: multiply both sides by the **inverse** to isolate ⟨x, y⟩ = M⁻¹·⟨5, 10⟩. Same answers, matrix machinery.

When the determinant is **zero**, the matrix method signals trouble: the system has either **no solution** (parallel lines) or **infinitely many** (the same line). A zero determinant is exactly the algebraic sign that elimination would stall — the two viewpoints agree (recall se's special cases).

A matrix is a **transformation of the plane**: feed it every point ⟨x, y⟩ and it maps them to new points ⟨x′, y′⟩ (recall the mapping notation from geometry). The matrix-vector product IS the rule (x, y) → (x′, y′). Scaling, reflecting, and rotating all become single matrices.

Here's the key to READING a transformation matrix: its **columns are the images of the basis vectors**. The first column is where ⟨1, 0⟩ lands; the second is where ⟨0, 1⟩ lands. Know where the two arrows go, and you know the whole matrix — every other point follows.

Rotation by angle θ (counterclockwise, about the origin) is the matrix

[[cos θ, −sin θ], [sin θ, cos θ]].

Its columns are where the basis vectors swing to: ⟨1, 0⟩ → ⟨cos θ, sin θ⟩ and ⟨0, 1⟩ → ⟨−sin θ, cos θ⟩ (recall the unit circle). Every point rotates rigidly around the origin.

Special rotations are clean: **180°** is [[−1, 0], [0, −1]] (negate everything — point reflection through the origin), and **360°** returns the identity [[1, 0], [0, 1]]. Rotation preserves length and angle: it's a **rigid motion** (recall geometry), so magnitudes never change.

To do one transformation **then** another, **multiply the matrices**. For 'apply B, then A,' the combined matrix is A·B (the second one goes on the LEFT). Matrix product:

[[a, b], [c, d]]·[[e, f], [g, h]] = [[ae+bg, af+bh], [ce+dg, cf+dh]].

Each entry is a row of A dotted with a column of B.

**Order matters**: A·B and B·A usually differ, because doing a reflection then a rotation is not the same as rotation then reflection. This mirrors geometry — the sequence of rigid motions changes the outcome. Matrix multiplication is **not commutative**.

Metric units step by powers of ten. A kilometer is 1000 meters, a meter is 100 centimeters, a kilogram is 1000 grams, a liter is 1000 milliliters. Going from a **bigger** unit to a **smaller** one, multiply: 3 km = 3 × 1000 = 3000 m.

Going the other way — **smaller** unit to **bigger** — divide. 3500 grams in kilograms: 3500 ÷ 1000 = 3.5 kg. The number gets smaller because each bigger unit holds many small ones. Multiply going down the ladder, divide going up.

Customary units use their own factors — not tens. A foot is 12 inches, a yard is 3 feet, a pound is 16 ounces, a gallon is 4 quarts. The direction rule still holds: bigger unit to smaller, multiply. 3 feet = 3 × 12 = 36 inches.

Going from a smaller unit up to a bigger one, divide. 48 ounces in pounds: 48 ÷ 16 = 3 lb. Same as before — down the ladder multiply, up the ladder divide — only the factor changes with each pair of units.

Some conversions need two jumps through a middle unit. Yards to inches goes through feet: 3 yd = 3 × 3 = 9 ft, then 9 × 12 = 108 in. Plan the chain first — name the middle unit — then convert one rung at a time.

Capacity chains work the same way. Gallons to cups goes through quarts: 1 gal = 4 qt, and 1 qt = 4 cups. So 1.5 gal = 1.5 × 4 = 6 qt, then 6 × 4 = 24 cups. Write the middle unit down — most multi-step mistakes are a skipped rung.

A line plot stacks an X above a number line for each measurement. When we measure lengths in fractions of a foot, the line is marked in quarters. Here are eight ribbons: 1/4 → XX, 1/2 → XXX, 3/4 → X, 1 → XX. Each X is one ribbon measured at that length.

Two more readings. The **total** number measured is all the X's added up. The **range** is the longest minus the shortest length on the plot. On our plot the shortest is 1/4 and the longest is 1, so the spread runs from 1/4 to 1 foot.

A line plot isn't just for reading — you can compute with it. To find the **total** length, multiply each measurement by how many X's it has, then add. For the plot 1/4 → XX, 1/2 → XXX, 3/4 → X, that's 2×(1/4) + 3×(1/2) + 1×(3/4).

Two more questions a plot answers. The **difference** between the longest and shortest is a subtraction (3/4 − 1/4). And if you pooled everything and split it **equally** among the items, each share is the total ÷ the number of items. Both are just fraction arithmetic on the data.

**Volume** is the amount of space a solid shape fills. To measure it, we fill the shape with **unit cubes** — little cubes that are 1 unit long on every edge. One unit cube takes up exactly **1 cubic unit** of space. So volume is really just a count: how many unit cubes fit inside?

When the cubes have real sizes, the count gets a label. If each cube is 1 centimeter on every edge, one cube is **1 cubic centimeter (cm³)**, and the volume in cm³ equals the number of cubes. Bigger cubes give bigger units: **cubic inches (in³)** or **cubic meters (m³)**. The little **3** means three dimensions — length, width, and height.

Counting cubes one by one is slow for a big box. Here's the shortcut: a box packed with cubes is made of equal **layers**. Count the cubes in **one layer**, then multiply by the **number of layers**. If the bottom is 3 cubes long and 2 cubes wide, each layer holds 3 × 2 = 6 cubes. Four such layers hold 6 × 4 = 24 cubes.

You can slice a box into layers from any direction and get the same count. That's why volume is just **length × width × height**. Take a box 2 cubes long, 2 wide, and 3 tall: one layer is 2 × 2 = 4 cubes, and 3 layers give 4 × 3 = 12. Multiplying all three edges — 2 × 2 × 3 — gives the same 12.

Last chapter's shortcut has a name. The cubes covering the bottom of a box form the **base layer**, and the number of cubes in it is the **area of the base** — a 4-by-3 base holds 4 × 3 = 12 cubes. Stack that layer once per unit of height: 5 layers hold 12 × 5 = 60 cubes.

You don't have to count the base cube by cube. If the **base area** is known — say 10 square units — then 10 cubes fit in each layer, and the volume is simply **base area × number of layers**. Area covers the floor; height repeats it upward.

The layer method fits in one line. The base layer holds **length × width** cubes, and there are **height** layers. So the volume of a box is **V = l × w × h** — multiply the three edge lengths. A box 6 long, 3 wide, and 2 tall: V = 6 × 3 × 2 = 36 cubic units.

Two useful facts. **Units:** if the edges are in centimeters, the volume is in **cm³** — a 4 cm × 2 cm × 3 cm box holds 24 cm³, the same as 24 one-centimeter cubes. **Order:** multiplying in any order gives the same result, so (4 × 2) × 3 and 4 × (2 × 3) both equal 24. Pick the easiest pairing.

Group the formula differently. In V = l × w × h, the first pair l × w is the **area of the base, B**. So the same formula reads **V = B × h**: base area times height. If a problem hands you B directly — "the base area is 15 square units" — skip straight to B × h. One formula, two groupings.

When B isn't given, compute it first. A base 6 units by 2 units has B = 6 × 2 = 12; with height 3, V = 12 × 3 = 36. Check the other grouping: 6 × 2 × 3 = 36 too. **Both routes always land on the same number** — choose whichever grouping the problem hands you.

Not every solid is a single box — but many are **boxes glued together**. Volume is **additive**: if a solid is made of two boxes that don't overlap, its volume is the first volume **plus** the second. Box A at 4 × 2 × 3 = 24 joined to box B at 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 makes a solid of 24 + 12 = 36 cubic units.

The one rule: the pieces must **not overlap**, so every unit cube is counted exactly once. Then combining is always **addition** — never multiplication. And order doesn't matter: A + B equals B + A, just like any sum.

An **L-shaped** solid isn't a box, so no single l × w × h fits it. The trick: **cut it into boxes yourself**. Our L: a bottom slab 5 units long, 2 wide, 2 tall, with a 2 × 2 × 2 block sitting on top of its left end. Cut along the block's base, find each box's volume, add.

Here's the satisfying part: **a different cut gives the same answer**. Slice the same L straight down at the block's edge instead. Now the pieces are a tall box 2 long, 2 wide, 4 tall, and a short box 3 long, 2 wide, 2 tall. Every cube still gets counted exactly once — so any legal split must agree.
Volume is a count: each unit cube fills one unit of space, so the number of cubes that pack a solid IS its volume.
This is the same idea as area, one dimension further on. Area counts equal squares covering a surface; volume counts equal cubes filling a space.
A prism is layers of the same base stacked up. Each layer is a complete copy, so the height MULTIPLIES rather than adds.
A base of 12 cubes, four layers tall, holds 48 cubes — not 16. That distinction is the whole of the volume formula.
V = l × w × h records the counting in order: l × w builds one layer, and h stacks it.
The formula is not a rule to memorise separately from the cubes — it IS the cube count, organised so you never have to draw them.
V = B × h says the same thing more generally: whatever shape the base is, find its area and stack it.
For a rectangular prism B is just l × w, so the two formulas agree. But B × h keeps working when the base is a triangle or an L-shape.
If the volume and the base are known, the height follows by division: how many base-layers fit inside the volume?
This is the formula run in reverse, and it is the same move as recovering a missing side from an area.
Composite solids are built from simple ones: find the full block, then subtract what has been cut away.
A notch is space removed, so every cube it takes lowers the count by one. The subtraction happens once, on the whole solid.
Volume word problems name the dimensions in words. Find the base, find the height, and the plan writes itself.
The commonest slip is stopping at the base area — a flat answer to a question about space.
Two solids can be compared without imagining either one: compute both volumes and the larger count wins.
Different shapes can hold identical volumes, which is exactly why the count settles the question and appearances do not.
A two-step problem hides a question inside itself. The story never states the middle quantity — you have to build it before the real question can be answered.
Find the hidden question first. It is always the one whose answer the final question needs but the story refuses to give you.
Add then multiply: when the story changes a group COUNT before the groups are counted up, the addition has to happen first.
One more van arrives, then every van is filled. The arrival changes how many groups there are, so it belongs inside the parentheses.
Multiply then subtract: build the whole from equal groups, then remove what the story takes away — once, from the total.
The classic error removes the loss from EVERY group. Read carefully: 3 chairs broke in total, not 3 at each table.
Divide then add: share the total into equal groups first, then add what joins afterward — and notice WHERE it joins.
If two apples go into each bag, the addition lands on one group's share. If two apples join the pile, it lands on the total instead.
When a quantity is unknown, give it a letter. The letter is not a mystery — it is a placeholder standing exactly where the number will go.
Writing 6 × n = 42 says 'six groups of something make forty-two'. Solving it just asks which number the letter is hiding.
Writing the equation makes the ORDER visible. Parentheses are not decoration — they say which step happens first.
(5 × 4) − 3 and 5 × (4 − 3) use the same three numbers and mean completely different stories. The brackets carry the meaning.
A bar model turns a story into a picture: equal parts for the groups, and a crossed-off piece for what leaves.
The picture makes the hidden question visible — you can see the total being built before anything is removed from it.
Estimating first gives you a neighbourhood for the answer. Round each number to something friendly, run the same two steps, and you know where you should land.
The estimate is not the answer — it is the guard. Anything far outside the neighbourhood is a mistake worth catching before you trust it.
Checking with rounding compares your exact answer to the neighbourhood. Close means plausible; wildly outside means something went wrong.
An estimate can never prove an answer exactly right — but it catches the big errors: a lost carry, a dropped zero, a step done backwards.
Some answers are impossible before you check any arithmetic: more apples than ever existed, or a leftover bigger than the total.
Ask what the story ALLOWS. If eight crates hold nine apples each, nothing that happens afterwards can push the count above seventy-two.
Stories often carry numbers the question never uses. Reading for the QUESTION, not for the numbers, is what keeps them out of your equation.
Three red bags are real, but if the question asks only about blue bags, the red ones never enter the arithmetic.
Writing your own two-step problem is the real test: you must invent a story whose hidden question is genuinely hidden and whose order actually matters.
Start from the equation. (5 × 6) + 4 needs equal groups first and a single addition after — and the story must make that order the only sensible reading.
